Prologue · P.1
The most fundamental question
What is money, really?

We all use money every day. But asked "what is money?" most people pause for a moment. The answers that come up are usually: the paper in your wallet, the number in your banking app, or the coins in your desk drawer. All of it is true. But all of it is also only the form, not the essence.

Money, at its core, is a social technology. Not a physical object, not a precious metal, not a digital number. Money is an agreement, a collective belief that something has value and can be exchanged.

A Rp 100.000 note has no value because of its paper. It has value because millions of people agree that it has value. If that agreement collapses, the money is nothing more than paper.

To understand why this agreement arises, we need to go far back to a time before money existed at all.

Imagine a small village. The farmer has rice. The fisherman has fish. The carpenter has chairs. They need one another, and the only way to get what they need is barter: trading goods for goods directly.

The problem is simple but fatal: what if the fisherman needs rice, but the farmer doesn’t need fish and instead needs a chair? The transaction can’t happen. Economists call this the coincidence of wants, a coincidence of needs that must meet in both directions at once. Barter only works in very small communities.

The solution is to find something everyone is willing to accept, not because they need that object directly, but because they know others will accept it too. This is the origin of money.

Throughout history, humans have used shells, salt, giant stones on the Yap Islands, animal furs, copper, silver, and gold. Not just because those objects are pretty or rare, but because the community agreed to trust them as a medium of exchange.

From this long experiment, economists formulated three main functions of good money:

Medium of exchange. Money must be usable to buy and sell. It removes the need for a coincidence of wants.

Store of value. Money must be storable and stay valuable into the future. Fresh fish can’t be good money because it rots.

Unit of account. Money must serve as a unit for measuring value. How much is a cow worth? Thirty sacks of rice, or one number everyone agrees on?

Gold lasted thousands of years as the best money that ever existed. Naturally scarce, durable, divisible, and hard to counterfeit. But gold has one big weakness: it is heavy and hard to move.

So humans created paper, proof of ownership of gold stored in a vault. More practical, easier to carry. And this is where the story begins to change. Because paper is far easier to print than gold is to mine.

Money isn’t about the object you hold. Money is about the trust that you and others agree on, and who holds control over that agreement.

This last question is the one we will chase throughout this Prologue, and the one that ultimately gave birth to Bitcoin.

Prologue · P.2
Money that changes quietly
A History of Money Manipulation

Have you ever asked your parents or grandparents how much a pack of instant noodles used to cost? Or how much they paid for gasoline the first time? The answer is sure to make you shake your head. Not because the noodles changed. Not because the gasoline changed. But because the money changed.

This is no coincidence. And this is not fate.

From gold to paper

For thousands of years, money had an anchor. That anchor was called gold. Every paper note in circulation had a gold equivalent stored in the government’s vault. This system was called the gold standard. It meant no one could carelessly print more money than the gold they held.

This kept money honest. Its value was stable. The government couldn’t do whatever it pleased.

But that anchor was cut.

August 15, 1971

U.S. President Richard Nixon stood before the television cameras and announced something that changed the world’s financial system forever. The United States would no longer tie the dollar to gold. This decision is known as the Nixon Shock.

The reasoning at the time sounded sensible: the economy was struggling, the Vietnam War was draining the budget, and America’s gold reserves were thinning as other countries began exchanging their dollars for real gold.

So Nixon cut the rope. The dollar was no longer guaranteed by gold. And because nearly every currency in the world was tied to the dollar at the time, that one decision changed the entire global financial system all at once.

From that day on, the money you hold is backed by nothing. Its value rests on one thing: the belief that the government will manage it responsibly.

When the printing press turns on

The problem is, that trust is often betrayed.

Without a gold anchor, governments and central banks gained a new ability: to print as much money as they want. And the temptation is enormous, especially in a crisis.

When the economy collapsed in 2008, big American banks nearly fell apart. The government’s response? Print money. Trillions of dollars were pumped into the financial system in a program called quantitative easing.

When the Covid-19 pandemic struck in 2020, the same thing happened again, on a far larger scale. America printed more than 40% of all the dollars that had ever existed in history, in just two years.

The result? Inflation exploded. Prices rose. The purchasing power of the money you keep in savings fell, without you doing anything, without anyone asking your permission.

Who is hurt the most?

Not the wealthy. The wealthy keep their wealth in the form of assets, stocks, property, gold, things whose value rises along with the money being printed.

The ones hurt the most are ordinary people. Those who keep their money in a savings account. Whose salaries don’t rise as fast as prices. Who work hard saving for years, only to watch the purchasing power of their savings slowly erode.

Inflation is a tax that is never collected in the open. There is no notice. There is no vote. It works quietly, every day, and is almost never questioned.

The question that begins to surface

If money can be printed at any time by whoever holds power, can it still be called honest? If the value of your savings can be eroded by decisions made without your knowledge, do you truly own that money?

These are the very questions that began to make some people think: there has to be another way.

Prologue · P.3
What does healthy money look like?
Austrian Economics & sound money

Have you ever felt like this: you’ve worked hard, you’ve been frugal, you’ve saved, yet somehow it never feels like enough? Prices keep rising, but your savings sit still. Something is wrong. But where is the fault?

Some economists have had an answer for more than a hundred years. They weren’t from Wall Street. Not from Washington. They were from Vienna, Austria.

What is Austrian Economics?

Austrian Economics, or the Vienna School, is a tradition of economic thought born in the late 19th century. Its figures include Carl Menger, Ludwig von Mises, and Friedrich Hayek. The last even won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1974.

But set those names aside for now. What matters is one core idea they fought for: good money is honest money.

Honest in the sense that its value can’t be manipulated at the whim of those in power. Its quantity can’t be increased arbitrarily. It reflects real hard work, not numbers printed on paper.

Cantillon Effect: who wins, who loses

When new money is printed, it doesn’t spread evenly to everyone at once. It flows from the top down. The central bank receives it first, then the big banks, then business owners, and only then does it reach workers and retirees.

The problem is, prices have already risen before the money reaches the bottom. So whoever gets the money first can buy at the old prices. Whoever gets it last is already too late.

Economists call this the Cantillon Effect, named after the economist Richard Cantillon who first described it in the 18th century. Try simulating it yourself below.

Sound money: healthy money

The opposite of money that can be manipulated is what’s called sound money, healthy money. Its criteria are simple:

Scarce. Its quantity is limited and can’t be increased arbitrarily. Gold is the classic example, because to obtain new gold someone has to mine it, requiring real time, effort, and cost.

Durable. Its value doesn’t rot, doesn’t decay, and can be stored over the long term.

Cannot be manipulated. No single party can change the rules of the game midway.

Sound money isn’t about gold or precious metals. It is about a principle: money should function as an honest store of value, not a tool the powerful can use to quietly transfer wealth.

Why does this matter for Bitcoin?

Satoshi Nakamoto, the creator of Bitcoin, did not appear out of a vacuum. He emerged from a tradition of thought that had long questioned the existing monetary system.

Bitcoin was designed with sound money principles as its foundation. The amount of Bitcoin is capped at just 21 million coins, forever. There is no Bitcoin central bank. No one can print more because they feel the need.

For the first time in history, humans have a choice: digital money that is scarce, open, and cannot be manipulated by anyone.

Prologue · P.4
The biggest problem of digital money
The Double-Spend Problem

Imagine you have a photo file. You can send it to one person, then send it again to another, then to a thousand people at once. The original file remains. Everyone gets a copy.

Now imagine digital money worked the same way. You have Rp 100.000 in the form of a digital file. You send it to Store A. Then you send the same file to Store B. The same money, used twice. This is what’s called the double-spend problem.

In the physical world, this problem doesn’t exist. If you hand a Rp 100.000 note to someone, you no longer have that money. The transfer is real and can’t be repeated. But in the digital world, everything is a copy. There is no such thing as an original.

The old solution: trust the bank

The solution all along has been to place a third party in the middle. The bank makes sure the money is actually deducted from your balance before it reaches the recipient. No one can double-spend because the bank controls the records.

But this comes at a price: you have to trust that the bank is honest, won’t go bankrupt, and won’t freeze your account. History proves that hope is not always met.

Attempts before Bitcoin

DigiCash, b-money, Bit Gold, all tried to build digital money without a bank. All failed at the same point: how to ensure no one spends the same money twice, without trusting anyone in the middle?

What was needed was a ledger open to all, owned by no one, and impossible to manipulate. That is what Satoshi created in 2008. Its name: blockchain.

Bitcoin solves the double-spend problem without a bank, without a third party. It makes digital money behave like cash: when you send it, it truly moves. You no longer have it.

Prologue · P.5
Ownership without identity
The Public-Key Cryptography Revolution

Cash solves double-spend physically. But it cannot prove ownership in the digital world. If you have cash and someone steals it, there is no mathematical way to prove that money is yours.

Bitcoin solves both at once. Resistant to double-spend like cash, while also able to prove ownership digitally. The secret lies in an invention from the 1970s that changed the world: public-key cryptography.

Two keys, one identity

Imagine you have a padlock and a key. You can hand out the padlock to anyone. Anyone can use it to lock a message for you. But only you have the key. Only you can open it.

That is how public-key cryptography works. The public key is your padlock, free to share with anyone. In Bitcoin, this is like your account address. The private key is your key, which no one may know. It proves that you are the rightful owner of that public key.

When you send Bitcoin, you sign the transaction with your private key. The network can verify that signature using your public key, without needing to know who you really are.

For the first time, someone could prove ownership of something digitally, without giving a name, without an ID card, without a bank to verify it. Mathematics proves it. Not an institution.

The entire Bitcoin system stands on this principle. Your private key is your identity. Whoever holds the private key holds the Bitcoin. Not a name in a ledger, not an ID card, not a signature on paper.

Prologue · P.6
Resistance written in code
The Cypherpunk Movement

Some realized it earlier.

Not by taking to the streets. Not with speeches. They sat in front of their screens, writing code, slowly building something that couldn’t be censored, couldn’t be stopped, and needed no one’s permission to run.

They called themselves Cypherpunks.

The internet was built too wide open

When the internet was born in the ARPANET era in 1969, it was designed to connect academic and military institutions that trusted one another. No one thought about privacy, because all of its users really were a small community who knew each other.

But the internet grew. The public came in. And its foundation did not change with it.

Data moves in the open, unencrypted. Anyone on the path of your connection can read what you send, exactly like reading a postcard rather than a letter in a sealed envelope. Governments can monitor. Corporations can collect. No one needs permission to peek.

The internet isn’t broken. It was simply never designed to protect you.

Where did they come from?

The year 1992. Three people met in San Francisco: Eric Hughes, Timothy C. May, and John Gilmore. They began gathering like-minded people into a mailing list. At its peak, more than 700 people were active in it, including several names who would later reshape the world’s technology landscape.

They were mathematicians, programmers, and cryptographers. Not street activists. But they held a sharp conviction: privacy is a right, not a privilege granted by the state.

The Cypherpunk Manifesto

In 1993, Eric Hughes wrote a manifesto. Calm, but firm to the bone:

"Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age."

Privacy is not about hiding something. It is about the ability to choose, what you reveal, to whom, and when. And their solution was not to ask. Their solution was to build.

An invisible legacy

Many of the technologies you use every day grew from seeds planted by this movement. The HTTPS that secures your browsing. End-to-end encryption in chat apps. Networks that make communication without surveillance possible.

And the most impactful of all: on October 31, 2008, someone under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto sent a paper to a cryptography mailing list. Its title was simple. Its impact was not.

"Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System."

Satoshi did not appear out of a vacuum. He was the end of a long thread woven over decades by people who didn’t wait for the world to change, but chose to change it themselves, one line of code at a time.

Cypherpunks write code. Not petitions. Not lobbying. They believed real change doesn’t come from permission granted by those in power, but from technology that is already up and running.

Bitcoin was not the first attempt

If cypherpunks really do write code, it is fair to ask: what code did they write before Bitcoin? In the Double-Spend Problem section we mentioned DigiCash, b-money, and bit gold in a single line as attempts that failed. Now we stop there for longer, because what is interesting is not that they failed but how close they had already come.

The earliest attempt came from David Chaum, who founded DigiCash in 1989. His money was genuinely private, using cryptography that stopped the bank from seeing who spent what. Technically it worked. But DigiCash was still a company, and its money was still issued by a single party. When the company went bankrupt in 1998, the money went with it. The lesson was harsh: privacy alone is not enough while a single point of failure remains.

In 1997 Adam Back built Hashcash, which we return to in 5.2. The idea was simple: before sending an email, your computer had to complete a small piece of work that took a little time. For an ordinary person that is imperceptible; for someone sending millions of spam messages it becomes expensive. For the first time there was a way to make something in the digital world genuinely costly. But Hashcash proofs could not be handed on. Each was spent once, could not be given to anyone else, and there was no total supply. It was a postage stamp, not money.

A year later, in 1998, two proposals arrived almost together. Wei Dai wrote b-money, which proposed that every participant keep a copy of the record of who owns what, with new money born from computational work. Nick Szabo wrote bit gold, which chained the results of that work together so their order could be proven.

Read those two sentences again and something strange emerges: both sound almost exactly like Bitcoin. A record everyone keeps, money born from work, a chain that proves the order. It was all on paper a decade before Satoshi.

So what was missing? One thing, and it was the hardest. If everyone keeps their own record, what happens when those records disagree? Who gets to decide which version is true? Both b-money and bit gold saw the problem and offered answers, but every answer ended at some set of chosen parties who had to be trusted. Precisely the problem they had set out to escape. It is the same double-spend problem from the earlier section, seen from another angle.

What Satoshi actually added

Here is the leap, and it is both smaller and larger than people usually imagine. Satoshi did not invent proof of work, did not invent digital signatures, did not invent hash chains. All of it already existed.

What he did was realise that proof of work could carry two jobs at once. His predecessors used it only to make something expensive to produce. Satoshi also used it to decide whose record counts: the version with the most accumulated work behind it wins. There is no need to choose who has authority, because authority is replaced by something that cannot be faked, namely energy that has already been burned.

That is why the question "why 2009, when the ingredients existed in 1998" has an answer that is both disappointing and reassuring. What was missing for those ten years was not a component, not a new mathematical discovery, and not a faster computer. What was missing was a way of looking at components that were already lying in plain sight.

This history also explains something you will meet again and again in this book. Bitcoin rarely adds anything new. It almost always rearranges what already exists, very carefully, because every part added is a part that can fail.

Prologue · P.7
The day it all began
The Genesis Block & Satoshi’s Message

January 3, 2009.

The world had just emerged from one of the worst financial crises in modern history. Giant banks in America and Europe nearly collapsed. Governments poured trillions of dollars of taxpayer money to rescue the very institutions that caused the crisis itself.

Somewhere unknown to anyone, someone switched on a network.

The first block

In the Bitcoin system, all transactions are recorded in units called blocks. Each block links to the previous block, forming a chain that cannot be manipulated. This chain is called the blockchain.

The first block that ever existed is called the Genesis Block. Block #0. The beginning of everything. And inside it, Satoshi left a message written forever:

"The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks"

This is the front-page headline of The Times newspaper on that day. The day Bitcoin was born.

Why that message matters

The message is no coincidence. Not merely a timestamp. On one hand, it serves as proof that the Genesis Block was truly created on that date. On the other, it is a statement. A calm but sharp critique of the financial system being rescued by the people’s money on that very same day.

Who is Satoshi?

No one knows. Satoshi Nakamoto communicated through email and forums for two years after Bitcoin was born. Then, in April 2011, he sent his final message to a developer: "I’ve moved on to other things." And vanished.

His identity was never confirmed. All that remains is his code. His whitepaper. And the Genesis Block that still stands to this day, with the same message, unchanged, impossible to change.

Bitcoin is the only financial system in the world whose creator chose to disappear. No CEO. No founder holding control. No one to contact to change its rules. This is not a weakness. It is the most important feature of all.

Prologue · P.8
Closing the Prologue
A Trustless System

The entire financial system that exists today stands on trust.

You trust that your bank won’t go bankrupt. You trust that the government won’t freeze your account. You trust that the transfer company won’t withhold your money. That trust has no guarantee; it depends only on the good intentions of the institutions in control.

History proves that good intentions are not always enough.

Trustless doesn’t mean there is no trust

The word trustless is often misunderstood. It does not mean you don’t need to trust anyone at all. It means you don’t need to trust any particular person or institution, because what you trust is mathematics and code that anyone can verify.

In Bitcoin, there is no director who can change the rules. No board meeting decides monetary policy. No headquarters can be lobbied or pressured. Its rules are written in code, open to all, and apply equally to everyone in the world.

Decentralized trust

If you send Bitcoin to someone, that transaction is verified not by one bank, but by thousands of computers around the world at the same time. None of them holds more authority than the rest. To manipulate the system, someone would have to control more than half of the entire network at once, a task that is practically impossible.

This is what makes Bitcoin different from every financial system before it. Not because it is digital. Not because it is new. But because, for the first time, trust no longer depends on human subjectivity that can be wrong, can be bribed, and can change its mind.

Bitcoin doesn’t ask you to trust Satoshi. It doesn’t ask you to trust its developers. It doesn’t ask you to trust anyone. It only asks you to verify for yourself. And that is what makes everything different.

Chapter 1 · 1.1
Setting straight a common misconception
What is Bitcoin, really?

Ask ten people about Bitcoin and you’ll get ten different answers.

Some say Bitcoin is an investment. Some say speculation. Some say a scam. Some say the future. All of those answers talk about price, not about what Bitcoin really is.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, but it is not part of the "crypto" industry.

This is important to understand from the start. Bitcoin is technically a cryptocurrency because it uses cryptography as the foundation of its technology. But the term "crypto" you hear every day is something different.

"Crypto" is a label born from where a thing is traded, not from how it works. Exchanges and financial media group Bitcoin with thousands of other tokens because they all change hands on the same venues, sit in similar wallets, and get reported in the same news column. As a commercial grouping, that makes sense and there is nothing wrong with it.

The trouble starts when that commercial grouping is read as a technical statement. Because technically, the contents of that basket differ enormously from one another. Some tokens have a CEO. Some have a whitepaper that can be rewritten at any time. Some were built to be sold to the public rather than to solve a real problem. Putting them all under one word makes the differences that matter most invisible.

Bitcoin has no CEO. No marketing team. No early investors waiting to exit. No rules that anyone can change unilaterally.

Bitcoin is a protocol. Just as HTTP is a protocol for the web, or TCP/IP is a protocol for the internet. A protocol is owned by no one, can be shut down by no one, and needs no one’s permission to be used.

That Bitcoin uses cryptography in how it works makes it technically fit the definition of a cryptocurrency. But calling it part of the "crypto" industry is like calling email part of the spam industry just because both use the same protocol.

Bitcoin is three things at once

A network. Bitcoin is a network of computers spread around the world, running without a central server, without a head office, and without anyone who can shut it down. Anyone can join, anyone can leave. The network keeps running as long as even a single node is alive.

A protocol. Bitcoin is a set of rules agreed upon by all network participants. Rules about how transactions are created, verified, and recorded. Rules about how much Bitcoin can ever exist. Rules that cannot be changed unilaterally by any single party.

A currency. Bitcoin is a unit of value that can be sent from one person to another, anywhere in the world, without an intermediary, without permission, and without operating hours.

If the internet is a protocol for moving information, Bitcoin is a protocol for moving value. Both are open, both are owned by no one, and both change how the world works. And like the internet, Bitcoin doesn’t care who misunderstands it. It just keeps running.

Chapter 1 · 1.2
From click to confirmation
How Do Transactions Happen?

Imagine you want to send money to a friend who lives in another city.

The usual way: you open your banking app, type the account number, type the amount, click send. Behind the scenes, your bank contacts your friend’s bank, both update their respective records, and after a process involving several intermediary institutions, the money "arrives" in anywhere from minutes to days. You don’t know exactly what happens in between. You simply trust that the system works.

In Bitcoin, there is no one in the middle.

What actually happens

When you send Bitcoin, you create a digital message containing three things: how much you’re sending, to which address, and a digital signature from your private key as proof that you are the rightful owner of that Bitcoin.

This message is broadcast to the entire Bitcoin network. Thousands of nodes around the world receive it, verify it, and pass it on to other nodes. Within seconds, your transaction is known to the whole network.

But it’s not done yet.

Getting into a block

Your transaction then waits to be included in a block by miners. Miners are computers competing to solve a very hard mathematical puzzle. The first to succeed earns the right to write the next block, and also receives a reward in the form of new Bitcoin.

Once your transaction is included in a block, it is recorded permanently on the blockchain. It can’t be deleted, can’t be changed, can’t be reversed.

How long does it take?

A Bitcoin block appears on average every 10 minutes. For a transaction considered final and safe, people generally wait for 6 confirmations, meaning 6 consecutive blocks after the block containing your transaction. About one hour.

Compared to a cross-border bank transfer that can take 3 to 5 business days, one hour is a significant improvement. And no one can block, delay, or cancel it along the way.

In Bitcoin, there is no one you need to contact if something goes wrong with your transaction. No customer service. No "cancel" button. A confirmed transaction is a finished transaction, forever.

Chapter 1 · 1.3
No boss, no central server
Who Runs the Network?

No one runs it. And that is exactly what makes it run.

This sounds like a paradox. Every system we know has someone behind it. Servers have administrators. Banks have boards of directors. Apps have developers who can update or shut them down at any time. But Bitcoin has none of that.

What runs Bitcoin is the network itself, made up of three kinds of participants:

Node

A node is a computer that stores a complete copy of the entire Bitcoin blockchain and verifies every incoming transaction. Anyone can run a node, with relatively affordable hardware. Nodes are not paid. They run because they want to participate in the network and verify for themselves that Bitcoin’s rules are being followed correctly.

Nodes are the guardians of the rules. If a transaction is invalid, the node rejects it. If a miner tries to cheat, the node rejects its block. There is no central authority to contact.

Miner

A miner is a computer competing to solve a mathematical puzzle to earn the right to write the next block. They invest real hardware and electricity. In return, the miner who succeeds receives new Bitcoin, called the block reward, plus the transaction fees from the transactions they include in the block.

Mining is the process that makes the blockchain secure. To forge a single old transaction, someone would have to redo the entire proof of work from that block until now, faster than the whole network that is currently running. Practically impossible.

Users

Users are anyone who holds or sends Bitcoin. They don’t need to run a node or a miner. Just having a wallet and a Bitcoin address is enough.

Why can’t it be shut down?

Because there is no single point that, if removed, would make everything stop. Nodes are spread across hundreds of countries. Miners operate in various jurisdictions. There’s no central server to attack, no CEO to arrest, no office to shut down.

Bitcoin runs because thousands of people around the world choose to run it, not because some single entity forces it to run. And as long as even one node is still alive somewhere on this earth, Bitcoin still exists.

Chapter 1 · 1.4
A ledger that cannot be manipulated
What is a Blockchain?

Before getting into how it works, there’s one thing we need to clear up first.

The word "blockchain" has suffered the same fate as the word "crypto". The industry took it, used it to sell everything, and its meaning grew blurry. "Blockchain for supply chains." "Blockchain for voting." "Blockchain for healthcare." Almost none of those need a blockchain at all, and could be solved more efficiently with an ordinary database.

So before learning how it works, it’s important to know: not everything called a blockchain is a blockchain.

Bitcoin’s blockchain vs the industry’s "blockchain"

Bitcoin’s blockchain is a genuinely decentralized system. No one controls who may write or read. There’s no admin who can change the rules. There’s no company behind it. There’s no off button. Its security comes from proof of work and the consensus of thousands of independent nodes around the world.

Most of the "blockchains" sold by the crypto industry are centralized databases with a blockchain look. There’s a company that controls them. There’s a team that can change their rules at any time. There are servers that can be shut down. This isn’t a blockchain in the sense Satoshi meant. This is marketing.

Not everything called a blockchain is necessarily a blockchain. But Bitcoin’s blockchain is the real thing.

What is a block?

Imagine a large ledger of transaction records. Each page contains a list of transactions that occurred in one period of time. Each new page refers back to the previous page, forming a chain that can’t be broken. That’s a blockchain. But no one owns it, and everyone can see it.

Each block contains three main things:

Transaction data. A list of all the transactions that occurred in that period. Who sent how much to whom.

This block’s hash. A kind of digital fingerprint of the entire block’s contents. If even one character changes, the hash changes completely.

The previous block’s hash. This is what forms the chain. Each block is bound to the previous block through its hash.

Why can’t it be manipulated?

Imagine someone wants to forge a transaction in block #500. They have to change that block's contents. But the moment its contents change, the hash of block #500 changes. That means block #501, which stores the hash of #500, is now invalid. Block #502 is invalid too. And so on, up to the latest block.

To forge a single old transaction, someone would have to recompute the entire chain from that block until now, faster than the whole network that is adding a new block every 10 minutes. Practically impossible.

Who stores it?

Everyone who runs a Bitcoin node stores a complete copy of the entire blockchain. Not on one server, but on thousands of computers around the world. There’s no single point that can be attacked to delete or change the record.

A blockchain isn’t magic technology. It’s a simple combination of cryptography, consensus, and economic incentives working together to create something that never existed before: an honest record, with no guardian who needs to be trusted.

Chapter 1 · 1.5
Scarcity that cannot be faked
Why 21 Million?

When Satoshi designed Bitcoin, he made one unusual decision: the amount of Bitcoin that will ever exist in this world is capped. Exactly 21 million. No more, no less, forever.

Not a policy that can be changed in a meeting. Not a regulation that can be amended. It is written directly into the code, and changing it would require the agreement of the entire network, something that is practically impossible.

Why 21 million?

There is no definitive mathematical answer for this number. Satoshi never explained it specifically. What’s clear is the principle behind it: Bitcoin must be scarce. Scarcity that can be verified, not scarcity that is merely promised.

This is fundamentally different from fiat money. No one knows how many dollars, rupiah, or euros will be in circulation tomorrow. The figure can change anytime a political or economic decision calls for it. Bitcoin can’t.

How is new Bitcoin born?

New Bitcoin isn’t printed by a central bank. It is born through the mining process. Each time a miner successfully finds a new block, they receive an amount of Bitcoin as a reward. This is the only way new Bitcoin enters circulation.

But this reward isn’t fixed forever.

Halving

Every 210,000 blocks, roughly every four years, the mining reward is cut in half. This process is called the halving.

When Bitcoin was first born in 2009, the reward per block was 50 BTC. After the first halving in 2012, it became 25 BTC. Then 12.5 BTC. Then 6.25 BTC. And so on, halved again and again, until around the year 2140 when the reward approaches zero and all 21 million Bitcoin are in circulation.

This mechanism is what ensures Bitcoin’s supply can’t be manipulated. No one can speed up this schedule. No one can change its rules midway.

Gold is scarce because it’s hard to mine. Bitcoin is scarce because its mathematics doesn’t allow more than 21 million. One depends on nature, one depends on code. Neither can be faked.

Chapter 1 · 1.6
Money that cannot be deceived
Bitcoin vs Ordinary Money

Good money should be impossible to deceive.

It can’t be printed in secret. It can’t be frozen arbitrarily. It can’t be censored for political reasons. Its value can’t be diluted by the decisions of a handful of people in a closed room.

For thousands of years, humans searched for a form of money that met all of that. Gold came close, but it could be seized. Paper money is practical, but it can be printed. Digital money is more efficient, but it’s controlled by institutions.

Bitcoin is the first experiment that successfully answered all of that at once. Not because it generates profit. Not because its price goes up. But because, for the first time in history, there is a form of money whose rules can’t be manipulated by anyone.

That is what is meant by honest money.

Chapter 2 · 2.1
Not a place that stores Bitcoin
What is a Wallet?

The name is misleading.

A wallet in Bitcoin doesn’t store Bitcoin. This is the first thing to clear up. Bitcoin isn’t inside the app on your phone. It isn’t stored on your device. It’s on the blockchain, and the blockchain lives on thousands of computers around the world.

What a wallet stores is something far more important: keys.

Imagine Bitcoin as a safe locked in a public place that everyone can see. Everyone knows how much is inside. But only the person with the key can open it and move what’s inside. The wallet is where you keep that key.

Not an account, not a balance

A bank account stores your records on the bank’s servers. The bank knows who you are, how much your balance is, and can change or freeze it at any time.

A Bitcoin wallet isn’t like that. There’s no name, no identity, no institution holding your data. All there is is a pair of mathematical keys that prove you are the rightful owner of the Bitcoin at a particular address.

What is actually inside a wallet?

It all begins with a single number, and everything else descends from it in a chain:

Private key. A very large random number, generated once and impossible for anyone to guess. This is the proof of ownership. Anyone who knows your private key can move your Bitcoin. Anyone.

Public key. Derived mathematically from the private key. It isn’t a secret, but it isn’t what you hand to other people either. Its job is to prove to the network that your transaction really came from you.

Address. Derived once more from the public key, shorter and more resistant to typos. This is what you share when you want to receive Bitcoin. Like an account number, but with no identity of yours behind it.

A wallet isn’t a place to store Bitcoin. A wallet is a place to store the keys that prove you own Bitcoin. If you lose the keys, your Bitcoin isn’t lost from the blockchain, but no one can ever access it again, forever.

Chapter 2 · 2.2
A number no one can guess
Private and Public Keys

Behind every Bitcoin wallet, there is a number.

Not an ordinary number. This is a very large random number, 256 bits, or about 78 decimal digits. This number isn’t created by a human, isn’t chosen by a server, and isn’t registered with anyone. It is born from pure randomness on your own device, at the moment the wallet is created.

This is your private key.

How random?

The number of possible private keys is 2²⁵⁶, or roughly 1.2 × 10⁷⁷. For comparison: the number of atoms in the entire observable universe is estimated at around 10⁸⁰. The private key space isn’t quite that large, but it sits in the same class of numbers, and that is already far beyond anything a computer could ever sweep through, now or later. The chance of two people accidentally producing the same private key is, practically, zero. This isn’t a promise. This is mathematics.

From the private key, a public key is born

A private key is never shared with anyone. But from a private key, a public key can be derived through a one-way mathematical process.

One-way means: going from the private key to the public key takes a fraction of a second. Going the other direction has no shortcut known to anyone. Not because information is lost along the way, since the public key is entirely determined by your private key and nothing gets dropped. But because reversing it demands an amount of computational work that, with the best methods we have today, would not finish within the lifetime of the universe.

Easy to compute forward, impossible to trace back. The whole security of Bitcoin rests on this imbalance.

So what is the public key actually for?

So far we only know that the public key is safe to share. But why does it need to exist at all?

To answer that, there is a third object we haven’t named yet: the digital signature.

When you send Bitcoin, your wallet doesn’t send your private key anywhere. What it does is take two ingredients, your private key and the contents of the transaction (how much, and to which address), and work them into a single new number. That number is the signature.

Two properties of that signature are what make the whole system work.

It is bound to one transaction. Because it is born from the contents of that transaction, it is only valid for that transaction. Change the amount slightly, swap the destination address, and the same signature no longer matches. It cannot be cut from one transaction and pasted onto another.

It can be checked without the private key. This is the most important part. Anyone holding your public key can confirm that the signature was made by whoever holds the matching private key, without ever learning that private key. Checking does not require the same secret as creating.

This is where the division of labour becomes clear. The private key creates signatures, and only it can. The public key checks signatures, and anyone can. One to prove, one to verify.

And that is the real reason the public key is safe to share. Not merely because it doesn’t leak your private key, but because what it hands to other people is only the ability to check, never the ability to create.

Exactly how that number is computed, and why checking is so much cheaper than forging, is what we take apart in Chapter 4 when we get to ECDSA and Schnorr.

Why does this matter?

Because the entire system of Bitcoin ownership rests on this principle. No username. No password. No email verification. Your ownership is proven solely by your ability to produce a valid signature using the private key, and the network can verify it using the public key without needing to know who you are.

A private key is your identity in Bitcoin. Whoever holds it, holds your Bitcoin. There’s no "forgot password," no "reset via email," no customer service that can help you. It is an absolute responsibility.

Chapter 2 · 2.3
One key, many faces
From Key to Address

A private key produces a public key. But a public key can’t be used directly as an address to receive Bitcoin. There’s one more step.

The public key is processed through a series of hash functions, producing a shorter, more readable string. This is the Bitcoin address. This address is what you share with others when you want to receive Bitcoin. Not the private key, not the public key, but an address derived from both.

Why not use the public key directly?

Two main reasons. First, security. By hiding the public key behind a hash, there’s an extra layer of protection in case some computational advance one day becomes a threat. One important caveat: this protection only holds as long as you have never spent from that address. The moment you send funds from it, your public key is revealed on the blockchain. This is the real reason behind the advice you often hear about not reusing a single address, and we go further into it in 10.5. Second, practicality. A public key is a long string that’s hard for humans to read. An address is far shorter and has a checksum mechanism that detects typos.

Different address formats

If you’ve ever seen a Bitcoin address, you may have noticed some start with the number 1, some with 3, and some with bc1. Each represents a different generation of technology with different capabilities and efficiencies. The technical details behind each format we’ll cover in Chapter 6.

A single private key can produce many different addresses depending on the format used. But all of those addresses still belong to the same private key. This is why modern wallets can show several addresses at once without making you lose control.

How does a wallet know which addresses are its own?

That last sentence leaves one question open. If a single key can produce many addresses across several formats, how does a wallet know exactly which ones to watch? The old answer was a mess: every wallet had its own conventions, and moving a backup from one application to another often ended with a balance that appeared to have vanished when it had merely gone undetected.

The modern answer is the output descriptor, a single line of text that states the rule in full. It looks roughly like this:

wpkh([d34db33f/84h/0h/0h]xpub6.../0/*)

Read piece by piece, it makes sense. wpkh gives the format, P2WPKH or bc1q, which we cover in 6.4. The part in square brackets is its origin, marking which device and which derivation path it came from. xpub6... is the parent public key from which all the children descend. And /0/* means "every address on the receiving branch", with the star standing in for an unbounded sequence number.

That one line holds everything needed to find all of your funds again, and contains no secret at all. It uses an xpub, not an xprv, so it can scan but cannot spend. You can store it alongside your seed phrase, and the two complement each other: the seed phrase grants the ability to sign, the descriptor says where to look.

Descriptors can also express rules more elaborate than a single key, including the multisig we cover in 6.5. That is where they meet the Miniscript from 6.2: a descriptor becomes a way of writing spending conditions that humans can read and software can understand at the same time. Which is why, if you use any scheme involving more than one key, keeping the descriptor is no longer a nice extra but part of the backup itself. Without it, a seed phrase alone may not be enough to rebuild a multisig wallet.

Chapter 2 · 2.4
Words that hold everything
Seed Phrase

The private key is everything in Bitcoin. But there’s one practical problem: a private key is a 64-character hex string that’s impossible for a human to memorize.

No one can remember that. And if it’s lost, your Bitcoin is lost forever.

The solution is the seed phrase, also called a mnemonic phrase or recovery phrase. The order is actually the reverse of what most people picture. The wallet does not turn a private key into words. What happens is this: the wallet generates the initial randomness, writes it out as a series of ordinary words, and it is from those words that every one of your private keys is then derived. The seed phrase comes first, the private keys follow.

How does it work?

A seed phrase usually consists of 12 or 24 words chosen from a standard list of 2048 words called the BIP-39 wordlist. These words aren’t random in just any way. They’re chosen because they’re easy to tell apart, avoiding words that look or sound similar.

With 2048 words and 12 positions, the number of possible word combinations is 2048¹². But not all of those combinations are valid: the final word carries a checksum, so a 12-word phrase actually represents 128 bits of entropy, and a 24-word phrase represents 256 bits. That last figure is exactly the size of the private key space we worked out in 2.2, roughly 1.2 × 10⁷⁷ possibilities. The chance of two people accidentally producing the same seed phrase is, practically, zero. Twelve unremarkable-sounding words carry exactly the same weight as the 256-bit number from the previous chapter.

From this seed phrase, the wallet can regenerate the entire hierarchy of keys. Not just one private key, but hundreds or even thousands of addresses at once. This is what’s called an HD wallet, or Hierarchical Deterministic wallet.

One seed phrase, one wallet

A seed phrase is a complete representation of your entire wallet. Anyone who has your seed phrase has access to all the Bitcoin in that wallet, across all addresses, all formats, all networks.

This means two important things. First, backing up the seed phrase is backing up the entire wallet. There’s no need to back up each private key one by one. Second, the seed phrase must be stored offline, in a safe place, never photographed, never typed on an internet-connected computer, and never given to anyone for any reason.

No legitimate wallet company will ever ask for your seed phrase. No support needs your seed phrase. No form requires you to fill in your seed phrase. If someone asks for it, it’s a scam. Always.

The problem we have not solved yet

The standard advice about seed phrases sounds simple: write it on paper, keep it somewhere safe. But think it through and you will find the advice pulls in two directions at once. The more copies you make, the smaller the risk of losing it, but the greater the chance one of them is found. The fewer and better hidden the copies, the safer from thieves, but the easier to lose to fire, flood, or simply forgetting where you put it.

No number of copies solves both. As long as a single sheet holds the entire secret, all you can do is choose which risk frightens you more.

Splitting the secret into pieces

There is a way out of that tug of war, and it is called Shamir Secret Sharing. The secret is split into several pieces, say five, with any three of them enough to rebuild it. What makes it interesting is not the splitting but its mathematical property: one or two pieces reveal nothing at all. Not part of it, not a narrowed set of guesses, genuinely nothing. Until the third piece joins them, their contents are as useless as random numbers.

That means you can scatter five pieces across five places. Two may be lost without you losing anything, and two may be found without the finder gaining anything. The tug of war is over.

But there is a weakness that gets mentioned far less often. To use it, the pieces have to be brought back together on one device, and for those seconds your whole seed phrase exists intact in one place again. If that device is compromised, all of the earlier care counts for nothing. The multisig we cover in 6.5 does not have this problem, because the keys are never combined: each one signs separately on its own device. That is why many people consider multisig safer for large amounts, and Shamir better suited to backups that are rarely touched.

And if you die?

This is a question Bitcoin books rarely address, even though it is the one that happens most. The very property that makes Bitcoin truly yours, that nobody can take it without your key, applies to your family too. There is no bank to call, no death certificate to present, no legal process that can compel the network to hand over anything. If the knowledge dies with you, so do the coins.

What is surprising is that the hardest obstacle is usually not technical. Your heirs need to know three things, and only the third is about technology: that the Bitcoin exists, where the pieces are kept, and how to use them. Many losses happen not because the cryptography was hard, but because the family never knew there was anything to look for.

The approaches vary. Some entrust individual Shamir pieces to a lawyer or to different family members. Some use a multisig where one key is held by a third party who only co-signs once a death is proven. Others use timelocks, so that a transaction to the heirs becomes valid automatically after a period passes without being refreshed. That last approach is covered in Chapter 15.

One warning is worth closing on honestly: complexity is itself a risk. Overly elaborate inheritance schemes have lost more Bitcoin than simple ones, because the owner forgot how their own plan worked, or the heirs gave up partway through. A plan genuinely understood by the people who will have to carry it out is worth far more than a sophisticated one on paper.

Chapter 2 · 2.5
Where is your private key stored?
Types of Wallets

A wallet is a place to store keys. But not all wallets are created equal. Some are more convenient, some are more secure, some are both with certain trade-offs.

The main difference between wallet types isn’t in their appearance, but in one question: where is the private key stored?

Hot Wallet

A hot wallet is a wallet connected to the internet. The app on your phone, a browser extension, an online desktop app, all fall into this category.

Its advantages are easy access, fast for everyday transactions, and usually free. Its drawback is that because it’s connected to the internet, it’s more vulnerable to attack. Malware, phishing, or a security flaw in the app could expose your private key.

A hot wallet is suited for small amounts used often, like the wallet in your pocket. You don’t keep all your savings in a physical wallet you carry everywhere.

Cold Wallet

A cold wallet is a wallet that is never connected to the internet. The private key is generated and stored on a fully offline device.

The most common type is the hardware wallet, a dedicated physical device like a USB stick that stores the private key inside an isolated chip. To sign a transaction, you connect this device to a computer, but the private key never leaves the device.

The simplest is the paper wallet, where the private key and seed phrase are printed or written on paper and kept in a safe place. Nothing can hack it digitally because it isn’t digital.

But paper wallets have long stopped being recommended, and the reason matters before you make one. To spend the funds, you have to load that private key onto an internet-connected device, and at that moment the entire offline advantage disappears. They also don’t support the address hierarchy that modern seed phrases do, so one sheet of paper serves only one address. If your goal is long-term storage, a handwritten seed phrase kept offline gives you the same security without any of those drawbacks.

A cold wallet is suited for storing large amounts long-term, like a safe at home.

A practical rule

There’s nothing wrong with using both. Many Bitcoin users keep a small portion in a hot wallet for daily transactions, and keep most in a cold wallet for the long term.

Bitcoin security isn’t about the most sophisticated platform or app. It’s about how well you keep your private key out of others’ reach and away from internet connections.

Fully disconnected: air-gapped signing

An ordinary hardware wallet still plugs into a computer over USB when it signs. The private key does not leave the device, but there is still a data path between your secret hardware and a machine that may be infected. For some people that path is already one too many.

Air-gapped signing removes it entirely. The signing device never touches the computer, not over USB, not over Bluetooth, not over anything. The only thing that crosses between them is an image: a QR code shown on one screen and photographed by the other device’s camera.

The flow rests on the PSBT we cover in 3.6. Your computer assembles an unsigned transaction and displays it as a QR code. The air-gapped device scans it, shows the contents on its own screen so you can check the amount and destination, then signs it. The result is displayed as a new QR code, scanned back by the computer, and only then broadcast to the network.

Notice that what travels back and forth is only the transaction, never the key. And because the path is an image, malware on the computer has no channel through which to reach the signing device at all. Some devices are sold with no data port whatsoever, only a camera, a screen, and a microSD slot.

There is one step that must never be skipped, and it is where the real strength lies. The signing device shows the amount and destination on its own screen before you approve. Check it there, not on the computer screen. If your computer is compromised and quietly swaps the destination address, the only place that lie becomes visible is the screen of a device connected to nothing.

Chapter 2 · 2.6
Who holds the keys?
Custodial vs Non-Custodial

There’s one question more important than choosing which wallet app is best: who holds your private key?

The answer determines everything.

Custodial wallet

Custodial means another party holds your private key on your behalf. Exchanges like Binance, Coinbase, or Indodax are the most common examples. When you buy Bitcoin there and don’t withdraw it, that Bitcoin is in their wallet, not yours.

You only have a balance in their ledger. Like saving at a bank.

This is convenient. No need to deal with a seed phrase, no fear of sending to the wrong place, there’s customer service if something goes wrong. But there’s a price to pay: you don’t truly hold your Bitcoin.

The exchange can freeze your account. The exchange can go bankrupt. The exchange can be hacked. All of this has happened, again and again, on various platforms around the world.

Non-custodial wallet

Non-custodial means you yourself hold the private key. No third party can block, freeze, or take your Bitcoin.

But the responsibility is entirely in your hands. There’s no customer service. There’s no account recovery. If the seed phrase is lost, the Bitcoin is lost forever.

"Not your keys, not your coins"

This isn’t just a slogan. It’s a fundamental principle of Bitcoin. As long as the private key is in someone else’s hands, you don’t truly own Bitcoin. You own a promise from someone else that they will give you Bitcoin if you ask.

And promises can be broken.

A custodial wallet isn’t an equal alternative to non-custodial. It’s a conscious trade-off: you trade sovereignty over your money for convenience. Understand the consequences before choosing.

Chapter 3 · 3.1
Not a balance transfer, but a cryptographic chain
What is a Transaction?

If you’ve ever transferred money through a bank, you’re used to a simple model: a balance decreases in one account, increases in another. The bank records the change. Done.

Bitcoin doesn’t work that way.

In Bitcoin, there’s no such thing as a "balance." There is no number stored somewhere that reads "you have 1 BTC." What exists is a history of transactions, and from that history is calculated how much Bitcoin you can use right now.

A transaction is a transfer instruction

Every Bitcoin transaction is a cryptographically signed message containing two main things: where this Bitcoin comes from, and where this Bitcoin is going.

"Where it comes from" is a reference to a previous transaction that gave Bitcoin to you. "Where it goes" is an instruction for whom this Bitcoin is sent to and how much.

The network verifies that you really have the right to move the Bitcoin you reference, then broadcasts the transaction to all nodes. If it’s valid, it enters a block and becomes a permanent part of the blockchain.

Not a number, but a chain

This is what makes Bitcoin fundamentally different from conventional financial systems. Your ownership isn’t a number in a database. It’s a cryptographic chain that can be traced all the way back to the first block, the Genesis Block, mined by Satoshi in January 2009.

Every Bitcoin in this world can have its origin traced. Nothing can appear out of nothing.

In Bitcoin, "owning" Bitcoin means having the ability to sign a transaction that references an unspent output. Not a number in a database, but a key that unlocks an output. This concept will become much clearer in 3.2.

Chapter 3 · 3.2
Digital banknotes that can’t be cut
UTXO — Unspent Transaction Output

UTXO stands for Unspent Transaction Output. This is the most important concept in Chapter 3, and perhaps one of the most frequently misunderstood concepts in Bitcoin.

Forget the concept of a balance

In the banking system, your ownership is represented as a number: a balance. The bank stores that number in their database and changes it every time there’s a transaction.

Bitcoin has no balance. What Bitcoin has is a collection of unspent transaction outputs. Each output has a certain value and can only be used once, by the person who has the right key. That is a UTXO.

The banknote analogy

The easiest way to understand a UTXO is to imagine physical banknotes. If you have a Rp 100.000 note, you don’t have "a balance of Rp 100.000." You have a single piece of paper worth Rp 100.000 that physically sits in your hand.

If you want to pay Rp 30.000, you can’t cut the banknote. You hand over the entire Rp 100.000, the merchant takes Rp 30.000, and returns Rp 70.000 to you. A UTXO works exactly like that. You can’t spend a portion. You have to spend the whole thing, and the remainder comes back to you as a new UTXO.

What a Bitcoin "balance" really is

If your wallet shows "0.55 BTC," that’s not one number in one place. It might be the sum of several UTXOs: for example one UTXO worth 0.05 BTC from Alice, one worth 0.12 BTC from Bob, one worth 0.08 BTC from a mining reward, and one worth 0.30 BTC from Charlie. Your wallet adds up all the UTXOs you can sign for, and displays them as a single number.

Why UTXO?

The UTXO model has several advantages. First, it makes verification easy: to check whether a transaction is valid, a node only needs to make sure the referenced UTXO exists and hasn’t been used. Second, it prevents double-spending naturally: once a UTXO is used, it disappears from the active UTXO set and can’t be used again.

The entire state of Bitcoin can be summarized in one set of data: the UTXO set. This is the list of all unspent transaction outputs across the whole network. As of mid-2026 its size is around 11 GB, holding more than 170 million UTXOs. Every full node stores it and uses it to validate every new transaction.

Who picks the UTXOs for you?

In the simulation above you chose which UTXOs to spend yourself. In everyday use you never do that. You type an amount and an address, then press send. But the decision still has to be made by someone, and that someone is your wallet. The process is called coin selection, and it explains a lot of the things that feel strange to new users.

Why does it matter? Because as we saw in 3.4, the cost of a transaction is set by its shape, not its value. Every UTXO drawn in adds one input, and every input adds size. Picking three small UTXOs instead of one large one can multiply the fee for a payment of exactly the same amount.

A wallet is juggling goals that pull against each other. It wants the fee as low as possible, which argues for using as few inputs as it can. It also wants to avoid leaving change that is too small, because tiny change today becomes an expensive UTXO to spend tomorrow. And ideally it leaks no more information than necessary, because every pair of UTXOs combined in one transaction tells the world they belong to the same person. We look at the privacy consequences in Chapter 10.

The ideal outcome is finding a combination that adds up exactly, so no change output is needed at all. The transaction comes out smaller, cheaper, and leaves no change trail to analyse. Bitcoin Core calls this search branch and bound, and it does try for that exact match first. The trouble is such matches are rare, so when the search fails the wallet falls back to methods that accept change.

This is where several things that puzzle new users start to make sense. Why is sending a small amount sometimes far more expensive than usual? Because your funds are scattered across many tiny UTXOs and the wallet is forced to combine a lot of inputs. Why can the fee differ when the amount sent is identical? Because the shape of the transaction differs, even though the value does not.

It is also why many wallets offer a way to pick UTXOs by hand, usually called coin control. For ordinary use, letting the wallet decide is fine. But once you care about privacy, or you are facing high fees, taking that decision back can matter a great deal. And if your funds are already scattered across many small UTXOs, there is a specific way to tidy them up that we cover in 10.4.

Chapter 3 · 3.3
The anatomy inside a transaction
Inputs and Outputs

Every Bitcoin transaction has two main parts: inputs and outputs. An input is a reference to a UTXO you consume. An output is an instruction for where Bitcoin goes after this transaction.

Input

An input isn’t a number. An input is a pointer to an unspent output of a previous transaction. It contains two things: a reference to which UTXO is consumed, and proof that you have the right to use it in the form of a cryptographic signature from your private key.

A single transaction can have many inputs. This happens when you need to combine several small UTXOs to pay a larger amount, like combining several small banknotes to pay for something more expensive.

Output

An output determines where Bitcoin goes. Each output contains two things: the amount of BTC sent, and the condition that must be met to spend this output in the future. That condition is usually simple: anyone who can prove they hold the private key matching this address may spend this output.

A single transaction can also have many outputs. You can send to several addresses at once in one transaction, and the change output back to yourself also counts as a separate output.

The hidden fee

There’s one interesting thing: the miner fee isn’t written explicitly inside the transaction. The fee is the difference between the total input value and the total output value. If you have inputs worth 0.1 BTC and create outputs worth 0.099 BTC, then the remaining 0.001 BTC automatically becomes the fee for the miner who includes your transaction in a block.

This is why it’s so important to always check the total output before signing a transaction. If you forget to create a change output and only create one output to the recipient, the entire difference becomes the miner fee. There are real cases where someone paid thousands of dollars in fees because they forgot to add a change output.

Beyond amounts and destinations, a transaction can also carry conditions about time: the earliest it may enter a block, or how long a UTXO must wait before it can be spent. Bitcoin has four mechanisms for this, and we take all of them apart in Chapter 15.

Chapter 3 · 3.4
Not a tariff, but an offer to miners
Transaction Fee

Fees in Bitcoin don’t work like a bank’s transfer fee. There’s no fixed tariff, no percentage of the amount sent, and nothing sets it centrally.

Fees in Bitcoin are determined by the market.

How fees are calculated

In Bitcoin, fees are calculated based on the size of the transaction in bytes, not based on the value of the Bitcoin sent. Sending 1 BTC and sending 0.00001 BTC can have exactly the same fee if the transaction size is the same.

The unit used is satoshis per vbyte (sat/vB). One satoshi is the smallest unit of Bitcoin: 0.00000001 BTC. One vbyte is the transaction size in virtual bytes, a unit that accounts for the efficiency of modern transaction formats.

Why fees rise and fall

Each Bitcoin block has limited capacity, about 1-4 MB per block, and a new block appears on average every 10 minutes. When many people want to transact at once, the space in a block becomes contested.

Miners choose which transactions go into their block. They’ll prioritize transactions offering the highest fee per vbyte because that maximizes their revenue. Transactions with low fees will wait longer, or even not make it into a block at all if the network is very busy.

The relationship between fees and UTXOs

The more inputs in a transaction, the larger the transaction size in bytes, the higher the fee that needs to be paid. This is why modern wallets try to manage UTXOs efficiently, consolidating small UTXOs when fees are cheap, so they don’t need to use many inputs when fees are expensive.

RBF (Replace by Fee)

If your transaction has already been broadcast to the network but hasn’t entered a block and its fee is too low, there’s a mechanism called RBF, or Replace by Fee. You can resend the same transaction with a higher fee, and miners will prioritize the new version. One condition is easy to miss: the original transaction must have been marked as replaceable when it was created. If it wasn’t marked, many nodes will reject the replacement. The details of the mechanism, including what to do if you are the recipient rather than the sender, we cover in 9.3.

Fees aren’t a charge taken by "Bitcoin." A fee is an incentive you offer to miners so they prioritize your transaction. No company, no platform, no third party receives it. The fee goes directly to the miner who finds your block.

Chapter 3 · 3.5
The queue before entering the blockchain
Mempool

When you send a Bitcoin transaction, it doesn’t go straight into the blockchain. It goes into a queue first.

That queue is called the mempool, short for memory pool. Every node in the Bitcoin network keeps its own mempool, a list of transactions that have been broadcast, validated, but not yet confirmed into a block.

The journey of a transaction

Once you sign and broadcast a transaction, it spreads to all nodes in the network within seconds through a process called gossiping. Each node forwards valid transactions to its neighboring nodes. But entering the mempool doesn’t mean it’s done. Your transaction still waits there until a miner decides to include it in the block they’re mining.

Miners choose transactions

Miners aren’t required to include every transaction in the mempool. They choose which transactions yield the highest total fee for their block. The most common strategy is to pick the transactions with the highest fee per vbyte first until the block’s capacity is full. This is why the fee rate you choose determines how quickly your transaction is confirmed.

The mempool can fill up

When the network is very busy, the mempool can swell to hundreds of megabytes. Transactions with fees that are too low can get stuck there for hours, even days. Some nodes will even drop transactions with very low fees from their mempool when memory is full.

Confirmation

Once your transaction enters a block, it gets one confirmation. Each new block mined on top of that block adds one more confirmation. The more confirmations, the harder it is to reverse that transaction, the more final your transaction. For small everyday transactions, one confirmation is usually enough. For large transactions, most people wait for 6 confirmations before considering a transaction truly final.

The mempool isn’t one global queue that’s the same for everyone. Each node has its own mempool with rules and capacity that can differ. But because nodes share transactions with one another, in practice most nodes have similar mempool contents.

Chapter 3 · 3.6
From creation to final
The Lifecycle of a Transaction

We’ve learned all the components: UTXO, inputs, outputs, fees, the mempool, confirmation. Now let’s put it all together in one complete picture.

This is the full journey of a Bitcoin transaction, from beginning to end.

1. Creation

The wallet chooses UTXOs sufficient to cover the amount to be sent plus the fee. It assembles a transaction with inputs referencing those UTXOs, an output to the recipient, and a change output back to the sender if there’s a remainder.

2. Signing

The sender’s private key is used to create a cryptographic signature that proves ownership of the referenced UTXO. This signature is unique to this transaction and can’t be reused for another transaction.

3. Broadcast

The signed transaction is broadcast to the network. The first node that receives it validates: do its UTXOs exist and are they unspent? Is the signature valid? If yes, it forwards it to its neighboring nodes.

4. Mempool

The transaction enters the mempool on every node that receives it. It waits there alongside thousands of other transactions. The fee rate determines how quickly a miner picks it.

5. Miner selection

When a miner is assembling a new block, it chooses transactions from the mempool based on the highest fee per vbyte. Your transaction enters the candidate block being mined.

6. Block found

The miner finds a valid proof of work and broadcasts the block to the network. Other nodes verify it and add it to the blockchain. The referenced UTXOs are marked spent. The new outputs become fresh UTXOs belonging to the recipient.

7. Confirmations accumulate

Each new block mined on top of that block adds one confirmation. The more confirmations, the deeper the transaction is embedded in the blockchain, the more impossible it is to reverse.

PSBT: Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction

The lifecycle above describes a transaction signed by one party. But what if a transaction needs to be signed by several parties, for example a 2-of-3 multisig, or if signing is done on a hardware wallet separate from the wallet that assembles the transaction?

PSBT (BIP 174) is a standard format for a transaction that is "in the process" of being signed. It separates two roles that were previously always combined: the role of the transaction assembler (who chooses the UTXOs, determines the outputs, and computes the fee) and the role of the signer (who has the private key). With PSBT, these two roles can be performed by different devices or parties.

The flow: the wallet software assembles the transaction and exports it as a PSBT file. This file contains all the information needed to sign: which inputs need to be signed, the script that must be satisfied, and additional metadata. A hardware wallet or another signer reads the PSBT file, verifies its details, adds its signature, and returns the partially signed PSBT. Once all signatures are collected, the PSBT is combined and finalized into a transaction ready to broadcast.

This entire process, from creation to the first confirmation, can finish in 10 minutes if the network isn’t busy and your fee is sufficient. No bank, no permission, no business hours, no holidays. Anywhere in the world, anytime.

Chapter 4 · 4.1
A deterministic shredding machine
Hash Functions

Imagine a magic machine. You can put anything into it: a piece of paper, a single word, or the entire contents of the national library. The machine will always output a card of the same size, containing a string of letters and numbers 64 characters long.

That is a hash function.

Like a fingerprint, but for data

Every piece of data has a unique hash "fingerprint." Like a human fingerprint, the hash of some data can be used to verify its identity without comparing its entire contents. And like a fingerprint, the original data can’t be reconstructed from the hash.

If you want to make sure a file you download isn’t corrupted or tampered with along the way, you can compare its hash with the hash provided by the source. If the hashes match, the files are identical. If even one bit differs, the hash is completely different.

First property: deterministic

The same input always produces the same output. SHA-256("Bitcoin") will always produce exactly the same hash, on any computer, anytime. No variation, no randomness.

Second property: the avalanche effect

Change just one small letter, and the entire hash changes completely. "Bitcoin" and "bitcoin" produce hashes with no similarity at all. No pattern can be guessed, no smooth transition. One small change, a huge earthquake in the output.

It’s like a cake recipe. If you swap one gram of sugar for salt, the taste changes drastically. There’s no way to guess how much was swapped just from tasting the result.

Third property: one-way

From the output, it’s impossible to reconstruct the input. This isn’t about a secret key or encryption. It’s about mathematics. There’s no equation that can be reversed. The only way to find the input from a hash is to try every possibility one by one. For SHA-256, with every computer in the world working together, it would take longer than the age of the universe. Not hyperbole.

Fourth property: collision resistant

SHA-256 produces a 256-bit output, meaning there are 2²⁵⁶ possible different outputs. The chance of two different inputs producing the same hash is, practically, zero.

SHA-256 in Bitcoin

Bitcoin uses SHA-256 almost everywhere. To generate an address from a public key. To link blocks to one another on the blockchain. As the core of the mining process. Every block contains the hash of the previous block, forming a chain that can’t be manipulated without recomputing the entire chain that follows.

SHA-256 isn’t encryption. Encryption can be reversed if you have the key. A hash can’t be reversed at all. This is a fundamental difference that’s often misunderstood, even by people who have long worked in technology.

Chapter 4 · 4.2
A jump that can’t be reversed
Elliptic Curve Cryptography

In Chapter 2 we learned that a private key produces a public key through a one-way process. Now it’s time to understand why that process can’t be reversed.

The answer lies in a branch of mathematics called Elliptic Curve Cryptography, or ECC. But we won’t start from the math. We’ll start from the problem.

The problem to be solved

Imagine you want to build a system where someone can prove their identity without revealing the secret that proves that identity. Like this: you want to prove that you know the way to a hidden place, without having to show anyone the map. You simply arrive there. Others can verify that you arrived, but can’t reconstruct the route you took.

For that, you need a mathematical operation with one crucial property: easy to perform in one direction, but impossible to reverse.

The combination lock analogy

Imagine a combination lock with dozens of digits. Turning the dial according to a combination you already know: easy, a few seconds. Finding the combination when you don’t know it: there is no route except trying, and the number of attempts required runs far past the time available to anyone.

Notice that what blocks you is not lost information. The combination is still there, intact, fixing the position of the dial exactly. What blocks you is the cost of finding it again. That is the difference from mixing paint, where the original composition really is destroyed. ECC behaves like a combination lock, not like paint: the result is entirely determined by the input, but tracing back demands work that would never finish.

Jumping along the curve

An elliptic curve is a mathematical line with a particular shape. On this curve, there’s one agreed-upon starting point everyone shares, called the generator point G. From point G, we can "jump" to the next point with certain mathematical rules. From there, jump again. And again. Each jump follows the same rules, but produces points scattered randomly across the curve.

The private key is the number of jumps you make. It can be a very large number, up to 2²⁵⁶ possibilities. The public key is the final point where you land. Computing the final point from the number of jumps: easy, takes milliseconds. Finding the number of jumps from the final point: computationally impossible. There’s no shortcut.

Public key format

The final point on the elliptic curve is a pair of coordinates (x, y). In Bitcoin, these coordinates are encoded into a hex string. The most commonly used format now is the compressed format: prefix 02 if y is positive, or 03 if y is negative, followed by the x coordinate in hex. Because the elliptic curve is symmetric, the recipient can recompute y from x and the prefix whenever needed.

SECP256K1

Bitcoin uses a specific elliptic curve called SECP256K1. This curve was chosen for its mathematical properties that are efficient, secure, and have no hidden backdoor.

The security of Bitcoin’s entire ownership system rests on one unsolved mathematical problem: from the final point, there’s no way to find how many jumps were made. As long as this problem remains unsolved, a private key can’t be derived from a public key.

Interactive simulation — Jumping Along the Elliptic Curve
Slide the slider to change the private key (number of jumps). Notice how the final point and the public key change completely even when adding just one jump.
