02...
Slide the slider to change the private key.
This simulation shows at most 32 jumps, and it’s already hard to guess where each jump goes. A real Bitcoin private key is 2²⁵⁶ jumps. That number can’t be imagined by any human brain, and can’t be cracked by any computer that has ever existed.
Public key formats: why half of it is enough
A point on the curve has an X and a Y coordinate. But the curve is symmetric about the X axis, so for any X there are only two possible Y values: one even, one odd. That means Y does not need to be stored, only which of the two it is.
Uncompressed
04X (32 bytes)Y (32 bytes)
65 bytes
The older format. Stores both X and Y.
Compressed
02/03X (32 bytes)
33 bytes
Prefix 02 if Y is even, 03 if odd. Y is recomputed when needed.
That saves 32 bytes per public key, nearly half, without losing any information at all. Y is not discarded, it can be derived back from X using the curve equation. This is why almost every modern wallet uses the compressed format.

Chapter 4 · 4.3
Proving without revealing
ECDSA

We already know that a private key produces a public key through ECC. Now the question: how is the private key used to prove ownership without revealing the private key itself?

The answer is a digital signature. In Bitcoin, this mechanism is called ECDSA, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm.

The sealed letter analogy

Imagine you send an official letter. You don’t want anyone to be able to forge your letter, and the recipient must be able to confirm it really came from you. In the physical world, you use a signature and a seal. In the Bitcoin world, you use ECDSA.

The difference from a physical signature: an ECDSA signature is unique for each message. Your signature for a 0.1 BTC transaction today is completely different from your signature for a 0.1 BTC transaction tomorrow, even though the private key used is the same. No one can copy your signature from one transaction and paste it onto another.

How signing works

When you send Bitcoin, the wallet takes the transaction data, combines it with your private key, and produces two numbers: r and s. Together they form the ECDSA signature. This process also involves a secret random number called the nonce. This nonce must be truly random and must never be used twice. If the same nonce is used to sign two different transactions, your private key can be recovered in full from those two signatures alone. This is not a theoretical weakness: implementation mistakes of exactly this kind have drained real wallets. Note also that this nonce has nothing to do with the nonce miners search for in Chapter 5. The name happens to be the same, the concept is not.

How verification works

Anyone who has the public key and the signature can verify that the signature was created by the owner of the corresponding private key, without needing to know the private key. The Bitcoin network performs this verification for every incoming transaction. If the signature isn’t valid, the transaction is rejected.

One input, one signature

Each input in a transaction must be signed separately. If your transaction has three inputs from three different UTXOs, you need to create three different signatures, each proving ownership of the corresponding UTXO.

ECDSA enables something remarkable: you can prove that you know a secret, without revealing the secret. The network knows you have the correct private key, but never sees your private key.

—
Nonce (k)
A random number created anew each time you sign. It must be truly unique — it must never be used twice for two different messages.
—
Signature (r, s)
The mathematical result of message + private key + nonce. Unique to this transaction only. Anyone can verify it using the public key, without needing to know the private key.
—
⚠️ The same nonce used twice for two different messages can mathematically expose your private key. This has happened in the real world and resulted in lost Bitcoin. The solution: modern wallets use a CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator) to ensure every nonce is truly random and never repeats. You don’t need to manage this manually, a good wallet handles it automatically.
Message received
The transaction data received by the network nodes.
Complete Stage 1 first.
Signature (r, s)
The signature included with the transaction. The node uses it together with the public key for verification.
—
Sender’s public key
Publicly known. The node uses this public key to verify the signature, without needing to know the private key.
—

Chapter 4 · 4.4
One signature, no matter how many people
Schnorr Signature

ECDSA has worked well for as long as Bitcoin has existed. But there’s another signature algorithm that’s more elegant, more efficient, and has properties that open up new possibilities: the Schnorr signature.

Schnorr was activated in Bitcoin through the Taproot upgrade in November 2021.

Why not Schnorr from the start?

For nearly two decades, the Schnorr signature was covered by a patent and almost nobody used it. That patent expired in 2008, a few months before Bitcoin was released. So the reason Satoshi chose ECDSA was not the patent. At the time, Schnorr had not been standardised, had not been widely tested, and was not available in OpenSSL, the cryptography library the earliest Bitcoin code leaned on. ECDSA met all three. It took years afterwards for the Bitcoin community to mature Schnorr and reach consensus to activate it safely.

First advantage: simpler

Schnorr has a stronger security proof that’s easier to analyze. ECDSA is more complex and has more corners that can be implemented incorrectly, like the nonce problem we discussed in 4.3.

Second advantage: linear and combinable

This is the most important one. Schnorr signatures can be combined mathematically. If two people each have a private key, they can create a single signature that represents both. An outsider can’t tell whether the signature is from one person or a hundred.

Third advantage: more private

Because signatures can be combined, a multisignature transaction looks identical to an ordinary transaction from the outside. No one can tell whether a transaction requires 2 of 3 signatures or just 1.

Fourth advantage: more efficient

A combined signature is smaller in size than a collection of separate signatures. This saves space in a block and lowers the fee for complex transactions.

MuSig

This ability to combine Schnorr signatures is implemented in a protocol called MuSig. With MuSig, several parties can collaborate to create a single signature without any one party knowing another party’s private key.

Taproot

Schnorr is the foundation of Taproot, the biggest Bitcoin upgrade since SegWit. Taproot allows complex spending conditions to be hidden behind a simple single signature. As long as all parties agree, the transaction looks like an ordinary transaction. Only if there’s a dispute are those complex conditions revealed.

Schnorr isn’t just a technical upgrade. It’s the foundation of the next generation of Bitcoin privacy and scalability. Every Taproot transaction that looks simple can hide very complex logic behind it.

Chapter 4 · 4.5
One hash that summarizes everything
Merkle Tree, Merkle Root, and Merkle Proof

Every Bitcoin block contains hundreds or even thousands of transactions. There’s one simple question that needs an efficient answer: how do you prove that a particular transaction is inside a block, without having to download and inspect the entire block?

The answer is the Merkle Tree.

A tree of hashes

A Merkle Tree is a tree-shaped data structure built from hashes. Here’s how it works: first, each transaction is hashed to produce a Transaction ID, or TXID. These are the "leaves" of the tree. Second, the leaves are paired up two by two. Each pair is combined and hashed again, producing one new hash at the level above. Third, this process repeats upward until only a single hash remains at the top.

That single hash at the top is called the Merkle Root.

The Merkle Root in the block header

This Merkle Root is what’s stored in the header of every Bitcoin block. Not the entire list of transactions, but the result of this hierarchical tree structure. The Merkle Root summarizes the entire contents of the block in a single 32-byte hash. If one transaction changes, its TXID changes, which changes the hash above it, all the way up to the Merkle Root. No one can manipulate a transaction without changing the Merkle Root.

Merkle Proof

What makes the Merkle Tree truly powerful is the Merkle Proof. To prove that transaction T is inside a block, you don’t need to see the entire block. You only need the TXID of transaction T, a few "sibling" hashes along the path from T to the root, and the Merkle Root in the block header. With those elements, anyone can verify that T really is in that block by recomputing the hash path from the bottom up.

SPV (Simplified Payment Verification)

The Merkle Proof is the foundation of SPV, how lightweight wallets like the one on your smartphone work. An SPV wallet doesn’t download the entire blockchain that’s hundreds of gigabytes. It only downloads the block headers, then requests a Merkle Proof for the relevant transaction. Enough to verify a payment without becoming a full node.

To prove one transaction in a block containing 2.000 transactions, you only need about 11 hashes. Not 2.000, not 1.999, but 11. This is because a binary tree grows logarithmically, an elegant efficiency from simple mathematics.

Chapter 4 · 4.6
How it all works together
From Cryptography to Network Security

We’ve studied all the cryptographic components that make up Bitcoin: the hash function, ECC, ECDSA, Schnorr, and the Merkle Tree. Now it’s time to see how they all work together as one whole system.

Hashing protects the integrity of the blockchain

Every block contains the hash of the previous block. This means if you want to change a transaction in an old block, you have to recompute the hash of the entire chain of blocks that follows. Meanwhile the network keeps mining new blocks. You will never be able to catch up. This is why the more confirmations a transaction has, the safer it is. Each new block mined on top of it makes an attack more impossible.

ECC and ECDSA protect ownership

Without the correct private key, no one can sign a valid transaction from your Bitcoin address. The network verifies every signature before accepting a transaction. No central authority, no password that can be reset, no "forgot password." Ownership is purely cryptographic.

The Merkle Tree keeps verification efficient

Without the Merkle Tree, to verify one transaction you’d have to download the entire block. With the Merkle Tree, you only need a few hashes. This is what lets Bitcoin be used on resource-constrained devices without having to trust a third party.

Schnorr protects privacy and scalability

With Schnorr, complex transactions look like ordinary transactions. Privacy improves, transaction size shrinks, and fees drop. This isn’t just a technical upgrade but a fundamental change in how Bitcoin can be used.

A system that locks together

What makes Bitcoin different isn’t any single cryptographic component, but how they all lock together. Hashing ensures history can’t be changed. ECC ensures ownership can’t be forged. The Merkle Tree ensures verification can be done efficiently. Schnorr ensures privacy and efficiency keep improving. There’s no single point of failure. There’s no single party that can manipulate the system. Trust is built from mathematics, not from institutions.

Satoshi didn’t invent all of this mathematics. SHA-256, ECC, the Merkle Tree, all existed before Bitcoin. What Satoshi did was assemble existing components into one system that, for the first time, solved the double-spend problem without a central authority. That’s what makes Bitcoin not merely a technology, but an invention.

So what about quantum computers?

Twice in this book we have leaned on the phrase "if some computational advance one day becomes a threat": once when covering addresses in 2.3, and again with P2PKH in 6.3. It is time to explain that phrase.

What is threatened is not all of Bitcoin’s cryptography, only one part of it. Hash functions like SHA-256 hold up relatively well: a quantum computer speeds up the search but does not collapse it, and lengthening the hash is enough to compensate. What is genuinely fragile is signatures. Shor’s algorithm, run on a large enough quantum computer, can compute a private key from a public key. That is precisely the reverse of the one-way property we covered in 4.2, and all of Bitcoin ownership rests on that property.

But note the condition: the public key has to be visible first. This is where the habit of hiding public keys behind a hash, which we covered in 2.3, turns out to be far more than tidiness.

How much is actually exposed?

Various analyses in 2026 estimate that roughly 6.5 to 6.9 million BTC, about a third of all supply, have already revealed their public key on-chain. That figure splits in two. About 1.9 million come from the earliest P2PK format, which put the public key directly in the output, including an estimated 1.7 million believed to belong to Satoshi. The remaining 4.1 million are exposed not because of their format but because of address reuse. This is the real price of the habit we discussed in 10.5.

Which means most of that exposure is not a protocol flaw. It is the result of user choices, and that means most of it was avoidable.

The debate underway

In February 2026 came BIP-360, proposing a new output type called P2MR. It resembles Taproot but drops the key path, so no public key appears on-chain when the output is created. That closes the exposure for new transactions, but does nothing for coins whose public keys are already visible.

Two months later came BIP-361, and this is where the argument turned heated. It proposes a staged schedule: after some years the network stops accepting outputs to legacy formats, and some years after that, ECDSA and Schnorr verification is switched off entirely. Coins that have not migrated become permanently frozen.

The reaction was fierce, and both sides have a case. Opponents call it confiscation: freezing other people’s coins because they could not or did not migrate, including owners who have died, contradicts the promise that nobody can take your Bitcoin. Supporters answer that doing nothing is not neutral either: if those coins are not frozen, they will be taken by whoever builds a quantum computer first, and what circulates will no longer be Bitcoin that is owned but Bitcoin that was stolen. The choice is not between confiscating and not confiscating, but between freezing and surrendering.

What will date, and what will not

As of mid-2026, both remain proposals and neither has been activated. If you are reading this some years later, the situation has very likely moved on. Perhaps one of them is active, perhaps both were replaced by something else, perhaps the argument is still running. The BIP names and numbers above will date, so will that figure of 6.9 million, and so will every estimate of when a sufficiently large quantum computer will actually exist. The history of such estimates is full of deadlines that came and went.

But the following four things will not date, and they are what you should actually carry away from this section. First, only signatures are threatened, not hash functions. Second, that threat only applies once a public key has been seen on-chain. Third, the largest share of exposure comes from address reuse, not from a protocol flaw. Fourth, every solution must ultimately choose between freezing coins that are already exposed or letting them be taken, and there is no third option that pleases everyone.

If you want to know the current state of things, what to look for is not news about quantum computers but two far more grounded questions: is there a quantum-resistant output type active on the network, and does the wallet you use support it. The rest is noise.

And whatever the answers to those two questions turn out to be, what you can do yourself stays just as simple: do not reuse addresses. As long as your public key has never appeared on-chain, you are not in the exposed group, today or ten years from now. Advice that sounded like a privacy matter in 10.5 turns out to be about long-term resilience too.

Chapter 5 · 5.1
How can thousands of parties who don’t know each other agree?
Consensus

Every morning, billions of people around the world wake up and agree on one thing without ever discussing it: what time it is. No one decides this. No meeting, no vote. But everyone in the same time zone sees the same clock and agrees that it’s seven in the morning. This is consensus.

Consensus is everywhere

Consensus is the process by which a group of parties reaches a shared agreement about something. It can happen formally or informally, with a central authority or without. In parliament, consensus is reached through voting. In the stock market, consensus about a stock’s price is reached through continuous buying and selling. On the internet, the TCP/IP protocol is a consensus about how data should be sent between computers. In society, language is a consensus about what a word means.

Easy consensus and hard consensus

Most of the consensus we know has one thing in common: there’s a central authority that serves as the anchor. The central bank sets the value of the currency. The government sets the laws. This authority makes consensus relatively easy. But what if there’s no referee? What if all parties are equal, none has more authority, and some of them might not even be honest? This is hard consensus. And this is exactly the problem Bitcoin faces.

Two consequences of not following consensus

In any consensus-based system, a party that doesn’t follow the shared agreement faces two choices. First, return to consensus. They realize their version differs from the majority, adjust, and continue together. Second, form their own faction. They keep their version, separate from the majority, and form a parallel system. In the Bitcoin world, this is called a fork.

Bitcoin’s consensus problem

Bitcoin has no central authority. What exists is thousands of nodes spread around the world, each keeping its own copy of the blockchain. The question: if two nodes get different information about the same block, who is right? How can thousands of computers that don’t know each other agree on one and the same version of history? Bitcoin’s solution to this problem is Proof of Work, which we’ll cover in 5.2.

Satoshi wasn’t the first to think about the problem of consensus without a central authority. Computer scientists had been wrestling with this since 1982 in what’s called the Byzantine Generals Problem. What Satoshi did was find the first practical solution that could work in an open system, without permission, and without prior trust between parties.

Interactive simulation — Network consensus
Choose a scenario to see what happens when nodes don’t agree on the correct chain.

Soft fork dan hard fork

When a change to the rules is proposed in Bitcoin, the way it’s changed determines whether the network stays united or splits permanently.

A soft fork is a rule change that is backward compatible. Old nodes can still communicate with new nodes, but new nodes have stricter rules. The key is this: the new rules are a subset of the old ones, so a block that is valid under the new rules is automatically valid under the old rules too. Old nodes do not reject it. And because the majority of hashrate enforces the new rules, it is their chain that grows longer. Thanks to the longest chain rule, old nodes eventually follow the longer chain, even without having to update their software. SegWit, activated in 2017, is an example of a soft fork.

A hard fork is a rule change that is not backward compatible. Old nodes can’t recognize blocks from new nodes, and vice versa. The split that occurs is permanent. Two chains grow side by side forever, forming two different networks and two different currencies. There’s no longest chain that can reconcile them because they’re already speaking different languages. Bitcoin Cash, which split off from Bitcoin in 2017, is an example of a hard fork.

The key difference: in a soft fork, old nodes don’t need to know there are new rules. In a hard fork, old and new nodes can no longer live on the same network.

Chapter 5 · 5.2
Very hard to create, very easy to verify
Proof of Work

Bitcoin’s consensus requires a way to prove that someone has done real work before they can propose a new block. That way is called Proof of Work.

An asymmetric puzzle

Proof of Work is a mathematical puzzle with a very specific property: very hard to solve, but very easy to verify. Find a number that, when combined with the block data and hashed with SHA-256d, produces a hash starting with a certain number of zeros. The number being sought is called the nonce. There’s no clever way to find it. The only way is to try one by one, billions of times per second, until a hash that meets the requirement is found.

Target and leading zeros

The Bitcoin network sets a target: the hash of the block header must be smaller than a certain number. In practice, this means the hash must start with a certain number of leading zeros. The more zeros required, the harder the puzzle. Currently, a valid Bitcoin block hash must start with around 19 to 20 zeros.

Why is this effective?

Because of the property of hash functions we learned in Chapter 4: the output can’t be predicted. There’s no way to know in advance which nonce will produce a valid hash. Each attempt is independent, the result of the previous attempt doesn’t help at all. This means the only advantage someone can have is computational speed.

A verifiable proof

Once a nonce is found, verifying it takes just a single hash computation. Other nodes simply take the block header, compute SHA-256d, and check whether the result meets the target. One second, done. This is the asymmetry: it takes trillions of attempts to find, but only one attempt to verify.

Proof of Work wasn’t Satoshi’s invention. The concept was first proposed by Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor in 1993, and popularized by Adam Back in the Hashcash system in 1997 to fight email spam. Satoshi adapted it as a consensus mechanism for Bitcoin, a use that far exceeds its original purpose.

Chapter 5 · 5.3
From transaction to block — the complete process
Mining

We already know that a miner has to find a nonce that makes the block header hash meet the target. But what’s actually inside that block header? And how does the mining process work from start to finish?

The anatomy of a block

Every Bitcoin block consists of two parts: the header and the body. The body contains the list of transactions collected from the mempool. The header contains 6 fields with a total size of exactly 80 bytes, and this is what the miner hashes trillions of times per second.

The mining process from start to finish

First, the miner collects transactions from the mempool and chooses those paying the highest fees. Second, the miner assembles the block candidate: computing the Merkle Root of all chosen transactions and filling in all header fields except the nonce. Third, the miner starts trying nonces from 0, 1, 2, and so on. If the entire nonce space is exhausted without a result, the miner changes the timestamp or the order of transactions, which changes the Merkle Root, then starts again from nonce 0. Fourth, once a valid hash is found, the miner immediately broadcasts the block to the entire network.

Coinbase transaction

Every block always contains one special transaction in the first position: the coinbase transaction. It has no input from any UTXO. It creates new bitcoin from nothing as a reward for the miner who successfully finds the block. The coinbase transaction also contains a free field called the coinbase data. Satoshi filled this field with a famous message in the genesis block: "The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks."

80 bytes. That is the size of a Bitcoin block header. No more, no less. The entire security of the network depends on hashing these 80 bytes trillions of times per second, around the world, every ten minutes.

Chapter 5 · 5.4
However many miners come or go, always 10 minutes
Difficulty Adjustment

Bitcoin is designed to produce one block every ten minutes. But how can the network maintain this rhythm when the number of miners keeps changing?

The problem to be solved

If more miners join, the network hashrate rises, and blocks are found faster than ten minutes. If miners leave, the hashrate drops, and blocks are found slower. Without an adjustment mechanism, the interval between blocks would be chaotic.

How difficulty adjustment works

Every 2016 blocks, Bitcoin automatically adjusts the difficulty. The number 2016 isn’t arbitrary: with a target of 10 minutes per block, 2016 blocks should take exactly 2 weeks. The formula is simple: compare the actual time it took to mine the last 2016 blocks with the ideal time. If it was faster, difficulty rises. If it was slower, difficulty falls.

Adjustment limits

To prevent overly extreme changes, Bitcoin limits the adjustment to a maximum of 4× up or 4× down in one period. This protects the network from very sudden surges or drops in hashrate.

Who decides?

No one decides. Each node computes this adjustment independently using the same rules, and the result is always identical. This is another example of consensus without a central authority.

Why ten minutes?

Satoshi chose ten minutes as a compromise. Fast enough that transactions don’t wait too long, but slow enough that a block can spread across the entire network before another miner finds the next block.

Difficulty adjustment is one of the most elegant mechanisms in Bitcoin. It ensures that no matter how much computation is thrown at the network, one block still appears every ten minutes. Bitcoin can’t be spammed with hashrate.

Chapter 5 · 5.5
The only way new bitcoin enters the world
Block Reward and Halving

Every time a miner successfully finds a valid block, they receive two types of income: the block reward and transaction fees. But there’s one part of the block reward that’s unique to Bitcoin: it halves once every four years.

Block reward

The block reward is new bitcoin created from nothing through the coinbase transaction. This is the only way new bitcoin enters circulation. There is no other way. When Satoshi mined the genesis block in January 2009, the block reward was 50 BTC. Every new block added 50 BTC to the circulation.

Halving

Every 210.000 blocks, the block reward is cut in half. With an average of 10 minutes per block, 210.000 blocks take about 4 years. The first halving happened in November 2012: the reward dropped from 50 to 25 BTC. The second halving in July 2016: down to 12,5 BTC. The third halving in May 2020: down to 6,25 BTC. The fourth halving in April 2024: down to 3,125 BTC. This process will continue until around the year 2140.

Why 21 million?

In 1.5 we said there is no definitive explanation for why Satoshi picked 21 million. That still holds, and it does not contradict what follows. What Satoshi never explained is why he picked 50 BTC per block and an interval of 210,000 blocks. Once those two numbers were fixed, 21 million stopped being a choice and became a consequence that follows on its own. If you sum all the eras from 50 BTC, 25 BTC, 12,5 BTC, and so on to infinity, the result approaches exactly 21 million BTC. This is a convergent geometric series.

Formula — Bitcoin total supply

After the reward reaches zero

If the block reward is zero, what motivates miners? Transaction fees. As the reward falls, fees are expected to rise because demand for block space increases. This is a gradual transition over more than 100 years from subsidy to a pure fee economy.

Halving is a disinflation mechanism that’s been programmed from the start. The term is worth getting right: Bitcoin’s supply still grows with every block, only the rate keeps slowing toward zero. What shrinks is the speed of issuance, not the amount in circulation. Unlike a central bank that can print money anytime, Bitcoin’s emission schedule can’t be changed by anyone. Every node verifies that the coinbase transaction doesn’t exceed the allowed reward.

Chapter 5 · 5.6
When an attacker controls the majority of the hashrate
51% Attack

Proof of Work ensures that to change the transaction history, someone would have to repeat all the computational work already done. But there’s one scenario that’s often discussed: what if someone controls more than half of the network’s hashrate?

What can an attacker do?

With more than 50% of the hashrate, an attacker can perform a double-spend. Here’s how: send bitcoin to another party, wait for confirmation, while secretly mining an alternative chain. Because they have more hashrate, the alternative chain grows faster. After receiving the goods, broadcast the alternative chain. Based on the longest chain rule, the network adopts the new chain, and the original payment transaction disappears. The attacker can also censor certain transactions, refusing to include transactions from certain addresses in a block.

What can an attacker not do?

Many people misunderstand this. The attacker can’t steal bitcoin from someone else’s wallet. Can’t forge cryptographic signatures. Can’t print new bitcoin outside the halving schedule. Can’t change the consensus rules. The cryptography underlying Bitcoin is untouched by this attack.

Why does this attack not make economic sense?

To control 51% of Bitcoin’s current hashrate, an attacker would have to operate more ASICs than all the honest miners in the world, with hardware, electricity, and infrastructure costs reaching billions of dollars. If the attack succeeds and is detected, trust in Bitcoin collapses, the price falls, and all the attacker’s hardware loses its value. The attacker destroys their own investment.

What if the motivation isn’t profit, but destruction?

This is a more serious question. Imagine a state-level actor willing to pour almost unlimited resources just to damage Bitcoin, without caring about economic losses. Can Bitcoin survive?

The answer: yes, but it requires an active response from the community. A sustained 51% attack would be detected very quickly. Thousands of nodes around the world would see an unnaturally large reorg. The developer community could propose changing the hashing algorithm through a hard fork. If the algorithm is changed, all the ASIC hardware used by the attacker instantly becomes useless. The attacker would have to buy new hardware all over again, while the community only needs to update software.

This is a deeply asymmetric war: defending is far cheaper than attacking. Every new attack requires a massive new hardware investment. Every response only requires a code update.

The 51% attack and decentralization

This is why decentralized mining isn’t just idealism, but a real defense. The more spread out the hashrate is around the world among thousands of independent operators, the more expensive and harder it is for one party to control the majority. There’s no single point that can be attacked, bribed, or forced to surrender.

Bitcoin’s resilience against a 51% attack isn’t just about cost. It’s also about incentives, decentralization, and the community’s ability to adapt. A network that can change its hashing algorithm within days is a network that’s very hard to destroy permanently, even by an actor with almost unlimited resources.

Chapter 6 · 6.1
A small program behind every transaction
What is Bitcoin Script?

Every Bitcoin transaction that has ever existed includes one question and one answer. The question is in the output: "Who can spend this bitcoin?" The answer is in the next transaction’s input: "Here is the proof that I’m entitled to spend it." Both of these are encoded in a small program called Script.

How Script works

Script is a stack-based language. No variables, no loops, no functions. There are only two things: data and commands. Data is pushed onto the stack (push). A command takes data from the stack, does something, and returns the result (pop). Execution runs left to right, one instruction at a time.

Imagine a stack of plates. You can place a plate on top (push) or take a plate from the top (pop). Script works exactly like this, but the contents are data and computation results.

Why not Turing complete?

Satoshi deliberately designed Script not to be Turing complete. No loops, no recursion, no conditions that can run without bound. This isn’t a shortcoming, but a very deliberate design decision. Every node in the network has to verify every transaction. If Script could contain unbounded loops, one malicious transaction could paralyze the entire network. With limited Script, execution time is always predictable and short.

scriptPubKey and scriptSig

scriptPubKey is the "padlock" placed on the output. It defines the conditions that must be met to spend that output. scriptSig is the "key" carried by the sender of the next transaction. It contains the data needed to satisfy the conditions in scriptPubKey. For SegWit transactions, scriptSig is replaced or complemented by the witness field, which works on the same principle but more efficiently.

Script is one of the most frequently misunderstood parts of Bitcoin. Many think Bitcoin can only do simple transactions. But with Script, Bitcoin can express very complex spending conditions, from multisig to time-locked transactions, all without a central server and without trust.

Chapter 6 · 6.2
The commands that run Script
Opcodes

Script consists of two kinds of elements: data and opcodes. Data is the value pushed onto the stack. Opcodes are the commands that operate on that data.

Categories of opcodes

Stack operations manipulate the stack contents without computation. OP_DUP duplicates the top value. OP_DROP discards it. OP_SWAP swaps the top two values. Arithmetic operations do simple math: OP_ADD adds, OP_SUB subtracts. Comparison operations compare values: OP_EQUAL pushes TRUE if equal, OP_EQUALVERIFY immediately fails the script if not equal. Crypto operations do cryptography: OP_SHA256 hashes, OP_HASH160 is used to make addresses, OP_CHECKSIG verifies signatures. Flow control directs execution: OP_IF for conditions, OP_VERIFY to ensure a value is TRUE, OP_RETURN to create an unspendable output.

Disabled opcodes

Bitcoin once had more expressive opcodes, including string operations, multiplication, and bitwise operations. Most were disabled in 2010 after security flaws were found. Operations like OP_CAT could make the stack grow exponentially and be used for DoS attacks. OP_MUL and OP_DIV could potentially crash nodes due to poorly defined edge-case behavior. This is an example of how Bitcoin chooses security over features.

OP_RETURN

OP_RETURN deserves a mention of its own. It stops script execution entirely and marks the output as provably unspendable, impossible to spend, not because of a wrong key, but because the script is designed never to produce TRUE. It’s used to embed small data into the blockchain: a document hash, a message, or other metadata. The data size limit is not a consensus rule but relay policy that can differ per node and implementation — long-standing convention: 80 bytes.

Miniscript

Writing Bitcoin Script manually is very error-prone. A script that looks correct can have subtle bugs that cause funds to be locked forever or stolen. Miniscript is a structured language that compiles to Bitcoin Script, designed so that scripts can be analyzed automatically: can they be spent, what’s the cost, are there conflicting conditions?

Miniscript defines a set of "fragments" that can be combined safely: single keys, multisig, timelocks, hash preimages, and their combinations with AND, OR, and threshold. Each fragment has a strict type so the compiler can verify that the resulting script can really be executed as intended. A wallet that supports Miniscript can read any script made with Miniscript and immediately know its spending conditions.

With about 200 defined opcodes, most of them inactive, Bitcoin Script looks simple. But it’s this simplicity that makes it safe. Every active opcode has been tested and audited for over a decade. No surprises.

Chapter 6 · 6.3
Bitcoin’s most classic transaction format
P2PKH

P2PKH stands for Pay-to-Public-Key-Hash. This is the most classic and most widely used Bitcoin transaction format since Bitcoin was born. If you’ve ever seen a Bitcoin address starting with the number 1, that’s P2PKH.

How P2PKH works

The idea is simple: instead of stating the recipient’s public key directly in the output, what’s stored is the hash of that public key. This is the "Public Key Hash" in P2PKH. When someone wants to spend a P2PKH output, they have to prove two things: first, that they know the public key that produces that hash. Second, that they have the private key matching that public key, proven with a digital signature.

scriptPubKey P2PKH

scriptPubKey is the "padlock" placed on the output. For P2PKH, its form is always the same: OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <Public Key Hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG. It means: anyone who can prove they know the public key whose hash is this, and can sign with the matching private key, may spend this output.

scriptSig P2PKH

scriptSig is the "key" carried by the sender. For P2PKH there are only two elements: <Signature> <Public Key>. Very simple.

The verification process

The node combines scriptSig and scriptPubKey, then runs them as a single script. The stack runs from left to right. OP_DUP duplicates the public key. OP_HASH160 hashes one copy of it. OP_EQUALVERIFY compares the hash result with the hash stored in the output. If they match, OP_CHECKSIG verifies the signature against the public key. If everything succeeds, the result is TRUE and the transaction is valid.

Why a hash, not the public key directly?

Because the hash provides an extra layer of security. As long as the output hasn’t been spent, the public key is never exposed on the blockchain. Only its hash appears. This means even if one day quantum computing can break elliptic curve cryptography, bitcoin that has never been spent is still protected by the hash.

P2PKH has existed since Bitcoin’s first block. Even though there are now more efficient formats like P2WPKH, P2PKH remains valid and is still widely used. Backward compatibility is one of Bitcoin’s core principles.

Chapter 6 · 6.4
Separating the signature from the transaction
P2WPKH and SegWit

P2PKH worked well for years. But as Bitcoin grew, there was an increasingly pressing problem: full blocks, expensive fees, and one technical flaw called transaction malleability.

Transaction malleability

Transaction malleability is the ability of a third party to change a transaction’s Transaction ID (txid) without invalidating the transaction. This is possible because the txid is computed from the entire transaction data including scriptSig, and scriptSig can be modified slightly without making the signature invalid. Malleability made the Lightning Network and more complex payment channels very hard to build on top of Bitcoin.

SegWit (Segregated Witness)

SegWit was activated in August 2017 through a soft fork. The idea is elegant: separate the signature data (witness data) from the main transaction data. In a SegWit transaction, scriptSig is emptied. The signature data is moved to a separate structure called the witness field. Because the txid is now computed only from the transaction data without the witness data, transaction malleability is fully resolved. As a bonus, witness data gets a fee discount: one byte of witness is counted as 0.25 vbyte, not 1 byte.

P2WPKH

P2WPKH stands for Pay-to-Witness-Public-Key-Hash, the SegWit version of P2PKH. Its scriptPubKey is far shorter: just OP_0 <Public Key Hash>. OP_0 marks this as SegWit version 0, followed by the 20-byte public key hash. The signature and public key are no longer in scriptSig, both are in the witness field which is processed separately.

P2WPKH address

P2WPKH addresses use the bech32 format starting with bc1q. This format uses only lowercase letters, contains no confusing characters like 0, O, I, and l, and has better error detection than Base58Check.

Compatibility

Old nodes that don’t understand SegWit see the scriptPubKey OP_0 <hash> as an output that’s always spendable. This is intentional as part of the soft fork design: old nodes don’t need to validate witness data, they just need to not reject it.

SegWit is one of the biggest upgrades in Bitcoin’s history. It resolved transaction malleability, made fees more efficient, and opened the way for the Lightning Network. All of this was achieved through a soft fork, without splitting the network.

Chapter 6 · 6.5
Hiding complex spending conditions
P2SH and Multisig

Imagine a company that wants to store bitcoin with a rule: no single person can move the funds alone. At least 2 of 3 directors are required to approve each transaction. How does Bitcoin express this rule?

P2MS (bare multisig)

Before P2SH, Bitcoin had a multisig format called P2MS or Pay-to-Multisig. The script places all public keys directly in scriptPubKey: OP_2 <pubkey1> <pubkey2> <pubkey3> OP_3 OP_CHECKMULTISIG. The problem is that all public keys are exposed on the blockchain from the moment the output is created. Worse, there’s no standard address format for P2MS. The sender has to know the full script structure, not just an address.

P2SH (Pay-to-Script-Hash)

P2SH was activated in 2012 as a soft fork. The idea is brilliant: hide the complex script behind a hash. The recipient creates a redeem script that defines the spending conditions, then hashes it. This hash is what’s put into scriptPubKey: OP_HASH160 <redeem script hash> OP_EQUAL. Only 3 elements. The actual script is only revealed when the output is spent.

P2SH address

The hash of the redeem script is encoded using Base58Check with a prefix that produces an address starting with the number 3. The sender only needs to know this address without needing to know the multisig structure inside it.

P2SH advantages

First, privacy: the complex condition script isn’t exposed until the moment it’s spent. Second, standardization: the recipient can give a normal address without having to explain their multisig structure to the sender. Third, the burden on the recipient: the cost of including the long script is borne by the recipient when spending, not the sender when creating the output.

P2SH-P2WPKH

P2SH can also wrap a SegWit script, called P2SH-P2WPKH or wrapped SegWit. It’s used as a middle ground for old wallets that don’t yet support bech32 but want to enjoy SegWit’s benefits. The address still starts with 3 but contains a witness program inside.

P2SH changed how Bitcoin expresses complex spending conditions. Instead of putting all the logic in the output, the logic is hidden behind a hash. This is an example of how Bitcoin evolves through elegant abstraction, without changing the basic rules.

Chapter 6 · 6.6
Prove only what needs to be proven
Taproot and P2TR

Taproot was activated in November 2021 through a soft fork. It’s the biggest Bitcoin upgrade since SegWit, and brings three changes at once: Schnorr signatures, MAST, and a new output format called P2TR.

The problem Taproot solves

Before Taproot, there were two nagging problems. First, privacy: multisig transactions, lightning channels, and simple transactions looked different on the blockchain. Anyone could see that an output was multisig or a smart contract just from the shape of its script. Second, efficiency: a complex script with many conditions had to include all the conditions when spent, even conditions that weren’t used.

Schnorr signature

Schnorr signatures replace ECDSA for Taproot transactions. Their main advantage is key aggregation: several public keys can be combined into a single public key. This means a 3-of-5 multisig can look exactly like an ordinary single-signer transaction on the blockchain. No one can tell them apart just from looking at the output.

MAST (Merkelized Alternative Script Trees)

MAST allows an output to have many alternative spending conditions, each as a branch of a Merkle tree. When spending, the sender only needs to reveal the branch used, not the entire tree. Unused branches stay hidden forever. This saves space on the blockchain and preserves the privacy of unused conditions.

P2TR (Pay-to-Taproot)

P2TR combines Schnorr and MAST in one elegant output format. Its scriptPubKey is very simple: OP_1 <tweaked public key>. OP_1 marks SegWit version 1, followed by a 32-byte public key that has been modified to include a commitment to the entire script tree. A P2TR output can be spent with the key path (a direct Schnorr signature) or the script path (revealing one of the MAST branches).

P2TR address

P2TR addresses use the bech32m format starting with bc1p. Unlike the bech32 used by P2WPKH, bech32m has an updated checksum to handle different witness program lengths.

Tapscript

Tapscript is the version of Script used inside the Taproot script path spending. It is not a new language, but a revision of the old Script with several important changes. OP_CHECKSIG remains and now works with Schnorr signatures. What was disabled is OP_CHECKMULTISIG, replaced by a new opcode called OP_CHECKSIGADD. This enables more efficient multisig because all signatures can be checked in parallel, not one by one like in the old Script.

Tapscript also introduces OP_SUCCESS: a group of opcodes that currently always produce success. This is not a bug, but a deliberate design to make it easier to upgrade Script in the future without a hard fork. If one day a particular OP_SUCCESS is given new meaning through a soft fork, old scripts using it automatically support the new semantics.

Taproot isn’t just a technical upgrade. It’s a philosophical shift: from "prove everything" to "prove only what needs to be proven." Unused conditions don’t need to be revealed. This makes Bitcoin more private, more efficient, and more expressive all at once.

Visualization — Key path vs Script path
A P2TR output can be spent two ways. Key path: a single Schnorr signature, looks like an ordinary transaction. Script path: reveal one MAST branch along with its Merkle proof.

Chapter 7 · 7.1
Why can’t Bitcoin handle millions of transactions per second?
The Scalability Problem

Bitcoin is by design slow and expensive for small transactions. Every transaction has to be confirmed on the blockchain, waiting 10 minutes per block, and competing with other transactions for limited block space. When the network is busy, fees can reach tens of dollars for a transaction worth a few cents.

This isn’t a bug. It’s a deliberate trade-off.

Why is the block limited?

A large block size means nodes have to store and process more data. The bigger the block, the more expensive it is to run a node. The more expensive a node is, the fewer people are willing to run one. The fewer nodes, the more centralized the network. Centralization is Bitcoin’s main enemy.

Satoshi understood this. Bitcoin was designed to be a secure settlement layer, not a retail payment system. Every transaction that enters the blockchain is a final, immutable transaction, like settlement between banks, not like swiping a card at a checkout.

The scalability trilemma

There are three desirable properties of a payment system: decentralized, secure, and scalable. Simultaneously, all three cannot be fully achieved in one layer. Bitcoin chooses decentralization and security. Scalability is solved in another layer.

Layer 2 as the answer

The solution isn’t to make blocks bigger, but to build a layer on top of Bitcoin that can handle transactions quickly and cheaply, while still inheriting Bitcoin’s security as the final settlement layer. The Lightning Network is the most mature implementation of this idea.

This debate is not a theoretical one. It split the Bitcoin community in 2017 and ended with a hard fork that gave birth to Bitcoin Cash, a separate network with much larger blocks.

Both are still running today, so you can see the consequences of the two choices for yourself. Bitcoin Cash does deliver far cheaper fees, exactly as promised. What also happened: the hash rate securing it is a small fraction of Bitcoin’s, and its adoption is far narrower. A chain with lower hash rate is cheaper to attack, and that is arithmetic, not opinion.

Whether that price is worth the cheaper fees is a question still argued in earnest by people who know exactly what they are talking about. What matters for this chapter is not who won, but why making blocks bigger is never a free choice. Every bit of added capacity is paid for with a higher cost of running a node, and nodes are what make Bitcoin’s rules enforceable without trusting anyone.

Chapter 7 · 7.2
Transact thousands of times with two on-chain transactions
Payment Channel

The Lightning Network is built on one simple concept: not all transactions need to be recorded on the blockchain. Only two things need to be recorded: when the channel is opened and when the channel is closed.

The basic idea

Imagine two people, Alice and Bob, who frequently transact with each other. Instead of every transaction going onto the blockchain, they can open a payment channel: locking some bitcoin in a shared multisig address, then transacting between themselves off-chain as much as they like, and only settling the final balance to the blockchain when done. While the channel is open, Alice and Bob can send each other bitcoin thousands of times without a single transaction touching the blockchain. Only two on-chain transactions happen: one to open the channel, one to close it.

Multisig 2-of-2: the foundation of a channel

Behind every payment channel is a 2-of-2 multisig. Unlike a regular multisig like in P2SH that can be 2-of-3 or 3-of-5 with tolerance for one party being absent, Lightning’s multisig has no tolerance at all. Both parties must sign to close the channel cooperatively. This isn’t a weakness, it’s a deliberate design. No single party can unilaterally take the funds except through a previously agreed mechanism.

Commitment transaction

Every time the balance changes within the channel, Alice and Bob exchange commitment transactions: unbroadcast transactions representing the current balance distribution. If one party wants to exit the channel, they can broadcast the latest commitment transaction to the blockchain.

Three channel-closing scenarios

First, cooperative close: both parties agree, sign a closing transaction together, the funds are split immediately according to the final balance. This is the most efficient. Second, force close: one party disappears or won’t cooperate. The honest party can unilaterally broadcast the latest commitment transaction, but has to wait for a time-lock to finish before they can take their funds. Third, penalty for cheating: if someone tries to broadcast an old commitment transaction that’s more favorable to themselves, the other party has a time window to detect it and broadcast the revocation key. The result: the cheating party loses all of their funds in the channel.

The incentive that makes cheating irrational

If Alice tries to cheat by broadcasting an old state, Bob can take all the funds in the channel as a penalty, not just his own. Alice loses everything. This makes cheating very expensive and economically irrational.

But what if Bob is asleep?

This is where the whole penalty mechanism has a condition we have not named yet. Bob can only punish Alice if he sees that old state appear on the blockchain, and he has to see it before Alice’s timelock expires, usually about a day. If Bob’s node is down, his phone is out of battery, or he is away for a week, Alice can cheat and simply get away with it.

This is not a theoretical gap. It is the clearest difference between on-chain Bitcoin and Lightning. Ordinary Bitcoin asks nothing of you once a transaction is confirmed: you can disappear for ten years and the coins are still yours. Lightning demands presence, because its security rests on someone watching within a fixed window of time.

The answer is a watchtower, a service that watches the blockchain on your behalf. You hand it a small encrypted blob for every state you revoke. That blob tells the watchtower nothing about who you are, what your balance is, or which channels you hold. It only becomes useful if a matching old state actually shows up on the blockchain, and at that moment the watchtower can assemble the penalty transaction and broadcast it for you.

The interesting part is that you do not have to trust it. A watchtower cannot steal your funds, cannot open your channels, and learns nothing at all as long as nobody cheats. Its worst failure mode is simply doing nothing, which leaves you exactly where you would have been without one. That is why many users register with several watchtowers at once.

So the earlier claim that cheating is irrational needs one honest addition: cheating is irrational as long as someone is watching. Providing that watcher, whether through an always-on node or through a watchtower, is the price Lightning pays for its speed.

Payment channels weren’t a Lightning Network invention. The seed of it was already in the earliest Bitcoin code: Satoshi included an nSequence-based transaction replacement mechanism that he explained in correspondence, not in the whitepaper. The idea was then developed further by several researchers before Lightning. Why that early mechanism failed to work is something we cover in 15.3. What Lightning did was connect many channels into a network that can route payments between parties that don’t have a direct channel.

Chapter 7 · 7.3
Pay anyone, through anyone, without trust
Routing and HTLC

A payment channel between two parties is already powerful. But imagine this: Alice wants to pay Carol, but Alice and Carol don’t have a direct channel. Should they open a new channel just for one transaction? Of course not. Lightning has a more elegant way.

Pay through an intermediary

If Alice has a channel to Bob, and Bob has a channel to Carol, Alice can pay Carol through Bob. Bob becomes the intermediary. No new channel needed, no on-chain interaction at all. But this immediately raises a very natural question: why should Alice trust Bob? What if Bob takes Alice’s money but doesn’t forward it to Carol? The answer: Alice doesn’t need to trust Bob at all. This is what makes Lightning extraordinary.

Key and secret

Imagine a padlock with a unique key. Carol made that padlock, and only Carol has its key. Carol gives a photo of that padlock to Alice, but keeps the key for herself. Alice says to Bob: "I’ll give you 0.01 BTC, but only if you can show the key that opens this padlock. If within 24 hours you can’t show it, the money comes back to me." Bob knows that Carol has the key. So Bob says to Carol: "I’ll give you 0.01 BTC, but only if you show me that key. If within 12 hours there’s none, the money comes back to me." Carol shows her key to Bob, takes 0.01 BTC. Bob now has that key, shows it to Alice, takes 0.01 BTC. Done.

In technical terms: HTLC

This "padlock and key" mechanism in the Bitcoin world is called an HTLC, short for Hash Time-Locked Contract. The "padlock" is the hash of a secret. The "key" is the secret itself. HTLC isn’t new technology. It’s ordinary Bitcoin Script, a combination of OP_HASH160 which we learned in Chapter 6 and OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY which is covered in full in Chapter 15. Lightning doesn’t change Bitcoin, it just makes use of what already exists.

Why is Bob’s timelock shorter than Alice’s?

Alice gives Bob 24 hours, but Bob gives Carol 12 hours. This isn’t a coincidence. Bob needs enough time to react after Carol reveals her key. If the times were the same, Bob might not have time to claim from Alice before the time-lock expires. The longer the chain of intermediaries, the more tiered the time-locks become.

Privacy through onion routing

Each intermediary only knows one thing: where the payment came from and where to forward it. Bob knows he received from Alice and must forward to Carol, but Bob doesn’t know whether Alice is the original sender or whether Carol is the final recipient. This technique is called onion routing, the same as what Tor uses.

HTLC is one of the most elegant cryptographic constructions in Bitcoin. It allows a payment to pass through many intermediaries that don’t trust each other, without any single intermediary being able to steal the funds. Everything is guaranteed by mathematics, not trust.

Chapter 7 · 7.4
What actually happens on-chain?
Opening and Closing Channels

In 7.2 we saw the three channel-closing scenarios conceptually. Now we look at the technical side: which transactions actually get broadcast to the blockchain, in what order, and at what cost.

Opening a channel: the funding transaction

Opening a channel is a single ordinary Bitcoin transaction. Alice and Bob each contribute funds to a 2-of-2 multisig output. This output is called the funding output. Before the funding transaction is broadcast to the network, Alice and Bob must already have exchanged their first commitment transaction. This is important: if the funding transaction is broadcast without a valid commitment transaction and one party suddenly becomes uncooperative, the funds could be trapped forever. So the order is: create the commitment transaction first, then broadcast the funding transaction.

Three ways to close a channel

First, cooperative close: both parties agree to close the channel. They sign a closing transaction together that immediately splits the funds according to the final balance. This is the best way: fast, cheap, and no need to wait for a time-lock. Second, force close: one party can’t be reached or won’t cooperate. The honest party broadcasts the latest commitment transaction. There’s a time-lock that must be waited out before the funds can be taken, usually a few hundred blocks. This gives time for the other party to detect any cheating. Third, penalty close: if someone broadcasts an expired commitment transaction, the honest party can broadcast a justice transaction and take all the funds in the channel as a penalty.

The cost of opening and closing a channel

Every time a channel is opened, there’s one on-chain transaction. Every time a channel is closed, there’s one more on-chain transaction. So the on-chain cost is always two transaction fees, no matter how many transactions happen within the channel. This is what makes Lightning very economical for routine use: pay for thousands of transactions with only two on-chain fees.

Channel capacity and liquidity

A channel has limited capacity. If Alice opens a channel with 0.1 BTC, she can’t send more than 0.1 BTC through that channel in total. Liquidity is a resource that must be managed carefully in the Lightning Network.

Opening a channel is an economic decision: how long it will be used, how much capacity is needed, and how much on-chain fee one is willing to pay. For casual users, modern Lightning wallets manage this automatically through channels managed by service providers.

Chapter 7 · 7.5
Scan, confirm, done — in one second
Invoices and Payments

So far we’ve understood how channels work and how payments can be routed. But how does an everyday user actually make a payment on Lightning? The answer is the invoice.

What is an invoice?

An invoice is a payment request created by the recipient. It contains all the information the sender needs to complete the payment: the amount to be paid, the hash of the HTLC secret, the recipient’s node ID, and the invoice’s validity period. An invoice is usually represented as a long text string starting with lnbc (for mainnet) or a QR code that can be scanned. The format is called BOLT-11, one of the Lightning protocol standards.

The payment flow

Carol wants to receive 0.001 BTC from Alice. Carol creates an invoice. Behind the scenes, Carol creates a secret R and computes H = hash(R), then puts H into the invoice. Carol shares the invoice with Alice via QR code or copy-paste. Alice opens the invoice in her wallet. The wallet automatically finds the best route to Carol. Alice confirms. The wallet performs HTLC payment routing. Carol reveals R to claim the payment. From the user’s point of view: scan QR, confirm, done. Less than one second.

Weaknesses of the classic invoice

BOLT-11 invoices have some limitations. First, single-use: each invoice can only be paid once. Second, the recipient has to be online when the payment arrives to reveal R. Third, there’s no proof of payment that a third party can verify.

BOLT-12: offers

A new, developing standard, BOLT-12, introduces the concept of an "offer": a static code that can be used many times. When a sender wants to pay, their wallet contacts the recipient’s node to request a new, unique invoice. This solves the single-use problem and enables recurring payments like subscriptions.

LNURL: one address, used many times

Outside the BOLT standard, there’s another approach already widely used: LNURL. Unlike the one-time BOLT-11 invoice, LNURL is an HTTP-based protocol that lets the sender’s wallet request a new invoice each time it wants to pay, from just one static address. This means the recipient can share a single code or address like name@domain.com, and the sender can pay repeatedly without the recipient needing to create a new invoice each time. Using lnbc (BOLT-11) is still far more common in everyday transactions, but LNURL exists as a practical solution for cases like donations, tips, or recurring payments.

A Lightning invoice is the interface between a complex protocol and a user who just wants to scan and pay. Behind that simple QR code hides the payment hash, routing hints, and a cryptographic signature. Good abstraction makes complicated technology feel like magic.

Chapter 7 · 7.6
There’s no perfect solution — only honest trade-offs
Lightning’s Limitations and Trade-offs

The Lightning Network is an extraordinary technology, but not a perfect solution. Understanding its limitations is as important as understanding its strengths.

Locked liquidity

To open a channel, a user has to lock bitcoin inside it. This locked bitcoin can’t be used for anything else while the channel is open. For nodes that do routing, they have to lock liquidity in many channels at once. This is idle capital.

The inbound liquidity problem

If Alice opens a channel to Bob with 0.1 BTC, the entire capacity is on Alice’s side. Bob can’t send to Alice until Alice sends something to Bob first. To receive payments, a user needs inbound liquidity: a channel that has capacity on the recipient’s side. Getting inbound liquidity isn’t always easy and often costs money.

The need to be online

To receive payments on classic Lightning, the recipient’s node has to be online. If a phone is off when someone tries to pay, the payment fails. This differs from on-chain Bitcoin where the recipient doesn’t need to be online. BOLT-12 offers are starting to address this, but aren’t yet fully widespread.

Watchtower: delegating monitoring

To detect cheating, a user has to monitor the blockchain periodically. If a node is offline too long, a cheating party can broadcast an old state undetected. The solution is a watchtower: a third-party service that monitors the blockchain on the user’s behalf. But this introduces a new element of trust.

Routing doesn’t always succeed

Finding a route that has enough liquidity at every hop is a hard problem. Large payments often fail because there’s no route with enough capacity. Lightning works very well for small, routine payments, but is less suited for large value transfers.

Honest trade-offs

Lightning isn’t a replacement for on-chain Bitcoin. It’s a layer on top of it for frequent, small, and fast payments. For large, final payments that require maximum security, on-chain is still more appropriate. Both serve different needs.

Every technology has trade-offs. What matters is understanding those trade-offs and choosing the right tool for the right need. Lightning isn’t a better Bitcoin. Lightning is Bitcoin extended for a different use case.

Chapter 8 · 8.1
Thousands of computers enforcing the rules without a leader
What is a Bitcoin Node?

When people talk about "Bitcoin", they often only think about the price or the wallet. But behind all of that are thousands of computers around the world that keep running, verifying every transaction and storing a complete copy of the blockchain. These computers are called nodes.

A node is the keeper of the rules

A Bitcoin node isn’t just a database. It’s the keeper of the consensus rules. Every node independently verifies every transaction and every block using the same rules. No one can force it to accept an invalid block, even if that block comes from the largest miner. This is the heart of Bitcoin’s decentralization: there’s no central authority that decides what’s valid. Every node decides for itself, based on the same rules.

Types of nodes

A full node stores the entire blockchain from the genesis block to today, more than 700 GB as of mid-2026 and growing by tens of GB each year. It independently verifies every transaction and block. This is the node that provides the highest security. A pruned node is a full node that has deleted old data after verifying it. It still verifies all the rules, but only stores a few GB of the latest blocks. An SPV node only downloads block headers, it doesn’t fully verify transactions. A mining node is a full node that also actively mines new blocks.

Why run your own node?

Running your own full node means you don’t have to trust anyone. No SPV can deceive you with fake transactions if you have your own node. No exchange or wallet provider can hide information. This isn’t just about individual security. The more people run full nodes, the harder it is for anyone to change Bitcoin’s rules without majority agreement. A node is a vote in Bitcoin’s democracy.

Running a full node doesn’t require special hardware. A Raspberry Pi with an external hard drive is enough. The cost is less than a million rupiah, and its contribution to Bitcoin’s decentralization is real.

Chapter 8 · 8.2
No center, no single point of failure
The P2P Network

Bitcoin has no central server. No headquarters, no data center that can be shut down, no single point that, if attacked, would destroy everything. What exists is a peer-to-peer network: thousands of nodes connected directly to each other.

What is a P2P network?

In a traditional network like a bank or social media, there is a central server that serves all clients. If the server goes down, no client can connect. If the server owner decides to block someone, there is nothing to be done. A P2P network is different. Every participant is equal, none more "central" than another. Information spreads from node to node like gossip. There is no single point of failure.

How do nodes connect?

When a Bitcoin node first starts up, it needs to find peers to connect to. There are several ways: DNS seeds (servers that provide a list of active nodes), hardcoded seed nodes (a list of IPs embedded in the software), and peer exchange (asking an already-connected node to introduce it to other peers). Once connected, the node maintains about 8 regular outbound connections plus 2 block-only ones, and fills the rest with inbound connections. Bitcoin Core caps total connections at 125, which leaves roughly 115 slots for inbound.

How does information spread?

When Alice sends a transaction, her wallet broadcasts that transaction to its connected nodes. A node receives the transaction, verifies its validity, and forwards it to all its peers. Those peers do the same. Within seconds, the transaction has spread to thousands of nodes around the world. This process is called gossiping. Each node only forwards valid transactions.

Why does P2P make Bitcoin strong?

To censor Bitcoin, an attacker would have to block the connection to every node in the world. As long as there’s one accessible node, Bitcoin can be used. Bitcoin has been blocked in various countries, but users there continue to access the network through VPN, Tor, or satellite connections like Blockstream Satellite.

Decentralization isn’t a feature that can be added later. It’s Bitcoin’s fundamental architecture from day one. The P2P network isn’t just how Bitcoin operates, it’s the reason Bitcoin can’t be stopped.

Chapter 8 · 8.3
From one wallet to thousands of nodes in seconds
Transaction Propagation

You press send in your wallet. What happens next?

From wallet to network

The wallet creates a signed transaction and broadcasts it to one or several connected nodes. The first node to receive this transaction is called the origin node from the user’s point of view, even though the network doesn’t really record it that way.

Verification before forwarding

A node that receives a transaction doesn’t forward it right away. It performs a series of verifications first: is the transaction format valid, is the cryptographic signature correct, do the UTXOs being used really exist and are unspent, is the fee reasonable. If everything passes, the transaction enters that node’s mempool and is forwarded to all its peers. If verification fails, the transaction is discarded and not forwarded. This is a natural defense mechanism: spam and invalid transactions die at the first node that receives them.

Node policy vs consensus rules

There is an important distinction that is often misunderstood: consensus rules and node policy are two different things. Consensus rules are the rules that determine whether a transaction or block is valid by protocol. All nodes must agree on these, otherwise they will fork. Node policy is an individual node’s decision about which transactions it wants to accept into the mempool and forward to peers, regardless of whether the transaction is valid by consensus or not.

A concrete example: datacarrier and datacarriersize are two node policy settings available in node software such as Bitcoin Core and Bitcoin Knots. datacarrier controls whether the node will forward transactions that use OP_RETURN to embed arbitrary data. datacarriersize sets the maximum size of that data in bytes. That number is not a protocol rule — its default differs across implementations and has changed between versions. The long-standing convention was 83 bytes (80 bytes of data), and since 2025 it has been at the center of a major debate: one camp wants to relax relay limits, the other wants to keep the filters. Every node operator is free to set their own value. A node that turns off datacarrier will not put OP_RETURN transactions into its mempool and will not forward them to other peers. But if a miner still includes that transaction in a block, the node still accepts the block because OP_RETURN transactions are valid by consensus. Policy stops at the mempool, not at block validation.

This is also the basis of the debate about Ocean Pool that we discuss in Chapter 11: that pool applies transaction filtering based on their own policy, not because the filtered transactions are invalid. A single node or pool can choose a different policy from the majority without violating consensus, but the consequence is that the transactions they reject still end up on the blockchain through miners or other nodes that don’t apply the same filtering.

Flooding and deduplication

Transaction propagation uses a flooding mechanism: every node that receives a valid transaction forwards it to all peers. But this creates a problem because a node can receive the same transaction from many peers at the same time. The solution is deduplication. Each node keeps a list of transactions it has already seen. If the same transaction comes again, it is immediately discarded without being reprocessed.

How long until it reaches the whole network?

Under normal conditions, a transaction spreads to most nodes around the world in less than 5 seconds. Reaching 90% of nodes usually takes about 10-15 seconds. This is well before the transaction is confirmed on the blockchain, which takes an average of 10 minutes.

Privacy in propagation

There is an interesting privacy issue: the first node to broadcast a transaction is most likely the original sender or directly connected to it. An observer monitoring many nodes can try to identify the transaction’s origin. The most widely discussed solution for this is Dandelion++: the transaction is first forwarded quietly along a single path (stem phase) before finally being spread to the whole network (fluff phase). This makes the transaction’s origin much harder to trace. Worth noting, Dandelion++ has not been merged into Bitcoin Core, and we cover why in 18.6.

Transaction propagation is one of the most elegant processes in Bitcoin. Thousands of nodes that don’t know each other, no central coordination, but within seconds the information has spread to every corner of the world. All because every node follows the same rules.

Chapter 8 · 8.4
A new block must spread as fast as possible — milliseconds mean money
Block Propagation

Transaction propagation and block propagation have the same goal: spreading information to the whole network as fast as possible. But a block is much larger than a transaction, and the stakes are much higher: a miner who finds a new block wants the whole network to recognize it as fast as possible before another miner finds the next block.

From miner to network

When a miner finds a valid nonce, it immediately broadcasts the new block to all its peers. Every node that receives the block performs full verification: is the proof of work valid, are all the transactions inside it valid, does the block header connect to the previous block correctly. If everything passes, the block is accepted, added to the local chain, and forwarded to all peers.

The problem: blocks are too big

A Bitcoin block can be up to 4 MB with SegWit weight. Spreading 4 MB to thousands of nodes requires significant bandwidth. In Bitcoin’s early days this wasn’t a problem because blocks were rarely full. But when the network is busy, propagation delay can cause serious problems.

Compact Block and Header-First

The main solution is Compact Block (BIP 152): instead of sending the entire block, a node sends the block header plus a list of shortened transaction IDs. The recipient most likely already has almost all of those transactions in its mempool. It only needs to request the transactions it doesn’t yet have. This reduces the data sent drastically, from megabytes to kilobytes. Header-First propagation is another technique: a node broadcasts the block header first before the entire block is ready, allowing proof of work validation to start earlier.

Orphan blocks and why speed matters

There is a phenomenon called an orphan block: two miners find a valid block at almost the same time. The network is temporarily split into two versions of the chain. Eventually the longer chain wins, and the block in the shorter chain becomes an orphan, valid but not recognized. The slower the propagation, the greater the chance of an orphan block. Compact Block has already significantly reduced the orphan rate.

Block propagation speed is one of the most important health metrics of the Bitcoin network. Thanks to Compact Block, a new block can reach most of the network within seconds. In the era before Compact Block, the same process took many times longer because the entire contents of a block had to be resent to every peer.

⚠️ Block 840,001B is an orphan block. It’s cryptographically valid — its proof of work is correct, the transactions inside it are legitimate. But because the chain containing 840,001A is longer, the whole network chooses that chain. Miner B loses its entire block reward.
Why does Compact Block reduce the orphan rate?
A regular block takes several seconds to spread to the whole network. During that window, other miners who haven’t received the new block keep mining on top of the old block, increasing orphan risk. Compact Block shortens this window to less than 1 second and the orphan risk drops drastically.
What happens to the transactions in an orphan block?
The transactions in an orphan block are returned to the mempool and can be confirmed in the next block. No bitcoin is lost. The only one who loses is the miner who found the orphan block.
Chapter 8 · 8.5
How does a new node find its place in the network?
Connections and Peer Discovery

In 8.2 we mentioned three ways a node finds peers. This section takes each of them apart, because this is where one of the answers lives to why Bitcoin is so hard to block.

A new Bitcoin node starting up for the first time faces one fundamental problem: how does it find other nodes to connect to? It doesn’t know anyone’s address. The P2P network has no centralized directory. But within minutes, that new node is already connected to dozens of peers around the world.

DNS Seed

The first and most common way is through a DNS seed. Bitcoin node software, like Bitcoin Core, Bitcoin Knots, or other implementations, generally embeds a few special domain names in its code. When a node first starts, it does a DNS query to these domains and gets a list of IP addresses of nodes that are currently active. DNS seeds are managed by trusted people in the Bitcoin community. This isn’t a dangerous trust point because the node only uses it to find initial peers, and after that all verification is done independently.

Peer Exchange

After connecting to the first few nodes, the new node can request a list of known peers through the getaddr message. A node that receives this request replies with an addr message containing a list of IP addresses of other nodes it knows. From here the network of connections grows organically without central coordination.

Hardcoded Seeds

If the DNS seed can’t be reached, there’s a fallback: a list of IP addresses embedded directly in the software code. These are nodes known to be stable and long-running. This list is updated every few releases by each development team.

Maintaining connections

A Bitcoin node generally maintains about 8 outbound connections that it chooses itself and accepts inbound connections from other peers. Connections are kept alive with periodic ping and pong messages. A node that doesn’t respond is disconnected and replaced. A node also stores a peer address database locally so that when it’s shut down and started again, it can connect directly to known peers without having to start peer discovery from scratch.

Why is this important for decentralization?

Bitcoin’s peer discovery system is designed not to depend on a single point. The DNS seed can fail or be blocked, but there are still hardcoded seeds. Hardcoded seeds can become outdated, but there’s still the peer database from previous sessions. And if all of that fails, the user can enter a peer address manually.

One of the most effective ways to support the Bitcoin network is to run a node with open inbound connections. A node like this helps new nodes find peers and strengthens the network’s resilience as a whole.
