Chapter 8 · 8.6
Technical and social, both equally important
Keeping the Network Healthy

A healthy Bitcoin network isn’t just about the number of nodes. It’s about the quality of connections, diversity of locations, diversity of software, and the often-forgotten one: the diversity of the humans behind those nodes.

The network’s technical health

There are several technical health indicators that can be monitored. The number of reachable full nodes is the most basic indicator. The more there are, the stronger it is. The geographic distribution of nodes is also important: a network whose nodes are all concentrated in one country is far more vulnerable to regulation or an internet outage than a network spread evenly around the world. Software diversity is also crucial. If almost all nodes run the same implementation, a critical bug in that implementation could affect the network widely.

What you can do as a node runner

First, leave inbound connections open. A node that accepts inbound connections helps new nodes find peers and strengthens the network. Second, keep uptime up. A node that’s frequently offline doesn’t contribute much. A small device running 24 hours is far more valuable than a computer that only turns on occasionally. Third, update the software regularly, not because you follow one development team, but because security patches are important to protect yourself and the network.

The network’s social health

This is the part that is often ignored but just as important. Node runners are the people most committed to Bitcoin. They spend time, money, and energy running the infrastructure that makes Bitcoin work. And precisely because of that great commitment, debates among them can become very heated.

Debates about block size, mempool policy, soft forks, software choice, how to operate a node: all of these are legitimate and important debates. Disagreement is healthy. Disagreement is a sign that many people are thinking independently, not just following one leader.

But there’s a difference between disagreeing and being disrespectful. Someone can have a different opinion about mempool policy while still respecting that another person has spent time and energy running their own node. Someone can criticize a technical decision without attacking the person’s character.

The ecosystem isn’t a monolith

Bitcoin is an open protocol. No single entity can claim full authority over it. No single development team, no single software implementation, no single discussion forum holds the single truth. This isn’t a weakness. It’s one of Bitcoin’s greatest strengths. As long as people with different views can still find common ground in running the network, Bitcoin will keep surviving.

Running a node is a real action, not just an opinion on the internet. Whatever debate is happening out there, a node that stays on is a contribution that always matters. And treating fellow node runners with respect, even when you disagree, is part of keeping the network healthy.

Chapter 9 · 9.1
A waiting room with no center
What is the Mempool?

We met the mempool in 3.5 as one stage in a transaction’s journey. Now we stop there for longer, because the mempool is more than a waiting room: it is where the price of a transaction gets decided.

Every Bitcoin transaction that has been sent but not yet confirmed lives in a waiting room. This waiting room is called the mempool, short for memory pool. Every node has its own mempool, and there is no single "global mempool".

A waiting room with no center

Because every node manages its own mempool, two different nodes can have slightly different mempool contents. Node A might have received a transaction that hasn’t reached Node B yet. Node C might have already removed a transaction that’s still in Node D because of memory limits. This is normal and intentional. The mempool isn’t a synchronized global database, it’s a collection of transactions waiting for confirmation at each node independently.

What gets into the mempool?

Not all transactions are automatically accepted into the mempool. Every node has its own rules called mempool policy. Common rules that apply at most nodes: the transaction must be cryptographically valid, the UTXOs used must exist and be unspent, the fee must meet a minimum threshold, and the transaction size must be within a reasonable limit. If a transaction doesn’t meet the requirements, it’s rejected and doesn’t enter that node’s mempool.

How long can a transaction stay in the mempool?

A transaction that isn’t confirmed within a certain time is removed from the mempool. Most nodes remove transactions that are more than two weeks old. If a transaction is removed from the mempool before being confirmed, the funds aren’t lost. The UTXOs used return to their original state and the transaction can be rebroadcast.

The mempool and the fee market

The mempool is where the fee market forms naturally. Space in every block is limited. Miners choose which transactions to include in a block, and they have an economic incentive to choose the transactions with the highest fees. When the mempool is busy, users who want fast confirmation have to compete with higher fees.

The mempool is one of the most frequently misunderstood components of Bitcoin. Many people panic when they see their transaction stuck in the mempool. But as long as the transaction is valid and its fee is reasonable, it will be confirmed, whether now or later when the network is quieter.

Chapter 9 · 9.2
It’s not the biggest fee that wins, but the highest fee rate
Fee Rate and Priority

In the mempool, all transactions compete to get into the next block. But it’s not the transaction with the largest total fee that’s prioritized. What’s prioritized is the transaction with the highest fee rate.

What is fee rate?

Fee rate is the fee divided by the transaction size. Its unit is satoshi per virtual byte, written sat/vB. A transaction with a 1,000 satoshi fee and a size of 200 vbytes has a fee rate of 5 sat/vB. Another transaction with a 500 satoshi fee but a size of 50 vbytes has a fee rate of 10 sat/vB and will be prioritized higher, even though its total fee is smaller. This is logical from the miner’s point of view: a block has limited capacity in weight/vbytes, not in number of transactions. The miner wants to maximize revenue per unit of available space.

Virtual byte vs byte

Since SegWit was introduced, transaction size is measured in virtual bytes (vbytes) rather than ordinary bytes. Witness data (signatures) gets a 75% discount: every 4 bytes of witness counts as 1 vbyte. This is an incentive for users to use SegWit addresses because their transactions are lighter and their fee rate is more competitive for the same fee.

How do miners choose transactions?

Miners sort all transactions in the mempool by fee rate, from highest to lowest, then fill the block from the top until capacity runs out. In practice it’s more complex because there are dependencies between transactions: transaction B that uses the output of transaction A must come after A. But the basic principle holds: the highest fee rate means the highest priority.

What’s the right fee rate?

There’s no exact number. The right fee rate depends on how busy the mempool is at the time and how fast the transaction needs to be confirmed. When the mempool is quiet, even 1 sat/vB can be confirmed in the next block. When the mempool is very busy, fee rate can reach hundreds of sat/vB. Tools like mempool.space help you see the mempool conditions in real time.

Understanding fee rate is a basic skill every Bitcoin user needs. Too low and the transaction can be stuck for weeks. Too high and you pay more than you need to.

Chapter 9 · 9.3
Transaction stuck? There are two ways to fix it
RBF and CPFP

The transaction has been sent but its fee is too low and it’s stuck in the mempool. What can be done? There are two mechanisms that let a user speed up a transaction that’s already been sent: RBF and CPFP.

RBF: Replace-By-Fee

RBF lets the sender replace an unconfirmed transaction with a new version that has a higher fee. The new transaction uses the same UTXOs but pays a larger fee, so miners are more interested in including it in a block. To be replaceable, the original transaction must mark itself as replaceable by setting the sequence number to a certain value. This is called opt-in RBF. A node that receives the replacement transaction discards the old one and replaces it with the new, as long as the new transaction meets the requirements: a higher fee and a higher fee rate than the original.

Full RBF

There’s also full RBF, where a node accepts a transaction replacement even if the original transaction didn’t mark itself as replaceable. This is controversial because it touches the assumption that an unconfirmed transaction can be considered safe for small payments.

CPFP: Child Pays for Parent

CPFP is a different mechanism. If the original transaction (parent) is stuck because of a low fee, the recipient can create a new transaction (child) that uses the output of the parent transaction, with a very high fee. A miner who wants to take the fee from the child transaction has to include the parent transaction first because the child depends on the parent. Effectively, the high fee from the child subsidizes the confirmation of the low-fee parent. The miner calculates the combined fee rate of the parent+child package and compares it with other transactions in the mempool.

When to use RBF vs CPFP?

RBF is used by a sender who wants to replace their own transaction. CPFP can be used by a recipient, who can’t change a transaction that’s already been sent to them but can create a new transaction that pulls the parent into a block.

RBF and CPFP are proof that Bitcoin can be very flexible when it comes to fee management. Two different mechanisms to solve the same problem, with different trade-offs and assumptions. Understanding both makes users far more confident in managing their transactions.

The other side of that flexibility

Flexibility always has another side. The same rules that let you speed up your own transaction can be turned around to hold someone else’s in place. It is called transaction pinning.

The key is something we already covered in 9.1: the mempool is not part of consensus. It is simply each node’s policy about what it is willing to keep and relay. That policy has practical limits, such as how many descendant transactions may hang off a single unconfirmed one. Those limits exist to protect nodes from being flooded. But the same limits can be used to trap.

The shape of the attack is roughly this. The attacker creates a very large, very low-fee child transaction attached to the one they want to obstruct. The combination is too unattractive to mine, yet it has already filled the mempool policy quota. As a result the victim can no longer replace or accelerate their transaction, because the replacement is rejected by a policy that is already full. The transaction is not cancelled, it is simply pinned in place, stuck with no way to push it forward.

For an ordinary payment this is annoying. For Lightning it is dangerous. Recall from 7.2 that the penalty against cheating only works if the penalty transaction can reach the blockchain before the timelock expires. If an attacker can pin that transaction in the mempool until the deadline passes, the punishment mechanism that looked so solid in the simulation becomes powerless. The cryptography was not broken. The road to the blockchain was blocked.

This is a good illustration of two different layers of security. Chapter 4 dealt with security resting on mathematics, and mathematics does not negotiate. But at the mempool layer what governs is not mathematics but policy, and policy can always be exploited by someone who reads it more carefully than the people who wrote it.

So the fixes live at the policy layer too, not in consensus. One is package relay, which has nodes evaluate a transaction together with its descendants as a single package rather than one at a time, so that a low-fee transaction accompanied by a high-fee child is no longer turned away at the gate. Another is restricting the shape of transactions used by protocols like Lightning, so that the room an attacker has to attach a giant descendant becomes much narrower.

It is worth noting that fixes of this kind need no soft fork, because no consensus rule changes. Nodes simply update their policy. That makes them easier to deploy, but it also means the protection depends on how many nodes actually update.

Chapter 9 · 9.4
Why fees suddenly spike and what can be done
The Mempool When the Network is Busy

There are certain times when the Bitcoin mempool becomes very busy. Thousands of transactions pile up, fee rate spikes, and users paying low fees have to wait hours or even days. Understanding when and why this happens lets you anticipate and make better decisions.

What causes the mempool to get busy?

A busy mempool happens when the rate of incoming transactions exceeds the block capacity that can be confirmed. Every block has a capacity of about 4 million weight units. A weight unit is the formal unit of block capacity, and its relationship to the vbyte we used in 9.2 is simple: 1 vbyte equals 4 weight units. So 4 million weight units is the same as 1 million vbytes. Because witness data counts as a quarter, a single block can hold more raw bytes than that figure suggests, typically around 1.5 to 2.5 MB in practice. With an average block time of 10 minutes, the network generally processes about 3 to 7 transactions per second, depending on which transaction types dominate at the time. Some events that historically caused mempool spikes: the launch of Ordinals and Inscriptions in 2023, a bull market driving high trading activity, halving events that triggered massive speculation, and spam attacks that deliberately flooded the network with low-cost transactions.

What happens to low-fee transactions?

When the mempool is busy, miners can easily fill an entire block with only high-fee transactions. Low-fee transactions are pushed to the bottom of the queue and might not be confirmed for days. Some nodes will even drop low-fee transactions from their mempool to save memory, even though the transactions are valid.

How do you read mempool conditions?

There are several metrics that can be monitored. The mempool size in MB or the number of transactions shows how busy the queue is right now. The fee rate for confirmation within 1 block, 3 blocks, and 6 blocks shows how much you need to pay for different speeds. Tools like mempool.space display these visualizations in real time and are very helpful.

Strategies for dealing with a busy mempool

If it’s not urgent, wait until the mempool is quiet. Usually weekends or the middle of the night in Asia are quieter than peak hours. If you’ve already sent with a low fee, use RBF or CPFP. If you want to send a new transaction, monitor the mempool conditions first and use an accurate fee estimator.

A busy mempool isn’t a sign that Bitcoin is broken. It’s actually a sign that Bitcoin works exactly as designed: a free market that determines the price of block space based on demand. What you need to do is understand how it works and use it wisely.

Chapter 9 · 9.5
What’s the right fee for this situation?
Fee Estimation

Determining the right fee for a Bitcoin transaction isn’t an exact science. Too low and the transaction can be stuck. Too high and you waste money. Fee estimation is the process of estimating the minimum fee rate needed for a transaction to be confirmed within a certain target time.

How does a fee estimator work?

A good fee estimator analyzes the current mempool conditions and historical confirmation data to predict what fee rate is needed. There are two main approaches. The first is mempool-based: looking at the distribution of fee rates in the current mempool and estimating how many blocks are needed to clear the queue down to a certain fee level. The second is history-based: analyzing historical confirmation data to build a prediction model based on similar mempool conditions.

Confirmation target

Users can usually choose a confirmation target: next block (fastest, most expensive), 3 blocks (about 30 minutes), 6 blocks (about 1 hour), or even 1-2 days for non-urgent ones. The fee estimator gives the recommended fee rate for each target.

Limitations of fee estimators

Fee estimators have some important weaknesses. First, the mempool can change very fast so an accurate estimate from 5 minutes ago can already be irrelevant. Second, an estimator can’t predict a block that happens to be empty due to mining luck. Third, some wallets use a fee estimator that’s outdated or too conservative, so they always recommend a fee that’s too high.

Fee sniping

There’s also an interesting phenomenon called fee sniping: a situation where a miner might be more interested in re-mining a previous block that had high fees than mining a new block. This is addressed with a time-lock on transactions to ensure a transaction is only valid at a certain block height or higher.

Good fee estimation is a combination of real-time data and an understanding of how the mempool works. Tools like mempool.space provide the data needed, but it still takes human judgment to read the situation correctly, especially when mempool conditions are changing fast.

Chapter 9 · 9.6
When the block reward runs out, who pays the miners?
The Future of the Fee Market

Bitcoin is designed so that the block reward keeps decreasing with every halving. Eventually, around the year 2140, all 21 million bitcoin will have been mined and the block reward becomes zero. The only compensation for miners is transaction fees. This is one of the most fundamental questions about Bitcoin’s long-term sustainability.

Are fees enough to replace the block reward?

This is an open question with no definite answer yet. The optimistic camp argues that as Bitcoin adoption spreads, transaction volume will keep increasing. More transactions means more competition for block space, which means a higher fee rate. The Lightning Network and other layers don’t eliminate on-chain fees: every channel opening and closing still needs an on-chain transaction. The skeptical camp argues that the pressure for efficiency is always there. Transaction batching, SegWit, Taproot, and other technologies keep reducing transaction size. If fees are too low, miners will go out of business, hash rate drops, and network security is threatened.

Fee market and security

There’s a direct relationship between the fee market and network security that’s often misunderstood. Many people think: if miners leave, the difficulty adjustment will adjust, so the network stays secure. This is partly true, but misses the more important point.

The difficulty adjustment does ensure the network keeps functioning. If hash rate drops 50%, difficulty drops 50%, and block time returns to 10 minutes. Transactions keep being confirmed, the network doesn’t stop. What the difficulty adjustment doesn’t do is make an attack more expensive. Quite the opposite: if hash rate drops because miners aren’t profitable, the cost of launching a 51% attack drops proportionally too.

The analogy is simple: imagine a building’s security system. If half the guards are fired because the budget ran out, the building stays open and people can still enter. But that building is far easier to rob. The difficulty adjustment is a mechanism that ensures the building stays open, not a mechanism that maintains the number of guards. This is why a healthy fee market isn’t just about user convenience. It’s the foundation of long-term network security.

Not all fees last equally long

Not all demand for block space is equal in value over the long term. The healthiest demand comes from organic, widespread Bitcoin adoption: the more people transact, the more Lightning channels are opened and closed, the more institutions do on-chain settlement. High fees from these sources are a sign of a healthily growing ecosystem, and this is exactly the desired scenario: millions of ordinary users whose transaction needs create natural competition for block space.

Other sources are seasonal. The Ordinals and Inscriptions wave of 2023 we mentioned in 9.4 is the clearest example: fees spiked for months, then receded. For a security budget that has to hold for decades, spikes like that are hard to lean on, because nobody can guarantee the next wave will arrive.

This is where one of the most heated debates in recent Bitcoin history lives, and you deserve to hear both sides. One side argues that a transaction is a transaction: the Bitcoin protocol has never distinguished by purpose, whoever pays the fee has earned the block space, and miners get paid whether the data is a payment or a picture. The other side argues that block space is finite, and when it fills with things that do not need Bitcoin’s particular properties, people who do need to send money get pushed out by the fee spike.

This book will not decide for you. What you can hold onto as an analytical tool: what determines long-term security is not how high fees are today, but how reliably those fees come back next year and ten years from now. Every time you read news about a fee spike, the useful question is whether this is a wave or a rising tide.

Block space as a commodity

Bitcoin’s block space is a scarce commodity. There’s demand from various legitimate sources: financial transactions, Lightning channel management, layer-two protocols, and applications that provide real value. As long as meaningful demand exceeds capacity, the fee market will stay active organically.

The sustainability of Bitcoin’s fee market is one of the biggest economic experiments that has ever existed. What you can do is understand the incentives involved, distinguish healthy demand from unhealthy, and observe how the market responds over time.

Chapter 10 · 10.1
Bitcoin doesn’t store balances — it stores outputs
What is the UTXO Set?

Bitcoin doesn’t store balances. This is one of the things most often misunderstood by people new to Bitcoin. Your wallet doesn’t have a "balance of 0.5 BTC" stored somewhere. What it has is a collection of unspent transaction outputs that, when added up, give the number we call the balance.

UTXO recap

Every Bitcoin transaction consumes existing UTXOs as inputs and creates new UTXOs as outputs. A UTXO that has been spent can’t be used again. A newly created UTXO waits to be used in a future transaction. The UTXO set is the collection of all UTXOs that currently exist across the entire Bitcoin network, that is, all the outputs that have been created but not yet spent. This is Bitcoin’s current "state".

Why does the UTXO set matter?

The UTXO set is the single source of truth about bitcoin ownership. Every full node stores a complete copy of the UTXO set and updates it each time there’s a new block. When you send a transaction, the node verifies that the UTXOs you claim as input really exist in the UTXO set and haven’t been spent. This is the mechanism that prevents double spending: if you try to use the same UTXO twice, the node will detect that the UTXO no longer exists in the UTXO set after the first transaction is confirmed.

The size of the UTXO set

The UTXO set is far smaller than the full blockchain. The blockchain stores the entire history of all transactions since the genesis block, which as of mid-2026 is already more than 700 GB. The UTXO set only stores unspent outputs, and its size is around 11 GB. This is what allows a full node to verify a new transaction very quickly without having to read the entire blockchain.

The UTXO set and memory

A full node stores the UTXO set in memory or a database optimized for fast access. Each time a new block comes in, the node removes spent UTXOs and adds new ones. This operation must be very efficient because it happens every 10 minutes.

The UTXO set is one of the most elegant designs in Bitcoin. By only storing "what exists now" rather than "everything that ever happened", Bitcoin enables fast and efficient transaction verification without having to read the entire blockchain history.

Chapter 10 · 10.2
Every block changes Bitcoin’s state deterministically
How the UTXO Set is Updated

Each time a new block is added to the blockchain, the UTXO set has to be updated. This is an operation that happens thousands of times a day at every full node across the network, and it must run very efficiently.

Two basic operations

There are two operations that happen when the UTXO set is updated: removal and addition. Every transaction in a block consumes some UTXOs as inputs, and these UTXOs are removed from the set. Every transaction also creates new UTXOs as outputs, and these UTXOs are added to the set. Once all transactions in the block are processed, the UTXO set reflects Bitcoin’s new state.

Processing order

The processing order within a block matters. The first transaction in every block is always the coinbase transaction: a special transaction that has no input and only outputs. This is how the miner gets the block reward plus all the transaction fees in that block. The UTXO from the coinbase transaction is added to the UTXO set, but there’s a special rule: a coinbase UTXO can’t be spent for the next 100 blocks. This is called coinbase maturity. The following transactions are processed in order. If transaction B uses the output of transaction A in the same block, A must appear first. This is called topological ordering.

Rollback during reorganization

Sometimes a chain reorganization happens: a node finds a longer chain that differs from the chain it’s currently following. When this happens, the node has to roll back the UTXO set to its previous state, then apply the blocks from the new chain. This is a complex operation and requires the node to store information about the UTXO set changes in each block so they can be undone.

Database efficiency

The UTXO set is stored in a key-value database optimized for fast lookup. The key is the pair (txid, output index) that uniquely identifies each UTXO. The value is the UTXO data: the amount of satoshi, the script that must be satisfied to spend it, and the block height when the UTXO was created. This lookup must complete within milliseconds because the node has to verify every input of every incoming transaction.

The UTXO set update process is the heart of full node operation. Every node around the world performs the exact same operation when processing the same block, and the result is always identical. From the same state, the same input always produces the same state.

Chapter 10 · 10.3
A node verifies transactions with local data only
The UTXO Set and Transaction Verification

One of the most critical functions of the UTXO set is enabling fast and reliable transaction verification. When a new transaction arrives at a node, the node doesn’t need to read the entire blockchain to verify it. It only needs to check the UTXO set.

What gets verified?

When a node receives a new transaction, several things are checked in order. First, does every UTXO claimed as input actually exist in the UTXO set? If not, the transaction is rejected because it’s trying to spend something that doesn’t exist. Second, is the total input value greater than or equal to the total output value? The difference is the fee for the miner. Third, is the locking script of each UTXO satisfied by the unlocking script the sender provided? This is cryptographic verification that the sender is indeed entitled to spend that UTXO.

Verification speed

Because the UTXO set is stored in a database optimized for fast lookup, this verification can complete within milliseconds even for transactions with many inputs. The node doesn’t need to trace the entire blockchain history, just query the UTXO set with the txid and output index as the key.

Double spend detection

A double spend is an attempt to use the same UTXO more than once. The UTXO set makes this impossible for confirmed transactions: once a UTXO is consumed and removed from the set, it can’t be used again. For unconfirmed transactions in the mempool, the node watches whether two transactions claim the same UTXO and rejects the one that comes later.

Coinbase maturity

There’s one special exception in verification: the coinbase UTXO. A UTXO originating from a coinbase transaction can’t be spent for 100 blocks after the block in which that coinbase exists. This is called coinbase maturity. The purpose is to provide a time buffer in case a chain reorganization removes that block. Before 100 blocks, the coinbase UTXO does exist in the UTXO set but the node rejects transactions that try to use it.

The UTXO set design that enables fast verification is one reason Bitcoin can operate as a decentralized system without a central server. Every node can verify every transaction independently, using only local data that’s far smaller than the full blockchain.

Chapter 10 · 10.4
Every unneeded UTXO is a small burden carried by the whole network
Size and Growth of the UTXO Set

The UTXO set isn’t a static number. It keeps changing with network activity. Understanding how the UTXO set size grows and how that affects nodes is an important part of understanding the long-term economics and technicals of Bitcoin.

How big is the UTXO set right now?

As of mid-2026, the Bitcoin UTXO set contains more than 170 million UTXOs with a total size of around 11 GB. This is far smaller than the full blockchain, which is already more than 700 GB. But that doesn’t mean the UTXO set can’t become a problem in the future.

What makes the UTXO set grow?

The UTXO set grows when more UTXOs are created than consumed. This happens in several situations: transactions that produce many small outputs without good batching, dust outputs that aren’t economical to spend because their fee is larger than their own value, and lost coins, that is, UTXOs whose private key is already lost and will never be consumed but remain in the UTXO set forever.

UTXO bloat and dust

Dust is a UTXO with a very small satoshi value, often below 546 satoshi for a P2PKH transaction. These outputs appear in the UTXO set but might never be economically spendable. Every node has to store these entries in their database. Over time, accumulated dust contributes to unproductive growth of the UTXO set.

Why does the UTXO set size matter?

The UTXO set has to be accessible quickly, ideally entirely in RAM or fast SSD. If the UTXO set grows too large, nodes with limited hardware will struggle. This is one reason there’s pressure to keep the UTXO set lean: the smaller the UTXO set, the easier it is to run a full node, and the stronger the network’s decentralization.

UTXO consolidation

When mempool fees are low, users can do UTXO consolidation: sending many small UTXOs to themselves in a single transaction to combine them into one larger UTXO. This reduces the number of UTXOs in the set and prepares for more efficient fees in the future when the mempool is busy.

A lean UTXO set is in the common interest of the whole network. Every unnecessary UTXO created is a small burden that every full node in the world has to carry. Practices like transaction batching and UTXO consolidation aren’t just personal efficiency, but a real contribution to the network’s health.

Chapter 10 · 10.5
The way you manage your UTXOs can reveal more than you realize
The UTXO Set and Privacy

The UTXO set isn’t just about technicals and efficiency. There’s a privacy dimension important to understand. Because the UTXO set is public data that anyone can analyze, the way you manage your UTXOs can reveal more information about your finances than you realize.

UTXO as a trail

Every UTXO has a traceable history. Where it came from, what transaction created it, and who might be involved. Blockchain analysis can link different UTXOs to the same owner with several heuristics. The most common heuristic is common input ownership: if two UTXOs are used as inputs in the same transaction, blockchain analysts assume both are owned by the same person. This makes sense because to use a UTXO, you have to prove ownership by signing.

Change output and privacy

When you send Bitcoin and there’s change, that change creates a new UTXO at your address. Which address is the change and which is the payment can often be guessed by analysts: the change is usually the output with a non-round value, while the payment is a rounder number.

Address reuse

One of the most common privacy mistakes is using the same address repeatedly. If you receive Bitcoin at the same address twice, analysts can link both receipts and start building a picture of how much bitcoin you own in total. Modern wallets use HD wallets that generate a new address for every transaction, but not all users understand why this matters.

UTXO consolidation and privacy

The UTXO consolidation we discussed in 10.4 is very useful technically, but has a privacy trade-off. When you combine many UTXOs in one transaction, you confirm to analysts that all those UTXOs belong to the same person. If those UTXOs came from different sources, consolidation can reveal a pattern you didn’t want to reveal.

CoinJoin as a solution

CoinJoin is a technique where several users combine their transactions into one shared transaction. The result is a transaction with many inputs from many different users and many outputs with the same value. Analysts can no longer use the common input ownership heuristic because the inputs really do come from many people. This will be discussed in more depth in Chapter 12.

Privacy in Bitcoin isn’t about hiding something illegal. It’s about the basic right to manage your own financial information. Just as you don’t want everyone to know your bank account balance, you also have the right to choose who knows how much bitcoin you own and where it came from.

Chapter 10 · 10.6
Challenges and solutions for the long-term UTXO set
The Future of the UTXO Set

The UTXO set is a component that will keep evolving as Bitcoin develops. There are several challenges and solutions being discussed or developed regarding how the UTXO set is managed in the future.

Long-term growth

Imagine a ledger that has to be copied out by everyone who wants to verify Bitcoin transactions. The thicker that book, the longer the copying process and the more space needed. That’s the analogy for the UTXO set. If Bitcoin keeps being adopted massively, the number of UTXOs will keep growing. The UTXO set could reach tens of gigabytes within a few decades. This is still far smaller than the full blockchain, but enough to become a barrier for nodes with limited hardware, especially in developing countries where hardware is expensive and internet connections are slow.

Stateless validation and UTXO commitments

Currently, to verify a transaction, a node has to have a complete copy of the UTXO set on its own computer. This is like a cashier who has to memorize the entire list of goods in the warehouse before being able to serve a customer. There’s an idea being discussed called stateless validation: instead of the node storing the UTXO set, the transaction sender proves that their UTXOs really exist and are valid. This proof is called a UTXO commitment, a kind of cryptographic certificate that can be verified without checking a local database. The analogy: instead of the cashier memorizing all the stock, the customer brings an official receipt from the warehouse proving the goods exist. The cashier just verifies the receipt. This is still in the research stage and requires significant changes to the Bitcoin protocol.

Assumevalid and assumeutxo

Bitcoin already has a few ways to speed up a new node joining the network without having to re-verify the entire history from the start. Assumevalid is the first optimization: a new node can skip cryptographic signature verification for very old blocks. The reasoning is economically sound: if millions of nodes already agree that those old blocks are valid, it’s almost impossible they’re all wrong. Assumeutxo is a newer and more sophisticated optimization: a new node can directly use a previously verified UTXO set snapshot, and start operating normally within minutes. Meanwhile, in the background, the node slowly verifies the entire blockchain history from the start to make sure that snapshot is indeed correct.

Archival node vs pruned node

Not all nodes store the entire history of Bitcoin. An archival node stores everything from the genesis block to today, and this is what truly supports the network: without enough archival nodes, new nodes can’t join because no one provides the historical data. A pruned node only stores the UTXO set and a few hundred of the latest blocks. It can verify transactions for itself, but can’t help other nodes that are newly syncing. A pruned node is useful for personal verification purposes, not a replacement for an archival node.

The UTXO set as a health measure

The size and composition of the UTXO set is one of the network health indicators that can be monitored. A UTXO set that grows too fast can indicate spam or inefficient activity. A UTXO set that’s stable or even shrinking shows users who are efficient at managing their outputs. The dust limit, the minimum value of a UTXO accepted by a node as part of mempool policy, is one mechanism to prevent the UTXO set from being flooded with useless outputs.

The UTXO set is one of the most concrete resource constraints in Bitcoin. Unlike the blockchain which only needs to be stored, the UTXO set has to be quickly accessible and queryable. This creates a natural pressure to stay efficient, a pressure that ultimately benefits every user of the network.

Chapter 11 · 11.1
In Chapter 5 we learned why mining exists — now we see how the industry works
From Protocol to Industry

In Chapter 5 we already understood why mining exists: Proof of Work is the consensus mechanism that allows Bitcoin to reach agreement without a central authority. Every valid block represents real work that has been done, and that real work requires real energy.

In this chapter we won’t repeat that mechanism. What we’ll discuss is how mining operates as a real industry: what kind of hardware is used, how miners collaborate in pools, how the economics work, and what the implications are for energy and decentralization.

Mining in 2009 vs now

When Satoshi Nakamoto mined the first block in January 2009, he used an ordinary laptop CPU. There was no competition, no special hardware, no mining companies. One person, one computer, and a newly born protocol.

Today, Bitcoin mining is a global industry worth billions of dollars. Public mining companies are listed on stock exchanges. Warehouse-sized mining facilities operate in countries with cheap electricity. The hardware used is the ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit), a chip designed from scratch for one purpose only: to compute SHA-256 hashes as fast as possible. This chip can’t be used for anything else.

Why did this industrialization happen?

The answer is simple: economic incentives. As long as the block reward is valuable enough, there’s strong motivation to invest in more efficient hardware. More efficient miners get a larger share of the reward at a lower cost. This competition drives extraordinarily fast hardware innovation.

But this industrialization also brings consequences worth thinking about. Mining that anyone could once do at home now requires large capital and access to cheap electricity at industrial scale. This creates centralization pressure that conflicts with Bitcoin’s original spirit as a system everyone can participate in.

Bitcoin mining isn’t just "computers solving a puzzle." It’s an industry with a global supply chain, a complex hardware market, and unique economic dynamics. Understanding this industry helps us understand the resilience and vulnerabilities of the Bitcoin network in the real world.

This industrialization is a natural consequence of Bitcoin’s economic incentives. But it also raises an important question: if mining can only be done by large companies, how "decentralized" is the Bitcoin network really? We’ll keep discussing this question throughout this chapter.
Chapter 11 · 11.2
From laptop to factory — 15 years of the most dramatic hardware evolution in computing history
Evolution of Mining Hardware

The history of Bitcoin mining hardware is one of the most dramatic technology evolution stories in computing history. In less than 15 years, mining efficiency increased trillions of times over.

The CPU era (2009-2010)

In Bitcoin’s early days, everyone mined with an ordinary laptop or desktop CPU. Satoshi Nakamoto himself mined with a CPU. The hash rate of the whole network at the time was so low that anyone could mine a block with a regular computer. There was no meaningful competition and a block could be found in minutes with a standard laptop.

The GPU era (2010-2013)

Someone realized that the GPU (Graphics Processing Unit), the chip usually used for rendering game graphics, was far more efficient at computing SHA-256 than a CPU. A GPU can perform thousands of parallel operations at once. The hash rate jumped drastically and CPU mining was practically no longer profitable.

The FPGA era (2011-2013)

An FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array) is a chip that can be reprogrammed for specific tasks. More efficient than a GPU for SHA-256, but still reprogrammable for other purposes. This era was short because it was soon replaced by the ASIC.

The ASIC era (2013-present)

The ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) is a chip designed from scratch for one purpose only: to compute SHA-256 hashes as fast and efficiently as possible. It can’t be used for anything else at all. A modern ASIC like the Antminer S21 can reach more than 200 TH/s (terahashes per second) with an energy consumption of around 3,500 watts. This means hundreds of trillions of hash attempts every second.

The ASIC’s impact on decentralization

ASICs create a paradox: on one hand, ASICs make the network far more secure because the very high hash rate makes a 51% attack extremely expensive. On the other hand, ASICs make mining increasingly concentrated among players with large capital to buy hardware and pay for electricity at industrial scale. Mining that anyone could once do at home is now dominated by large mining companies with dedicated facilities.

The evolution of mining hardware reflects a simple economic law: as long as there’s a large enough financial incentive, innovation will keep pushing the limits of efficiency. What’s interesting is how this inadvertently changed who can participate in the Bitcoin mining process.

Chapter 11 · 11.3
Rather than struggling alone, join up and share the rewards
Mining Pools

When mining became very competitive, individual miners faced a problem similar to a gambler’s: they might never find a block even after working hard for months. The probability of finding a block for one small miner is very low, and their income becomes very uncertain. The mining pool emerged as a solution.

What is a mining pool?

A mining pool is a group of miners who combine their hash rate and share the rewards proportionally. Instead of each one struggling alone to find a block, they work together. When the pool finds a block, the reward is split among all members based on each one’s hash rate contribution. The analogy is like a lottery ticket: instead of one person buying one ticket with a very small chance of winning, a hundred people chip in to buy a hundred tickets and share the proceeds. The chance of winning is far higher, and although the prize is split, income becomes far more consistent.

How does a pool work?

The pool gives work to its member miners in the form of tasks that are easier than the actual network target. These tasks are called shares. Miners submit the shares they manage to find to the pool as proof that they really worked. Occasionally, a share a miner finds turns out to also meet the actual network target, meaning a new block is found and the pool gets the reward.

Payment methods

There are several ways pools split rewards. PPS (Pay Per Share): miners are paid for every valid share, regardless of whether the pool finds a block or not, and the pool bears the variance risk. PPLNS (Pay Per Last N Shares): payment is based on the shares contributed in the last period before a block is found, more volatile but advantageous when the pool is lucky. FPPS (Full Pay Per Share): like PPS but also accounts for transaction fees in the split.

The pool’s impact on decentralization

Mining pools create centralization concerns: a few large pools control a significant portion of the network’s total hash rate. But it’s worth noting that individual miners in a pool are still free to switch pools at any time. If a pool acts dishonestly, miners will leave it and move to another pool or mine on their own. Stratum V2 is the newest protocol that gives miners more control, including the ability to choose for themselves which transactions go into a block.

Mining pools are an innovation that makes mining more accessible to small miners, but at the same time create centralization pressure. This is a trade-off that’s continually debated in the Bitcoin community. Stratum V2 is one effort to preserve decentralization while still enabling efficient collaboration.

Chapter 11 · 11.4
Mining is a business — revenue must exceed costs
Mining Economics

Bitcoin mining is a business. Like any other business, its success is determined by one simple equation: revenue must exceed costs. But mining economics is far more complex than an ordinary business because some of its key variables keep changing dynamically.

Sources of miner revenue

Miners get two sources of revenue. First, the block reward: currently 3.125 BTC per block, and it will keep decreasing with every halving. Second, transaction fees: all the fees from transactions included in the block. When the mempool is busy, fees can become a significant portion of total revenue. A miner’s total revenue is calculated in USD or local currency, so the BTC price strongly determines profitability.

Operating costs

The biggest cost in mining is electricity. A modern ASIC needs thousands of watts to operate, and has to run 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. The electricity cost per kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the factor that most distinguishes profitable miners from unprofitable ones. Miners with access to cheap electricity (0.03-0.05 USD/kWh) can stay profitable even when the BTC price is low. Miners with expensive electricity (0.10-0.15 USD/kWh) can lose money even when the BTC price is high. Other costs include the ASIC hardware that needs replacing every few years, cooling infrastructure, facility rent, and labor.

Hash rate and difficulty

As more miners join the network with new hardware, the total hash rate rises and the difficulty adjusts so block time stays at 10 minutes. This means every miner gets a smaller share of the reward. Mining economics is a zero-sum game in the short term: if other miners become more efficient, less efficient miners come under more pressure.

Hashprice and break-even price

Hashprice is a metric that calculates how much USD is generated per terahash per second per day. This lets miners compare profitability regardless of the size of their operation. Break-even price is the minimum BTC price for a mining operation not to lose money, depending on the electricity cost and the efficiency of the hardware used.

Halving and its impact

At every halving, the block reward is cut in half. If the BTC price doesn’t rise enough to offset it, inefficient miners will shut off their hardware. The hash rate can drop temporarily, the difficulty adjusts down, and the remaining miners become more profitable. The halving is one of the most tense moments in Bitcoin’s mining economic cycle.

Mining economics is a very dynamic and self-correcting system. High profitability attracts more miners, which raises the difficulty, which reduces profitability. Low profitability pushes miners out, which lowers the difficulty, which increases profitability for those remaining. This is a balance that keeps moving.

Chapter 11 · 11.5
Large energy consumption — wasteful or meaningful?
Mining and Energy

No topic in the Bitcoin ecosystem is more frequently debated than mining’s energy consumption. Criticism comes from various directions, and the defenses are also varied. What matters is understanding the facts before drawing conclusions.

How much energy does Bitcoin use?

The energy consumption of the Bitcoin network cannot be measured directly, because there is no meter attached to it. All that exists are estimates, and the two most cited ones differ considerably. As of mid-2026 the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance estimates around 138 TWh per year, while Digiconomist puts it near 204 TWh. The gap is 66 TWh, and it is not carelessness.

Why two equally credible figures can differ that much

Because they answer slightly different questions. Cambridge builds from the bottom up: surveying mining companies, cataloguing the hardware actually in use, then computing its power draw. Digiconomist builds from the economics: assuming miners spend a fixed share of revenue on electricity, then working backwards. As a result the Digiconomist figure rises when the price rises, while the Cambridge figure stays anchored to physical hardware. Neither is wrong. What is wrong is quoting one number without saying which model it came from.

For context, that figure is roughly the electricity consumption of a mid-sized country such as Poland or Thailand, and sits around half a percent of all electricity worldwide. As another comparison, global data centres consumed roughly 485 TWh in 2025 and are growing about 15 percent a year, while Bitcoin’s figure stays broadly flat.

What will not change, whatever the number becomes

The figures above will certainly date, and any part of this book quoting TWh should be treated as a dated snapshot. But the following three things do not date. First, Bitcoin’s energy use follows miner revenue, not transaction count. Adding or removing transactions within a block does not change the energy at all, because what is paid for is finding the block, not filling it. This is why the widely quoted "energy per transaction" figure misleads: its denominator can move while the numerator does not.

Second, because it follows revenue, it rises and falls with the price. This is not theory: in December 2025 the annualised estimate approached 190 TWh at the market peak, then fell back into the 130s once prices weakened through 2026 and less efficient miners powered down. Third, hardware efficiency keeps improving, from around 98 J/TH in 2016 to roughly 13.5 J/TH in 2026. Energy per hash falls continuously while the number of hashes keeps climbing, and what settles the outcome is the price.

If you want a current figure, what to look for is not news coverage but one of those two indices directly, and what you should record is the date and which model you are quoting.

Energy and security

The energy used in mining isn’t wasted from Bitcoin’s perspective. It’s a cost that directly secures the network. The more energy used for mining, the more expensive it is to attack the network. This is a deliberate security mechanism: the work in proof of work must be real and expensive.

Mining energy sources

The composition of mining energy sources has shifted significantly. Because miners seek the cheapest electricity, they often head toward energy sources that are cheap because they’re in surplus or isolated: surplus hydro energy, flared gas from oil wells, geothermal energy, and other renewable sources. Recent estimates show about 50-60% of mining energy comes from renewable or low-carbon sources, although this figure is debated because of differing methodologies.

Comparison with other systems

Often overlooked in the debate is the energy consumption of the traditional financial system: banks, ATMs, offices, data centers, printing physical money, and transporting cash. This comparison is hard to do apples-to-apples because of the different scope, but it’s important to keep a balanced perspective.

Mining as a flexible energy buyer

There’s an interesting argument that mining can play a positive role in the energy grid. Miners can act as a very flexible energy buyer: they can be turned on when there’s an energy surplus and turned off when demand is high. This helps stabilize the grid and can make renewable energy projects more economical by being an always-present energy buyer even outside peak hours.

The Bitcoin energy debate has no simple answer. How expensive is a decentralized monetary security system worth paying for? This is a question of values, not just technicals. What you can do is make sure this debate is based on accurate facts, not numbers taken without context.

Chapter 11 · 11.6
Between centralization pressure and the spirit of decentralization — where will mining go?
The Future of Mining and Decentralization

Bitcoin mining sits at the intersection of two opposing forces: pressure toward centralization driven by economies of scale, and pressure toward decentralization driven by the spirit of the Bitcoin protocol itself. Where is this industry headed?

Current hash rate concentration

Today, most of the Bitcoin network’s hash rate is concentrated in a few large pools. This doesn’t mean the network is controlled by a handful of parties, because individual miners in a pool are free to switch at any time. But this concentration still creates a theoretical risk and questions about long-term resilience. Geographically, China once dominated with more than 60% of the hash rate, but the mining ban in 2021 drove a massive redistribution. Now the hash rate is spread across the United States, Kazakhstan, Russia, Canada, and many other countries. This broader geographic distribution is generally positive for the network’s resilience.

Who chooses the transactions?

In a traditional pool setup, the pool operator decides which transactions go into a block, not the individual miner running the hardware. For a long time this rarely became a problem because pools generally chose transactions based on the highest fee without filtering content.

But Ocean Pool changed this dynamic. Ocean is a pool that explicitly applies transaction filtering: they reject certain transactions they consider inconsistent with legitimate Bitcoin use, including some types of Ordinals and transactions that use OP_RETURN excessively. This isn’t cheating in a technical sense. By protocol, miners do have the right to choose which transactions go into a block.

But this opens a deeper debate: if large pools start censoring certain transactions based on content rather than just technical validity, is Bitcoin’s censorship-resistance threatened? On one hand, some argue miners have the right to choose based on their preferences. On the other hand, some worry this sets a dangerous precedent: if one pool may censor based on content, what stops other pools from censoring based on other, more political criteria?

Stratum V2 and decentralizing transaction selection

Stratum V2 emerges as a structural answer to this question. As an upgrade to the communication protocol between pool and miner, Stratum V2 gives individual miners the ability to choose for themselves which transactions they want to include in a block. This is a fundamental change: even if the hash rate is concentrated in large pools, the power to choose transactions is redistributed back to individual miners. If Stratum V2 is widely adopted, scenarios like Ocean Pool filtering transactions on behalf of all the miners in the pool become harder to happen without the miners’ explicit consent.

Home mining and small-scale mining

There’s a growing movement to bring mining back to small scale. Devices like the Bitaxe are small open-source ASICs that can run at home with a few watts of power. Their hash rate is very small compared to industrial ASICs, but their contribution to network decentralization is greater than the numbers suggest. The argument: a network with millions of small, geographically dispersed miners is more resistant to attack and regulation than a network that depends on a few hundred large industrial facilities.

Transaction fees as a long-term incentive

The block reward will keep decreasing with every halving. Eventually, there will be no more block reward. Miner incentives will depend entirely on transaction fees. If Bitcoin succeeds in becoming a system used by billions of people, the volume and aggregate fees might be more than enough. But if not, the hash rate could drop and network security could weaken. This is one of the most fundamental questions about Bitcoin’s long-term sustainability, and no one knows the answer for certain.

The future of Bitcoin mining depends on the balance between economic incentives, technological innovation, and community decisions. Questions about who has the right to choose transactions, how decentralized the hash rate should be, and whether fees are enough to replace the block reward are questions that will keep being debated. What’s interesting is that all of this happens without any single party who can decide the answer.

Chapter 12 · 12.1
Bitcoin isn’t anonymous, it’s pseudonymous — and the difference is enormous
Why Privacy in Bitcoin is Hard

Bitcoin is often called an anonymous currency. This is a fairly serious misunderstanding. Bitcoin isn’t anonymous, it’s pseudonymous. Every transaction is recorded permanently on the blockchain that anyone can read. What’s hidden is only the identity behind the address, not the transaction itself.

Transparency as a feature, not a bug

The full transparency of the blockchain is a deliberate design choice. Without this transparency, nodes can’t verify that no bitcoin was created from nothing or spent twice. Transparency is the price paid for decentralization and trustless verification. But this transparency has serious privacy consequences. If someone knows one of your addresses, they can see all the transactions going in and out of that address. And with heuristic analysis like we discussed in Chapter 10, they can start linking other addresses that are likely yours too.

Blockchain analysis heuristics

There are several heuristics blockchain analysts use to link addresses and identify owners. Common input ownership: if two UTXOs are used together as inputs, both are most likely owned by the same person. Change output detection: a transaction’s change can usually be identified from the non-round value or from the same script type as the sender. Address reuse: if the same address appears more than once, all its transactions are linked.

Why this matters

Financial privacy isn’t about hiding something illegal. It’s about a basic right: you don’t want your employer to know how much you earn from a side job, you don’t want your competitor to know who you transact with, you don’t want an attacker to know how much bitcoin you own. In countries with unstable governments, financial privacy can become a real safety issue.

The Bitcoin blockchain is a permanent public ledger. Every privacy mistake you make today can be re-analyzed years later with more sophisticated tools. Good privacy must be built from the start, not patched on afterward.

What leaks is not only who, but what you use

The heuristics above try to answer the question of who owns a given UTXO. There is another, subtler layer that is rarely noticed: your transactions also reveal which wallet you use. It is called wallet fingerprinting.

The cause is simple. The Bitcoin protocol leaves a lot of freedom in how a transaction is assembled, and every wallet makes slightly different choices. Those choices are consistent, and that consistency is the fingerprint.

Some of the easiest to read: output ordering, whether change always sits first or is shuffled. The transaction version number, some use 1, others 2. The nSequence value we cover in 15.3, whether the wallet flags its transactions as replaceable. How the fee is rounded, whether it is always a round number or the raw result of a calculation. And most visible of all, address types: a wallet that spends from bc1q and sends change to bc1q too has already narrowed the field.

Any single trait means little. Combined, though, the pattern is often enough to guess which wallet was used, and sometimes which version. To an observer that is valuable. If they know which wallet you run, they know your change patterns, they know whether you might be using certain privacy features, and they can filter the blockchain for other transactions carrying the same fingerprint.

There is a more uncomfortable consequence. Fingerprints can be used to unpick the CoinJoin we cover in 12.2. If only one of ten participants in a CoinJoin uses a wallet with a distinctive trait, the anonymity that was supposed to come from blending in with nine others thins out considerably.

What you can do about it is limited, and honestly not much. Using a popular wallet means blending in with more people. Using the same address type as most of the network helps too. But fundamentally this is not something a user can fix alone: what needs to change is the wallets themselves, and some developers are indeed converging on shared behaviour so that the fingerprints dissolve.

Chapter 12 · 12.2
Privacy without trust — several users, one transaction
CoinJoin — Mixing without Trust

CoinJoin is the most fundamental privacy technique in Bitcoin. The basic idea is simple but powerful: several users combine their transactions into one shared transaction with many inputs from many users and many outputs with the same value.

How CoinJoin works

Imagine Alice wants to send 0.1 BTC and Bob also wants to send 0.1 BTC. Instead of making two separate transactions, they join into one transaction: two inputs from Alice and Bob, two 0.1 BTC outputs to their respective recipients. Blockchain analysts can no longer use the common input ownership heuristic because the inputs really are from two different people. And because the outputs are the same value, it can’t be determined which output is Alice’s and which is Bob’s.

Without trust

What makes CoinJoin elegant is that no one needs to be trusted. Each participant signs the transaction only after verifying that their output is in that transaction. If someone tries to manipulate an output, the signature is invalid and the transaction is voided. No party can steal another participant’s funds.

CoinJoin implementations

There are several different CoinJoin implementations. Wasabi Wallet uses WabiSabi, a CoinJoin protocol that allows outputs with varying values, not just one denomination. JoinMarket is a marketplace where market makers provide liquidity for CoinJoin in exchange for a small fee. Whirlpool from Samourai Wallet uses fixed denominations and allows users to perform multiple mixing rounds.

CoinJoin’s limitations

CoinJoin isn’t a perfect solution. First, it needs coordination between several users willing to join at the same time. Second, if a user later combines a CoinJoin output with another UTXO that wasn’t CoinJoined, the privacy that was built can leak. Third, some exchanges and services are starting to reject bitcoin that originates from CoinJoin, creating a serious fungibility problem.

A note on Samourai Wallet

In April 2024, the founders of Samourai Wallet were arrested by US authorities on charges of money laundering and operating an unlicensed money transmitting service. This is a real example of how Bitcoin privacy tools sit in a legally contested area. Whirlpool is no longer active as a centralized service since then, although its protocol can still be run independently.

CoinJoin is proof that privacy can be built on top of Bitcoin without changing its underlying protocol. But the Samourai case shows that the line between privacy tools and financial services that need regulation is still an active debate across various jurisdictions.

Chapter 12 · 12.3
Privacy that leaves no recognizable trace
Payjoin — Invisible Privacy

CoinJoin requires coordination between several users who don’t know each other. Payjoin takes a different approach: privacy is built directly into an ordinary payment transaction between sender and recipient.

What is Payjoin?

Payjoin (also called P2EP or Pay-to-End-Point) is a protocol where the payment recipient also contributes input to the transaction. In an ordinary transaction, only the sender provides input. In Payjoin, the recipient also adds one or more UTXOs as additional input. The result: the transaction looks like an ordinary transaction from the outside, but the common input ownership heuristic now gives the wrong conclusion. An analyst looking at this transaction will assume all inputs belong to one person, when in fact the inputs come from two different parties.

Why is this better than ordinary CoinJoin?

CoinJoin is easy for blockchain analysts to identify because its transaction pattern is distinctive: many inputs from many addresses and many outputs with exactly the same value. Although the contents of the transaction can’t be deobfuscated, the existence of a CoinJoin itself can be detected and flagged. Some exchanges reject bitcoin that has been through CoinJoin even without being able to prove the funds are linked to illegal activity. Payjoin has no identifiable pattern. From the outside, a Payjoin transaction looks exactly like an ordinary payment transaction.

How Payjoin works technically

The process starts with a sender who wants to pay. The sender contacts the recipient through a special endpoint, usually a URL the recipient’s wallet provides. The recipient responds by adding their own UTXO to the transaction being constructed. The sender then verifies and signs the complete transaction. The result is one transaction that looks normal but contains input from both parties.

Payjoin’s limitations

Payjoin requires a recipient who supports this protocol. If the merchant or recipient’s wallet doesn’t support Payjoin, the transaction is done as usual without the privacy benefit. Adoption is still limited: BIP 78 defines the standard Payjoin protocol, and several wallets like BTCPay Server, Wasabi Wallet, and JoinMarket already support it, but it’s still far from universal.

Payjoin is an elegant privacy technique because it leaves no identifiable trace. If its adoption is widespread, it can improve the privacy of all Bitcoin users even those who don’t actively use it, because analysts can no longer assume all inputs in one transaction belong to one person.

Chapter 12 · 12.4
One static address, unlimited payments, nothing that can link them
Silent Payments — Privacy without Coordination

CoinJoin needs coordination between users. Payjoin needs a recipient who supports the protocol. Silent Payments takes a more radical approach: privacy that needs no coordination at all from the sender or recipient.

What are Silent Payments?

Silent Payments (BIP 352) is a protocol that lets someone publish a single static address that anyone can use to send payments, but every payment received goes to a different on-chain address that can’t be linked to one another just by looking at the blockchain. The analogy: imagine you have one bank account number you share with everyone, but every time someone transfers to that number, the money goes into a different sub-account that can’t be seen relative to each other from the outside.

How does it work?

The sender uses the recipient’s public key from the static address together with the sender’s private key to generate a unique payment address through a cryptographic operation called Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman. This address is unique for each sender and can’t be linked to the payment address of another sender, even by someone who knows the recipient’s static address. The recipient then scans the blockchain using their private key to find the payments addressed to them.

Advantages of Silent Payments

No coordination needed: the sender just needs to know the recipient’s static address, no additional communication required. No address reuse: every payment produces a unique on-chain address, even from the same static address. No third-party server that needs to be trusted. The static address can be published openly like an email address, but is safer privacy-wise because it doesn’t expose transaction history.

Limitations

Scanning the blockchain to find payments is more computationally heavy. A light wallet that relies on a third-party server will struggle to implement Silent Payments without losing privacy. Still fairly new: implemented in Cake Wallet and a few other wallets, but not yet available in the majority of popular wallets.

Silent Payments is one of the most interesting privacy innovations in the Bitcoin ecosystem lately. It addresses one fundamental problem: how can you receive a payment from anyone without revealing your transaction history, and without having to coordinate with the sender first.

Chapter 12 · 12.5
Lightning isn’t just faster and cheaper — it’s also more private
The Lightning Network and Privacy

The Lightning Network isn’t just a scalability solution. It also brings privacy characteristics very different from on-chain transactions. Understanding this difference is important for making the right decision about when to use Lightning and when to use on-chain.

Lightning privacy vs on-chain

On-chain transactions are recorded permanently on the blockchain that anyone can read. Lightning transactions aren’t recorded on the blockchain at all. What’s recorded is only the opening and closing of the channel. All the payments that happen inside the channel stay private from the public. If Alice and Bob have a Lightning channel and do thousands of transactions, what’s visible on the blockchain is only two transactions, not thousands of individual transactions.

Onion routing in Lightning

Lightning uses onion routing similar to Tor: each node in the payment path only knows where the payment came from and where it should be forwarded, but doesn’t know the whole path. The first node knows the sender but not the final recipient. The last node knows the recipient but not the original sender. This provides better privacy than an ordinary on-chain transaction, but isn’t perfect.

Lightning privacy challenges

There are several privacy challenges specific to Lightning. Channel balance visibility: a node connected to you can see the channel balance you hold together with them. Invoice reuse: if you use the same invoice to receive several payments, the payers can become aware of each other. Routing node surveillance: a large node routing many payments can collect data about payment patterns in the network.

BOLT 12 and Offers

BOLT 12 is a new standard that introduces the concept of offers, a more private replacement for the Lightning invoice. Offers let a recipient publish one code that can be used many times to receive payments, similar to Silent Payments but at the Lightning layer. Every payment generates a cryptographically unique invoice, preventing correlation between payments.

Lightning provides better privacy than on-chain for most everyday transactions, but isn’t without weaknesses. The best choice depends on context: for large values that need on-chain finality, use on-chain. For small, frequent transactions, Lightning offers better privacy along with lower fees.

Chapter 12 · 12.6
Privacy depends on your threat model, not one solution for everyone
Privacy is a Spectrum, Not an On/Off Switch

After discussing various privacy techniques in this chapter, it’s important to understand one thing: privacy in Bitcoin isn’t something that can simply be turned on or off. It’s a spectrum that depends on many small decisions you make every time you transact.

There’s no perfect solution

Every technique we discussed has limitations. CoinJoin’s pattern can be identified and some exchanges reject it. Payjoin needs a recipient who supports the protocol. Silent Payments aren’t available in all wallets yet. Lightning has its own limitations for large transactions. No single technique can solve all privacy problems at once.

Threat model: a threat from whom?

The first question to answer before thinking about privacy is: who do you want to protect yourself from? From blockchain analytics companies tracking transaction patterns? From exchanges that might freeze funds because of tainted coins? From people around you who don’t need to know how much bitcoin you own? Different answers require different strategies.

Basic practices everyone can do

There are a few simple steps anyone can take without needing special tools. Use an HD wallet that automatically generates a new address for every transaction. Avoid combining UTXOs from different sources in one transaction if you don’t need to. Use Lightning for small, routine payments. Be careful about who you share information with about your address or transactions.

Privacy and fungibility

There’s a close relationship between privacy and Bitcoin’s fungibility. Fungibility means every satoshi of bitcoin should be treated the same, regardless of its history. If some bitcoin can be tainted because it was once used in suspected activity and an exchange can reject that bitcoin, then bitcoin is no longer fully fungible. Good privacy helps maintain fungibility: if transaction history can’t be traced, no bitcoin can be tainted.

The future of Bitcoin privacy

The Bitcoin community keeps working on privacy improvements at the protocol level. Silent Payments are starting to be adopted. BOLT 12 is in the process of implementation. There’s discussion about cross-input signature aggregation that could make all transactions look more uniform. Bitcoin privacy in the future will likely be far better than today, but this is a slow and careful process because every protocol change requires broad community consensus.

Privacy isn’t about being a criminal. It’s about maintaining the basic right to manage your own financial information. Just as you don’t publish your bank account to everyone, you also don’t need to publish your entire Bitcoin transaction history. Good privacy is the foundation of true financial freedom.
