Chapter 13 · 13.1
How can a protocol with no owner change?
What is a Soft Fork and a Hard Fork?

We introduced the terms soft fork and hard fork briefly in 5.1 when covering consensus. Here we take both apart properly, because the whole of Chapter 13 rests on the difference. If the opening feels familiar, that is deliberate.

Bitcoin is a living protocol. It needs to evolve to fix bugs, add features, or respond to new threats. But how do you change a protocol that has no owner, no CEO, and is run by thousands of independent nodes around the world? This is where the concept of a fork becomes important.

Hard fork vs soft fork

A hard fork is a protocol change that isn’t backward compatible. Nodes that don’t upgrade can no longer follow the new chain. If some nodes upgrade and some don’t, the network splits into two permanently separate chains. Each has its own longest chain, but they don’t compete with one another because one side’s blocks are irrelevant to the other. A hard fork requires almost universal coordination from the entire ecosystem.

A soft fork is a protocol change that is backward compatible. Old nodes that don’t upgrade can still follow the new chain, because the new rules only tighten the existing rules. A block that’s valid under the new rules is also valid under the old rules. This means it’s still one network with two candidate chains, and the longest one wins. Because the majority of hash rate is usually on the upgraded nodes, their chain is always the longest.

A simple analogy

Imagine a card game with the rule: "a card worth more than 5 wins." A hard fork is changing the rule to "a card worth more than 3 wins"; old players who don’t know the new rule can’t play at the same table. A soft fork is changing the rule to "a card worth more than 5 wins, and it must be red"; the rule becomes stricter, but old players can still play at the same table even if they play suboptimally.

Why Bitcoin prefers soft forks

A soft fork is safer because it doesn’t force all users to upgrade at once. Old nodes can still participate in the network. This reduces the risk of community fracture and allows changes to be made gradually. A hard fork in Bitcoin is considered very risky and is almost never done for new features, only for critical fixes that truly can’t be done with a soft fork.

The choice between a soft fork and a hard fork isn’t just technical, but also political and social. A soft fork allows change without forcing universal consensus, but it also means new features must be designed very carefully to be backward compatible. This is one reason Bitcoin development feels slow compared to other crypto projects.

Visualization — Hard fork vs Soft fork
A hard fork splits the network in two permanently. A soft fork stays one network — the non-conforming candidate chain is abandoned because it loses the longest-chain race.
Hard fork: two separate networks. Each has its own longest chain — but the two don’t compete because one side’s blocks are irrelevant to the other.
Shared block (before the fork)
Chain A — upgraded nodes
Chain B — old nodes
Chain A’s blocks are irrelevant to node B, and vice versa — not because one loses the longest-chain race, but because the rules are already different. There’s no competition between the chains.
Upgraded nodes (Network A)
Network A has its own longest chain. Blocks from network B are irrelevant.
Separate network
Old nodes (Network B)
Network B has its own longest chain. Blocks from network A are irrelevant.
Separate network
Hard fork = two networks, two consensuses. Bitcoin Cash (2017) is a real example. After the fork, there’s no "winner" between the chains — both live on their own.
Soft fork: one network, two candidate chains. The longest one wins — and because the majority of hash rate is on the upgraded nodes, their chain is always the longest.
Shared block
Block valid under both rules (majority)
Non-conforming block (rejected by the majority)
This is still one network. Old nodes can follow the majority chain. The longest one wins — and the majority always grows faster because it has more hash rate.
Majority (upgraded nodes)
Largest hash rate, the chain grows fastest. Non-conforming blocks from the minority are rejected. This chain is always the longest.
✓ Longest chain — wins
Minority (not upgraded)
Their non-conforming blocks are rejected by the majority. Small hash rate makes their chain always shorter and abandoned.
Shorter chain — abandoned
A soft fork keeps one network. As long as the majority of hash rate supports the new rules, the non-conforming chain can never become the longest.
Chapter 13 · 13.2
No CEO, but there is a process — that’s how ideas get into Bitcoin
BIP — How Ideas Get into Bitcoin

Bitcoin has no CEO, no headquarters, no board of directors. But Bitcoin isn’t without process. There’s a formal mechanism to propose, discuss, and implement changes to the protocol. This mechanism is called a BIP, short for Bitcoin Improvement Proposal.

What is a BIP?

A BIP is a written document that proposes a change or addition to the Bitcoin protocol, its development process, or the standards used. The BIP was first introduced by Amir Taaki in 2011, inspired by the Python Enhancement Proposals (PEP) used by the Python community. Every BIP has a unique number: BIP 32 for HD wallets, BIP 141 for SegWit, BIP 340-342 for Taproot, BIP 352 for Silent Payments. This number becomes the way the community references a proposal consistently.

Who can submit a BIP?

Anyone. A BIP isn’t an exclusive document for core developers. Anyone can write and submit a BIP. But it’s the quality of the argument, the clarity of the technical specification, and support from the community that determine whether a BIP will be considered seriously or ignored.

The BIP process

A submitted BIP first goes through review by a BIP editor who ensures the document’s format and completeness. The editor doesn’t decide whether a BIP is technically good or bad. After being accepted as a draft, the BIP starts being discussed in various forums: the bitcoin-dev mailing list, GitHub, forums, and conferences. This discussion can last months or even years. There’s no formal voting, no single decision. Consensus forms organically from long discussion.

Types of BIPs

There are three types of BIPs. The Standards Track BIP is the most important: it proposes changes to the Bitcoin protocol that affect compatibility, further divided into several layers from the consensus layer to the applications layer. The Informational BIP provides information or guidance without proposing a new feature. The Process BIP proposes changes to Bitcoin’s development process itself.

Why is this process slow?

Because Bitcoin has no central authority that can decide. Every change to a protocol used by millions of people and storing billions of dollars in value must be considered very carefully. One bug in the consensus code could be catastrophic. The slowness is a feature, not a bug.

The BIP is how a decentralized community coordinates change without a central authority. The process is slow and often full of debate, but that’s what makes the legitimacy of the result depend on real consensus, not the decision of one party.

Chapter 13 · 13.3
Who has the power to activate a change?
Types of Soft Fork Activation

A soft fork is clearly safer than a hard fork. But how exactly is a soft fork "activated"? It turns out there are several different activation mechanisms, each with a different trade-off between speed, security, and who has the power to activate a change.

MASF: Miner Activated Soft Fork

MASF is the earliest activation mechanism used. Miners mark the blocks they create with a signal of support for a particular soft fork. This signal is placed in the version field of the block header. If a certain threshold, for example 95% of 2016 blocks in one difficulty period, is reached, the soft fork is activated automatically. The advantage of MASF is that the process is measurable and there’s certainty about when activation happens. Its weakness: miners have a de facto veto.

UASF: User Activated Soft Fork

UASF is a response to MASF’s weakness. Economic nodes, users, exchanges, and businesses that use Bitcoin activate the new rules on a certain date, regardless of whether miners have signaled or not. This creates back-pressure on miners: if miners don’t follow the new rules, their blocks will be rejected by the economic majority of the network, and their reward will be worthless. BIP 148, which activated SegWit in 2017, is the most famous and successful example of UASF.

URSF: User Resisted Soft Fork

URSF is the opposite of UASF. If UASF is users forcing activation, URSF is users forcing rejection. Economic nodes coordinate to reject a soft fork that has been activated by miners but is not wanted by the user community. URSF has never been used fully in Bitcoin’s history, but its existence as an option shows that users have the power to reject a change forced by miners.

Version Bits: How Miners Signal

Modern soft forks use the version bits mechanism defined in BIP 9. The block header has a 32-bit version field. Each bit can be used to signal support for a particular soft fork. This allows several soft forks to run in parallel without conflict. The miner’s signal is indicative, not binding: a miner can signal without actually implementing the new rules.

Speedy Trial: An Evolution of MASF

Speedy Trial is a variation of MASF used to activate Taproot in 2021. Its main idea: give a shorter activation window of about 3 months with a 90% threshold. If the threshold is reached within that window, the soft fork is activated. If not, the process can be repeated with a different mechanism. Speedy Trial worked: Taproot was activated in November 2021 after miners reached the threshold in a relatively short time, without drama like SegWit.

The choice of activation mechanism isn’t just a technical matter. It reflects who is considered most entitled to decide on changes in a decentralized network: the miners who provide computation, or the users who give economic value. Bitcoin’s history shows that both need each other, and no single party can fully impose its will.

Chapter 13 · 13.4
Two years of political war that changed how Bitcoin makes decisions
SegWit — The Most Controversial Soft Fork

If there’s one moment in Bitcoin’s history that truly tested whether a decentralized network can make hard decisions without a central authority, it’s the SegWit debate. Running from 2015 to 2017, this wasn’t just a technical debate, it was a political war involving developers, miners, exchanges, users, and Bitcoin businesses around the world.

What is SegWit?

SegWit, short for Segregated Witness, is a soft fork that separates the signature data (witness data) from the main transaction data. Technically, it moves the witness data to a separate part of the block that isn’t counted in the 1 MB block size limit. The result: transactions with SegWit become effectively smaller, increasing network capacity without explicitly changing the 1 MB limit. Besides capacity, SegWit also fixes transaction malleability, a weakness that was one of the main obstacles to implementing the Lightning Network.

Why was it controversial?

The debate began not because of SegWit itself, but because of the larger context: Bitcoin’s scaling debate. Part of the community, especially some miners and large businesses, wanted a simpler solution: just raise the block limit from 1 MB to 2 MB or more through a hard fork. They saw SegWit as too complicated and not enough. On the other side, core developers and most users wanted SegWit because besides capacity, it brought other important improvements and could be done without a risky hard fork.

The New York Agreement and UASF

In May 2017, a large group of Bitcoin businesses and miners signed the New York Agreement, promising to activate SegWit while also raising the block limit to 2 MB through a hard fork, known as SegWit2x. But many Bitcoin Core developers and users rejected this hard fork part. When miners appeared unwilling to activate SegWit without a hard fork guarantee, the user community launched BIP 148: UASF. Nodes running BIP 148 would reject miner blocks that didn’t support SegWit starting August 1, 2017.

The result

The pressure worked. Miners activated SegWit before the August 1 deadline. SegWit officially became active on August 24, 2017 at block 481,824. The hard fork part of the New York Agreement, SegWit2x, was eventually canceled in November 2017 due to insufficient support. Part of the community that wanted large blocks split off to create Bitcoin Cash through a hard fork on August 1, 2017.

SegWit taught several important lessons about Bitcoin governance: miners don’t have an absolute veto, users and economic nodes have real power through UASF, and consensus in Bitcoin can’t be forced by any single party. But the process also showed how hard it is to make a collective decision without a central authority.

Dec 2015
Developer
BIP 141 submitted — SegWit introduced for the first time
Pieter Wuille, Eric Lombrozo, and Johnson Lau submit the SegWit proposal as a soft fork.
SegWit separates witness data from the main transaction. This fixes transaction malleability and effectively increases network capacity without explicitly changing the 1 MB limit. This proposal was well received by developers but immediately sparked debate in the wider community.
2016
Community
The scaling debate heats up — the block size war begins
Part of the community wants a simpler solution: raise the block limit directly through a hard fork.
Two camps form. The big blocks camp, led by large miners and businesses like Roger Ver, want a hard fork to raise the block limit. The small blocks camp, along with Bitcoin Core developers, want SegWit as a more cautious solution. The debate runs fiercely on forums, social media, and at conferences.
2016-2017
Miner
Miners don’t signal SegWit — deadlock
Even though SegWit was technically ready, most miners refused to signal support.
Large miners, especially those based in China, refused to signal SegWit without a guarantee that the block limit would also be raised. This created a deadlock: developers didn’t want a hard fork, miners didn’t want SegWit without a hard fork. Transaction fees started spiking because network capacity was full.
Mar 2017
Community
BIP 148 submitted — UASF as a user weapon
Shaolin Fry submits BIP 148: supporting nodes will reject miner blocks that don’t support SegWit starting August 1, 2017.
BIP 148 is a grassroots movement, not from core developers. Users, exchanges, and businesses tired of the deadlock threatened to use their economic power. If enough nodes ran BIP 148, miners who didn’t signal SegWit would produce blocks rejected by the economic network.
May 2017
Community
New York Agreement — a compromise that didn’t last
More than 50 Bitcoin companies sign an agreement: activate SegWit, then raise the block size to 2 MB (SegWit2x).
The New York Agreement was signed by the majority of hash rate and many Bitcoin businesses. The plan: activate SegWit via MASF, then within 3 months do a hard fork to raise the block to 2 MB. Bitcoin Core developers refused to be involved because they opposed the hard fork part. This agreement created a fragile illusion of consensus.
Jul 2017
Miner
Miners start signaling SegWit — UASF pressure works
Under the threat of BIP 148, miners start activating the SegWit signal before the August 1 deadline.
In the weeks leading up to August 1, the percentage of SegWit signaling from miners jumped drastically. Not out of conviction, but out of economic calculation: producing blocks that might be rejected by the economic network is a risk that isn’t worth it. This moment proved that miners don’t have an absolute veto.
Aug 1, 2017
Split
Bitcoin Cash is born — a hard fork by the big blocks camp
The community that wanted large blocks splits off and creates Bitcoin Cash with an 8 MB block limit.
At block 478,558, Bitcoin Cash split off from Bitcoin. This was the first significant real hard fork in Bitcoin’s history. Bitcoin holders automatically received the same amount of BCH. Bitcoin Cash used replay protection to ensure a transaction on one chain isn’t valid on the other.
Aug 24, 2017
Result
SegWit officially active in Bitcoin — block 481,824
After almost two years of debate, SegWit was finally activated on the main Bitcoin network.
SegWit lock-in happened on August 8, 2017 after the threshold was reached, and became fully active on August 24 at block 481,824. This opened the way for the Lightning Network and other technical improvements. The network’s effective capacity increased and transaction malleability was fixed.
Nov 2017
Result
SegWit2x canceled — the hard fork doesn’t happen
The hard fork part of the New York Agreement was officially canceled due to insufficient community support.
The signatories of the New York Agreement announced the cancellation of SegWit2x on November 8, 2017. The reason: not enough support to split the community. This ended the most dramatic chapter in Bitcoin’s history. SegWit ran without a hard fork, exactly as Bitcoin Core developers wanted from the start.
Chapter 13 · 13.5
From concept to activation in 3 years, without a single drama
Taproot — A Smoother Soft Fork

After the SegWit drama, the Bitcoin community learned a lot about how a major upgrade should not be done. Taproot was a chance to prove that Bitcoin could change in a more mature and coordinated way.

What is Taproot?

Taproot is a package of three BIPs activated together in November 2021: BIP 340 (Schnorr Signatures), BIP 341 (Taproot itself), and BIP 342 (Tapscript). All three are interconnected and designed to work together. Schnorr Signatures replace ECDSA as Bitcoin’s signature scheme. Schnorr is more mathematically efficient and enables signature aggregation: several signatures in one transaction can be combined into a single signature. This reduces transaction size and improves privacy because a multi-signature transaction looks like an ordinary transaction from the outside.

Tapscript introduces a new way to write smart contracts in Bitcoin using the MAST (Merkelized Alternative Script Trees) structure. With MAST, only the script branch that is actually executed needs to be revealed on the blockchain. A complex contract with many conditions looks like an ordinary payment from the outside as long as the executed path is the "happy path".

Why smoother than SegWit?

Taproot was activated using Speedy Trial with a short activation window and a 90% threshold. No UASF drama, no threats, no split. Miners reached the threshold in just 6 weeks after the window opened. Several factors contributed: everyone was already tired of the SegWit drama, there was no controversial trade-off like the block size debate, Taproot’s technical benefits were clear, and Speedy Trial provided a fair mechanism with a clear time limit.

What changed after Taproot?

Taproot became active at block 709,632 on November 14, 2021. Initial adoption was slow because wallets and services needed to be updated to support the new P2TR (Pay-to-Taproot) address format. Taproot opened the way for a more private Lightning Network with PTLCs (Point Time Lock Contracts) replacing HTLCs, and for a richer smart contract ecosystem in Bitcoin.

Taproot is proof that Bitcoin can change without major conflict. But this doesn’t mean Bitcoin governance is already perfect. Taproot succeeded because its benefits weren’t controversial and no major economic interest was threatened. The next, more controversial upgrade could require a process just as hard as SegWit.

Chapter 13 · 13.6
No one decides — everyone influences
Bitcoin Governance — Who Really Decides?

After studying BIPs, soft forks, UASF, SegWit, and Taproot, a reasonable question arises: who actually has the power to change Bitcoin? The answer isn’t simple, and that’s what makes it interesting.

No one decides, everyone influences

Bitcoin has no formal governance. No voting, no board of directors, no defined decision mechanism. But change still happens, through an organic process in which various parties influence each other and ultimately reach consensus or not.

Developers

Developers who contribute to various Bitcoin implementations like Bitcoin Core, Bitcoin Knots, and others are the people who write and review the code that nodes run. They have great influence because they’re the ones who implement technical changes. But they can’t force anyone to run their code, and anyone is free to fork those implementations.

Miners

Miners are the party that produces blocks and secures the network. In MASF, the miners’ signal determines when a soft fork is activated. But the SegWit UASF case proved that miners can be forced by economic nodes: blocks rejected by economic nodes don’t generate real income.

Nodes

Nodes are the most often overlooked but most fundamental actor in Bitcoin governance. There are two kinds: independent nodes run by individuals, communities, or organizations without a direct economic motive, and economic nodes run by exchanges, wallets, and businesses. What matters: one home node has the same weight as one large exchange when it comes to validating and enforcing the consensus rules. They are the true guardians of the rules.

Users and Economic Actors

Ordinary users are the hardest to measure in influence, but in the long term they’re the ones who determine Bitcoin’s value. Economic actors and businesses like exchanges, merchants, payment processors, and institutions have significant economic power: exchanges can determine which chain gets liquidity, merchants who accept Bitcoin give the network real value. But they also have limitations, depending on user trust and unable to force a protocol change directly.

Why can no one force change?

Because Bitcoin is opt-in. Every node is free to choose what software it runs. If an implementation releases a new version the community doesn’t like, people can keep running the old version or fork the implementation. This informal governance process has advantages: there’s no single point of failure and no one can hijack Bitcoin for their own interest. Its drawback: the process is very slow and debates can last years.

Bitcoin governance isn’t a democracy, isn’t an autocracy, and isn’t anarchy. It’s a system where power is spread among many parties that don’t trust each other, but are forced to coordinate because they all depend on the same network. This may be the most interesting governance experiment of the digital era.

Chapter 14 · 14.1
184 billion bitcoin created in one block — and fixed in 5 hours
The 2010 Value Overflow Bug

On August 15, 2010, someone found a critical bug in the Bitcoin code: an integer overflow. By exploiting this bug, the attacker managed to create a transaction that appeared to create bitcoin far beyond the protocol’s rules. This transaction was briefly confirmed in block #74,638 before being rolled back by the community in about 5 hours. It’s important to understand: this was a bug in the code implementation, not a bug in the Bitcoin protocol itself. The 21 million BTC supply was never truly threatened.

Two things to distinguish

Bitcoin has two different limits that are often confused. First, MAX_MONEY: this is a Bitcoin protocol consensus rule that states no transaction output may exceed the total supply of 21 million BTC (2.1 quadrillion satoshi). Second, MAX_INT64: this is the mathematical limit of the 64-bit integer data type in computers, namely 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. This number has nothing to do with Bitcoin’s rules, it’s just the technical limit of storing numbers in computer memory. This bug isn’t about violating MAX_INT64, but about code that forgot to check MAX_MONEY before performing the addition.

How the bug works

The Bitcoin code at the time didn’t check whether the value of each transaction output exceeded MAX_MONEY before adding them up. The attacker took advantage of this by creating two outputs that each far exceeded 21 million BTC. When the two were added together, the total exceeded MAX_INT64 and an integer overflow occurred: the number "wrapped" into a large negative number. The validation code then checked whether the total output was less than the total input, and because the total output had become a negative number, this condition was always met. The transaction passed validation when it shouldn’t have.

The community response

Satoshi Nakamoto himself responded to this incident. In about 5 hours, Satoshi released a patch that added a check: if an output value is less than zero or exceeds MAX_MONEY, the transaction is immediately rejected. The Bitcoin community at the time, which was still very small, managed to organize an emergency soft fork: nodes upgraded and started ignoring block #74,638. The clean chain became dominant. The bitcoin that appeared to be "created" never really existed because it was immediately rolled back before anyone could use it.

This bug is an example of the important difference between a protocol bug and an implementation bug. The Bitcoin protocol defines the rules correctly, but the code that implements those rules had a gap. This is one reason Bitcoin’s consensus code is audited very strictly: a single missing line of code can create a dangerous gap.

Eight years later, it almost happened again

It is tempting to file the 2010 incident under growing pains: the code was raw, the users were few, gaps were to be expected. But in September 2018 Bitcoin came close to losing the 21 million cap a second time, and this time in a mature era, with code under far heavier review.

The bug is catalogued as CVE-2018-17144. It came not from a new feature but from an optimization. In Bitcoin Core 0.14.0, released in March 2017, a duplicate-input check was removed because it was believed to happen elsewhere already, so repeating it only cost time. That belief was wrong. As a result, nodes were willing to partly process blocks that spent the same input more than once.

In the 0.14.x versions the consequence was "only" that the node died abruptly, because a safety check deliberately halted the program on encountering an impossible state. But that check was rewritten in 0.15.0, and from then on the node no longer stopped. It carried on. Which meant a miner could spend one output twice inside a single block and claim its value twice as well. Repeated enough times, that is minting Bitcoin out of thin air.

The bug lay dormant for about a year and a half. What finally surfaced it was not the core team but a developer using the alias awemany, from the Bitcoin Cash camp, while reading code his project had inherited from Bitcoin Core. He disclosed it privately on 17 September 2018, and not only to Bitcoin Core but to other projects running the same code.

What he reported was only a crash bug. It was the Bitcoin Core developers themselves who then realised the same root cause carried something far worse: inflation. At that point they faced an uncomfortable choice. Full disclosure meant telling everyone how to mint Bitcoin before most nodes had a chance to update. Saying nothing meant leaving the hole wide open.

The path they took was staged disclosure: announce and patch the lesser crash bug in the open, so that people had an urgent reason to upgrade immediately, while quietly reaching out to miners and large businesses about the real issue. The fix shipped on 18 September in version 0.16.3, less than a day after the report arrived. The full impact was only announced on 20 September, once most of the network was safe.

The bug was never exploited. But its lessons cut deeper than those of 2010, and there are three. First, the most dangerous change is often not an addition but the removal of something believed unnecessary. Second, the person who found it came from a rival project reading inherited code, which makes open source not merely an ideal but a defence mechanism that demonstrably works. Third, Bitcoin’s security does not end with the mathematics we covered in Chapter 4. It also rests on humans reading code carefully, and on hard judgement calls about when a danger is best made public.

Chapter 14 · 14.2
When Bitcoin’s history is rewritten — and why that’s normal
Chain Reorganization (Reorg)

A reorg, short for chain reorganization, happens when a node finds that there’s an alternative chain longer than the chain they’re currently following. The node then switches to the longer chain, discarding the blocks that are no longer part of the longest chain. These discarded blocks are called orphan blocks.

Small reorgs are normal

A 1-2 block reorg is a routine event that happens almost every day in Bitcoin. This can happen when two miners find a valid block almost simultaneously: the network is temporarily split because some nodes receive miner A’s block first, while others receive miner B’s first. As soon as one of the miners finds the next block, its chain becomes longer and the whole network converges to that chain. The losing miner loses the block reward but the network stays safe.

A large reorg is dangerous

A deep reorg, 6 blocks or more, requires very large hash rate and can be exploited for a double spend. An attacker with enough hash rate can mine an alternative chain in secret, do a large transaction on the main chain (for example selling bitcoin to an exchange), then release the longer alternative chain that doesn’t contain that transaction. A merchant or exchange that already considered the transaction final could become a victim.

The history of reorgs in Bitcoin

The deepest reorgs ever recorded on Bitcoin mainnet were not attacks at all, but fallout from software bugs. Rolling back the 2010 overflow bug we covered in 14.1 required reversing dozens of blocks, and the March 2013 chain split we will cover in 14.3 ran for 24 blocks. Outside those two incidents, reorgs on Bitcoin are almost always just 1 to 2 blocks. Deliberate deep reorgs have happened on other networks like Ethereum Classic (a 100+ block reorg in 2019) and Bitcoin Gold, but both have far smaller hash rate than Bitcoin so the cost of attack is far lower.

The "6 confirmations" standard often mentioned in Bitcoin isn’t an arbitrary number. It’s an estimate that after 6 blocks, the cost of doing a reorg deep enough to cancel that transaction becomes very uneconomical for any attacker. For small everyday transactions, 1-3 confirmations is already safe enough.

Chapter 14 · 14.3
When two software versions produced two different realities for 6 hours
March 2013 Chain Split

On March 11, 2013, an unintended chain split occurred between nodes running Bitcoin 0.7 and Bitcoin 0.8. This wasn’t an attack, wasn’t a deliberate bug exploit, but an unexpected consequence of a difference in database implementation between two software versions that both claimed to follow the same rules.

The root cause: BerkeleyDB vs LevelDB

Bitcoin 0.8 switched the storage database from BerkeleyDB to LevelDB as a performance optimization. What wasn’t realized: BerkeleyDB had a limit of 10,000 keys that could be locked simultaneously. This wasn’t part of Bitcoin’s consensus rules, just an implementation detail. LevelDB didn’t have the same limit. Block #225,430, mined on the night of March 11, affected the status of more than 5,000 transactions at once, requiring more than 10,000 BerkeleyDB keys simultaneously. Bitcoin 0.7 nodes couldn’t process this block and rejected it. Bitcoin 0.8 nodes accepted it without issue.

Six hours with two Bitcoins

For about 6 hours, there were two versions of Bitcoin running in parallel. The 0.8 chain had about 60% hash rate so it grew faster. The split lasted for 24 blocks before being resolved. The split wasn’t detected immediately: it was only about an hour later, at 23:10 GMT, that a user named thermoman reported an anomaly on the bitcoin-dev IRC. One minute later, Mark Karpelès of Mt. Gox immediately halted block processing as a precaution.

An unusual solution

The community had to choose: upgrade everyone to 0.8, or go back to 0.7? The decision was to go back to 0.7, not because 0.7 was more technically correct, but because it was easier to coordinate a handful of large mining pools to downgrade than to force the entire ecosystem to upgrade at once. BTCGuild and Slush Pool downgraded even though they had to give up the reward they’d already earned on the 0.8 chain. At block #225,454, the 0.7 chain managed to surpass the 0.8 chain and the network reunited.

The recorded double spend

During the split period, one double spend was recorded. But according to BIP 50, the official post-mortem written by Gavin Andresen, this was done by someone experimenting to test whether it was possible, not with intent to steal.

This incident taught an important lesson: two implementations that claim to follow the same rules can still produce different behavior because of hidden implementation details. This is one reason Bitcoin is very careful about changing consensus code, and why there’s a big effort to ensure all implementations behave identically on every edge case.

Chapter 14 · 14.4
A mining strategy that’s profitable on paper — but has never been proven to work
Selfish Mining

Selfish mining is a strategy where a miner with significant hash rate hides the blocks they manage to find and doesn’t immediately broadcast them to the network. By withholding these blocks, they gain an advantage: they can start mining on top of the hidden block while the network is still mining on the previous block.

How selfish mining works

If the dishonest miner manages to find the next block before the network knows about their hidden block, they can release two blocks at once and turn the other honest block into an orphan. The honest miner who worked hard to find a block loses their reward, while the dishonest miner gets the reward of two blocks at once.

Formal analysis and the threshold

This attack was first formally analyzed by Ittay Eyal and Emin Gun Sirer in their 2013 paper. They showed that with about 33% hash rate, selfish mining can be economically profitable. With larger hash rate, the theoretical profit grows.

The real technical risks

Although it looks profitable on paper, selfish mining has serious technical risks. First, block secrecy is hard to maintain on a P2P network: once a block is found, the propagation signal on the network can leak before the dishonest miner is ready to release their hidden chain. Second, if an honest miner finds a block before the dishonest miner releases their chain, all the hidden work becomes wasted and the dishonest miner loses all the reward they’d invested. Third, the longer they hide blocks, the greater the risk that the hidden chain can never catch up to the public chain. Fourth, an abnormal orphan pattern can be detected by the community and cause a boycott of the suspicious pool.

Why it has never happened in Bitcoin

In practice, selfish mining has never been proven to happen at a significant scale. There are several reasons: it’s hard to maintain secrecy on a peer-to-peer network, the risk of losing rewards is far more real than the theoretical profit, the distributed mining pool landscape makes it very hard for one entity to reach 33% hash rate without being noticed, and the economic incentive for honest mining remains stronger in the long term.

Selfish mining is a reminder that Bitcoin’s economic incentives are designed to make dishonesty more expensive than honesty. But this isn’t an absolute guarantee: if the mining landscape changes drastically and one entity dominates the hash rate, these incentive dynamics could change.

Specific technical risks:
⚠️ Propagation leak: the signal of a found block can be detected by other nodes on the P2P network before the dishonest miner is ready to release their chain
⚠️ Race condition: if an honest miner finds a block before the hidden chain is released, all the hidden work becomes wasted and the reward is lost entirely
⚠️ Risk accumulation: the longer the hidden chain, the smaller the probability of catching up to the continuously growing public chain
⚠️ Pattern detection: an abnormal orphan rate around a particular pool can be detected and trigger an investigation or community boycott
Selfish mining is most dangerous when combined with an eclipse attack: the dishonest miner isolates certain nodes and forces them to follow the wrong chain. But this combination requires enormous resources and coordination.
Empirical evidence: selfish mining has never been proven to happen at a significant scale on Bitcoin mainnet. The economic incentive for honest mining remains stronger in the long term as long as no single entity dominates the hash rate.
Chapter 14 · 14.5
An attack that isolates one node, not the whole network
Eclipse Attack

An eclipse attack is an attack where the attacker controls all of a target node’s peer connections, so that node only communicates with nodes controlled by the attacker. It’s important to understand from the start: this is an attack against one specific node, not against the Bitcoin network as a whole. The Bitcoin network keeps running normally.

A simple analogy

Imagine you live in a big city but all your information sources, neighbors, friends, radio, and TV, are replaced by an attacker’s agents delivering fake news. You’re still in the same city, but you don’t know what’s really happening. The city itself keeps running normally without you. That’s an eclipse attack: the attacked node lives in a fake reality controlled by the attacker, while thousands of other nodes on the network keep operating correctly.

How an eclipse attack works

Every Bitcoin node maintains a number of connections to other peers. If the attacker can fill all these connection slots with nodes they control, the target node can no longer communicate with the real network. The attacker does this by flooding the network with IP addresses they control, waiting for the target node to restart and pick new peers, or exploiting weaknesses in the peer selection mechanism.

Possible impacts

An eclipsed node can be tricked into accepting fake transactions (a double spend against a merchant), wasting hash rate on a fake chain (for a miner), or exposing transaction information to the attacker before it’s broadcast to the real network. But once again, all these impacts only happen to the node that was successfully isolated, not to the network as a whole.

Mitigations in Bitcoin Core

Bitcoin Core has already implemented several mitigations. Anchor connections maintain 2 outbound connections to trusted nodes even during a restart. Limits on connections from the same IP subnet make it harder for an attacker to dominate all the slots. Tor support and multiple network interfaces make it harder to identify and isolate the target node.

An eclipse attack isn’t proof that Bitcoin is easy to attack or that its decentralization is weak. It’s an attack that requires great effort to target one specific node, and Bitcoin Core keeps improving peer connection resilience to make this attack harder. The network as a whole is actually very hard to attack precisely because it’s distributed across thousands of nodes that don’t depend on each other.

An eclipse attack doesn’t require large hash rate. All it requires is the ability to control all the network connections of one target node.
💥
Double spend against a merchant using the eclipsed node
The attacker sends a fake transaction that looks valid to the target node. The merchant thinks the payment is confirmed, when on the real network that transaction doesn’t exist. The attacker then spends the same bitcoin elsewhere.
💥
An eclipsed miner wastes hash rate on a fake chain
A miner whose node is eclipsed will mine on top of the attacker’s fake blocks. All the electricity and computation is wasted because the blocks produced won’t be recognized by the real network.
💥
The attacker monitors transactions before they’re broadcast
All transactions sent by the target node must pass through the attacker’s node first, exposing financial information that should be private.
🛡️
Anchor connections: maintaining 2 connections to trusted nodes
Bitcoin Core keeps 2 outbound connections to known nodes even during a restart, making it harder for an attacker to replace all connections at once.
🛡️
Limits on connections from one IP subnet
Limiting inbound connections from the same IP subnet makes it harder for an attacker to dominate all the connection slots from just one address block.
🛡️
Run the node via Tor or a different IP address
A node running via Tor or multiple network interfaces is far harder to isolate because the attacker can’t identify all the connection entry points.
An eclipse attack isn’t the end of Bitcoin’s decentralization. It’s a very specific and targeted attack that only affects one node. Thousands of other nodes around the world keep working normally. Bitcoin Core keeps improving peer connection resilience to make this attack harder.
The most vulnerable nodes: home nodes with few outbound peers or that are rarely maintained. The simplest solution is to run a node with connections to many geographically diverse peers.
Chapter 14 · 14.6
Not a perfect system — but a system that has been battle-tested for 15+ years
What Keeps Bitcoin Strong?

After studying the overflow bug, chain split, reorg, selfish mining, and eclipse attack, a reasonable question arises: if all these threats exist, why is Bitcoin still standing today?

Aligned economic incentives

Successfully attacking Bitcoin requires a cost far exceeding the gain that can be obtained. Selfish mining is more expensive than honest mining in the long term. An eclipse attack needs large resources for a very specific target. A 51% attack needs astronomical electricity and hardware costs. Honest miners get a larger and more consistent reward than dishonest ones because the system is designed that way.

Extreme network redundancy

There’s no single point of failure in Bitcoin. If one node is attacked, thousands of others keep running. If one implementation has a bug, another implementation can be a reference. If one mining pool is compromised, the remaining hash rate still secures the network. There’s no central server, no CEO to pressure, no off switch.

A vigilant and responsive community

The 2010 bug was found, reported, and fixed in 5 hours. The 2013 chain split was detected in an hour and resolved with extraordinary coordination between developers, mining pools, and exchanges. Developers, miners, node operators, and users all have an incentive to keep the network healthy because Bitcoin’s value depends on trust in the network.

Open source and total transparency

The Bitcoin code can be examined by anyone, anytime. No gap can be hidden for long because thousands of eyes keep watching. Every change is strictly audited before being implemented. Weaknesses that are found are fixed openly and the result becomes a lesson for the entire ecosystem.

Bitcoin isn’t a perfect system. It’s a system that has been battle-tested since 2009, attacked from various directions, and still standing. Every weakness found becomes a lesson. Every failed attack proves the resilience of its architecture. And every incident successfully resolved proves that a distributed community can coordinate without a central authority.

Mitigated
What happened
Security researchers demonstrated that a Bitcoin node can be isolated from the network by controlling all of its peer connections. An isolated node can be tricked into accepting fake information.
Community response
Bitcoin Core implemented anchor connections, per-subnet connection limits, and better Tor support. Research continues to strengthen peer connection resilience.
Lesson
Peer diversification is the best protection. A node connected to many peers from various geographic locations is far harder to isolate. Open source allows mitigation to be done transparently.
The four pillars of Bitcoin’s resilience:
💰
Economic Incentives
Attacking Bitcoin is more expensive than the gain. The system is designed so honesty is always more profitable than cheating in the long term.
🌐
Network Redundancy
There’s no single point of failure. Thousands of nodes around the world that don’t depend on each other make the network very hard to shut down.
👥
Vigilant Community
Every major incident is responded to quickly. Developers, miners, and users all have an incentive to keep the network healthy because Bitcoin’s value depends on it.
🔓
Open Source
The code is open for anyone to examine. No gap can be hidden for long. Every change is audited by many eyes before being implemented.

Chapter 15 · 15.1
No server clock, no time authority — yet the whole network still agrees
Time in Bitcoin — Not a Wall Clock

If you’ve ever wondered how Bitcoin "knows" when a transaction may or may not be processed, the answer is in how Bitcoin defines time. And this way is very different from the clock you use every day.

The problem: who do you trust to know the time?

In the real world, you trust the clock on your phone, or a globally synchronized time server. But Bitcoin is a system without a central authority. There’s no time server everyone can trust. If you let one party determine "the current time," you’ve just created a centralized point of failure that can be attacked or manipulated.

Bitcoin’s solution: don’t rely on a wall clock at all. Use two ways of measuring time that can be verified by all nodes independently.

First way: Block Height

Block height is the sequential number of a block in the blockchain. The first block is block #0, the next is #1, and so on. Every new block found adds one number. The analogy is like the pages of a book: if you want to refer to "chapter 5", you don’t need to know when the book was written, just "page 120". Block height works the same: "after block 800,000" is a specific point in time that anyone with a copy of the blockchain can verify.

The advantage: very simple and can’t be manipulated. The disadvantage: it isn’t directly related to real time because blocks don’t always arrive exactly every 10 minutes (it could be 2 minutes, could be 25 minutes).

Second way: Median Time Past (MTP)

Every Bitcoin block contains a timestamp, a number showing when that block was mined. But miners can lie a little about this timestamp within the limits allowed by the protocol. If Bitcoin directly trusted the timestamp of a single block, miners could manipulate "time" for their own benefit.

The solution: take the last 11 blocks, take the middle value (median) of their timestamps. This is Median Time Past (MTP). The analogy is like measuring the average temperature of the last week rather than trusting today’s thermometer that might be broken. One wrong reading doesn’t ruin the overall picture. By using the median of 11 blocks, one miner lying about their timestamp can’t shift the MTP significantly.

Why does this matter?

From these two ways of measuring time, Bitcoin can build time-based contracts that take effect automatically without needing a judge, notary, or third party. You can say to the Bitcoin network: "this money can’t be touched until block 900,000" or "this transaction is only valid after 6 months from now" and the whole network will enforce it automatically.

Bitcoin defines time by consensus, not based on a server clock. This isn’t a limitation, but a design choice that keeps the system decentralized. The result is a time mechanism that can be trusted by all parties without having to trust anyone in particular.

Chapter 15 · 15.2
For thousands of years humans needed a notary to manage time in contracts — Bitcoin doesn’t
nLockTime — A Check That Can’t Be Cashed Yet

Imagine you write a check but you write next month’s date in the top right corner. The bank won’t process that check until that date arrives. nLockTime works exactly like that, but it isn’t a bank that enforces the rule, it’s the entire Bitcoin network automatically, without anyone being able to intervene. Even the sender themselves can’t cancel or speed it up after the transaction is created.

For thousands of years, humans needed a third party to manage time in contracts: notaries, banks, lawyers, or judges. They’re the ones who ensure "this check can only be cashed next month" or "this escrow fund is returned if no one claims it within 6 months." nLockTime removes that need. Trust in humans is replaced by mathematics.

What is nLockTime?

nLockTime is a 4-byte field that has been in every Bitcoin transaction since day one. Its value determines when that transaction may be included in a block. If a miner tries to include a transaction with an nLockTime that hasn’t been reached, every node in the network will reject that block automatically.

Two modes: block or time

This is one of Satoshi’s early design decisions that still holds today. The way Bitcoin distinguishes whether you’re talking about "which block number" or "what time" is just by looking at the number. If the nLockTime value is below 500,000,000, it’s interpreted as a block height. A value of 800,000 means "this transaction isn’t valid before block #800,000." If the value is at or above 500,000,000, it’s interpreted as a Unix timestamp, the number of seconds since January 1, 1970. The number 500,000,000 in Unix time is around the year 1985, long before Bitcoin existed, so it’s safe to use as a dividing line.

One important condition that’s often forgotten

nLockTime is only effective if at least one transaction input has an nSequence other than 0xFFFFFFFF (the maximum value). This is a technical detail that often surprises new developers. If all inputs have nSequence 0xFFFFFFFF, the node will ignore nLockTime entirely and the transaction can be included at any time. In the simulation below, you can try turning off nSequence and see what happens.

Why is this powerful?

Scheduled payment: you can make a transaction that can only be confirmed starting next month. There’s no risk of a contractor not wanting to work after being paid, no risk of you not wanting to pay after the work is done. Escrow with a time limit: until now, escrow needed a third party you trust. With nLockTime, that trust is replaced by mathematics. The funds can’t go anywhere until the time condition is met. Dead man’s switch: a digital inheritance that can’t be blocked by anyone, not by a bank, not by a government, not even by the person who made the contract.

nLockTime is the simplest feature of Bitcoin’s timelock arsenal. It has existed since day one and is proven to work. But its power is limited because it only works at the transaction level. For more complex conditions like "Alice can claim anytime OR Bob can claim after 6 months", we need CLTV, which will be discussed in 15.4.

Chapter 15 · 15.3
A field designed for one purpose, failed, then became the foundation of the Lightning Network
nSequence — From a Failed Idea to Relative Timelock

There’s one field in every Bitcoin transaction input that has the most winding history of all the fields in the protocol. Its name is nSequence. It was designed for one purpose, failed to achieve it, then was recycled into something far more useful.

The original idea that didn’t work

Satoshi designed nSequence as a mechanism to update unconfirmed transactions. The idea: if two parties are negotiating, they can keep updating the transaction by raising the nSequence value. Miners were supposed to only include the version with the highest nSequence. The problem: there was no incentive for miners to follow this rule. A miner could just include the first version of the transaction if the fee was attractive enough. Without an enforcement mechanism, this idea couldn’t work. nSequence then became an almost useless field for years.

The difference from nLockTime

Before going further, it’s important to understand the fundamental difference between nLockTime and nSequence. Imagine you have two kinds of "dated checks." The first check reads: "valid starting January 1, 2026", this is nLockTime, an absolute time that doesn’t depend on when the check is held. The second check reads: "valid 30 days after being handed to the bank", this is nSequence, a relative time that only starts running after the transaction is confirmed. This difference sounds small, but it’s crucial for building more flexible contracts.

BIP 68: nSequence gets a new meaning

In 2016, BIP 68 — activated together with BIP 112 and BIP 113 in the CSV soft fork — gave nSequence a new meaning: relative timelock. Instead of creating a new field that would have required a hard fork, the Bitcoin community recycled an old, almost unused field.

Three "buttons" in nSequence

nSequence is a 32-bit number, but the way to read it is like a device with three buttons. The first button is on/off: a single bit that determines whether nSequence has any timelock meaning at all. If this button is off, the rest is ignored. The second button is the unit choice: whether the time delay is measured in blocks (about 10 minutes per block) or in time units (512 seconds per unit). The third button is the value: a 16-bit number that determines how long the delay is, maximum 65,535 units.

The analogy is like setting a phone alarm: choose on/off, choose AM/PM, fill in the hour. You don’t need to understand binary to use the concept.

Why is relative timelock powerful?

nLockTime can’t depend on when a UTXO is confirmed, it only knows absolute time. nSequence can. This is very important for the Lightning Network: when a channel is force-closed, there’s an nSequence-based waiting period that starts running from when the commitment transaction is confirmed, not from an unpredictable absolute time. This period gives the other party time to detect cheating and submit a penalty transaction.

nSequence is a beautiful example of recycling what already exists. Rather than adding a new field to the transaction format (which would need a hard fork), BIP 68 recycled an old, almost unused field and gave it a very useful new function. This is how Bitcoin evolves: carefully, backward-compatible, and without discarding the existing legacy.

Chapter 15 · 15.4
Time is no longer an external limit, but becomes part of the contract logic itself
CLTV — When the Script Itself Guards Time

So far we’ve seen two timelock mechanisms: nLockTime which works at the transaction level, and nSequence which works at the input level. Both are limits outside the script. But what if we want time to be part of the script condition itself? What if we want to say: "Alice can take these funds anytime, OR Bob can take them after 6 months"? For that we need OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY.

Analogy: a security guard vs a safe

nLockTime is like a security guard at a building’s entrance: they check whether you may enter based on the time. But once you’re in, anyone can take the things inside. CLTV is like a safe inside the building that has its own time-combination lock. No matter when you enter the building, that safe won’t open before its time. And what’s more powerful: that safe can have different rules for different people.

How CLTV works

OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY is an opcode added to Bitcoin Script through BIP 65 in 2015. When executed, it compares the value on the stack with the nLockTime value of the transaction being verified. If the stack value is greater than the transaction’s nLockTime, the script fails. This means: anyone who wants to spend a UTXO with CLTV must create a transaction that commits "I won’t spend this before time X."

Why is this powerful for real life?

Imagine this scenario: you send funds to your child who’s still in college, but you don’t want them to be able to access it until they graduate 4 years from now. With CLTV you can make a script: "my child can take this after block X (about 4 years), OR I can take it back anytime with an emergency key." No bank, no lawyer, no trustee. Mathematics enforces it.

Or imagine milestone payments for a contractor: "the contractor can claim payment after the agreed delivery date, but if the contractor doesn’t show up within 6 months, the client can refund." Automatic escrow without an escrow agent.

HTLC: the CLTV that powers the Lightning Network

A Hash Time Lock Contract (HTLC) is a combination of CLTV with a hash preimage. The recipient can claim the funds by revealing a secret that was hashed beforehand. If the secret isn’t revealed before the timeout, the sender can refund. This simple mechanism, without a third party, is the foundation of every payment that crosses the Lightning Network.

CLTV is a big leap from "when a transaction can be created" to "when a UTXO can be spent." This difference opens up room for far more expressive contracts. With CLTV, time is no longer an external limit, but becomes part of the contract logic itself.

Chapter 15 · 15.5
Without CSV, the Lightning Network in its current form couldn’t exist
CSV — The Relative Timelock That Powers Lightning

If CLTV is "not before date X", then CSV is "not before X days after this is confirmed." This difference that sounds small turns out to be very crucial for building a secure payment system without trust.

The analogy of two kinds of contracts

Imagine two kinds of apartment lease contracts. The first contract: "you may move out starting January 1, 2026." This is like CLTV, an absolute date that doesn’t depend on when the contract was signed. The second contract: "you may move out 30 days after giving notice." This is like CSV, a relative period that only starts running after a certain action happens. This difference sounds small, but it’s very important for contracts that can’t predict when their action will happen.

OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY

BIP 112 added the CSV opcode to Bitcoin Script, activated together with BIP 68 in 2016. CSV works similarly to CLTV but uses nSequence: it verifies that the nSequence of the input spending this UTXO has reached the specified minimum value. In other words, CSV forces the party who wants to claim a UTXO to wait at least X blocks or X time since that UTXO was confirmed.

Why CSV is the heart of the Lightning Network

The Lightning Network lets two parties do many off-chain transactions with only two on-chain transactions: opening and closing the channel. The security of this system depends on the ability to punish a party who tries to cheat with an old commitment transaction.

Here’s how it works: when Alice and Bob open a payment channel, they create a commitment transaction that represents the latest state. Every time the state is updated, the old commitment must be revoked by providing a revocation key. If Bob tries to close the channel with an old commitment that’s more favorable to him, Alice has time to detect the cheating and submit a penalty transaction that takes all the channel funds.

The time Alice has to detect cheating is what CSV controls. Usually 144 blocks (about 1 day). During this period, Bob’s funds are locked in an output that Alice can take if Bob is proven to be cheating. Without CSV, Bob could claim immediately before Alice had a chance to react.

CSV beyond Lightning

Beyond Lightning, CSV is useful for vaults with a cooldown period before funds can be moved, escrow that automatically refunds after a relative waiting period, and multisig systems with a backup key that only activates after a certain period of inactivity.

CSV provides a fairness mechanism that lets two parties who don’t trust each other transact repeatedly without needing to trust one another. It’s enough to trust mathematics and the Bitcoin protocol. Without CSV, the Lightning Network in its current form couldn’t exist.

Chapter 15 · 15.6
Timelock isn’t an exotic feature — it’s the foundation of a financial system that’s truly trustless
Timelock in Practice — from Inheritance to Vaulting

After understanding nLockTime, nSequence, CLTV, and CSV, it’s time to see how all these mechanisms can be combined to build powerful real use cases. Timelock isn’t an exotic feature for cryptography developers, but the foundation of many things that make Bitcoin more than just a simple payment system.

Dead man’s switch: a digital inheritance that can’t be blocked

Imagine you want to ensure that if you’re inactive for 1 year, your bitcoin can be accessed by someone you trust. In the traditional banking system, this needs a will, a notary, a legal process, and potential family conflict. In Bitcoin, this can be implemented with a script: "the main key can move the funds anytime, OR the backup key can claim after 52,560 blocks since the UTXO was last touched." The owner just needs to periodically move the funds to reset the clock. If inactive for 1 year, the backup key held by the heir can claim the funds automatically.

Vault: an extra security layer

A vault is a pattern where funds can’t simply be moved right away. There’s a cooldown period that provides time to cancel if a private key is compromised. The simple pattern: to spend funds from a vault, you must first create an "unvault transaction" that’s CSV-locked for 144 blocks. During those 144 blocks, you can still cancel with an emergency key and send the funds back to cold storage. If a hacker steals the private key, you have about 1 day to notice and cancel.

Escrow and milestone payments

With a combination of nLockTime, multisig, and CLTV, you can build an escrow system that’s truly trustless. No need to trust an arbiter, a platform, or anyone. Milestone payments let a contractor receive automatic payment after the agreed date without having to wait for the client’s "approval" which could be denied.

Limitations to understand

Bitcoin Script can’t see conditions outside the chain. It doesn’t know whether goods have been delivered or work has been completed. Timelock can only manage time, not real-world conditions. To connect off-chain conditions to on-chain, an oracle or minimal trust in a third party is needed. Besides that, complex scripts tend to be larger and require higher fees, although Taproot already helps hide this complexity.

Timelock is proof that Bitcoin isn’t just a "send and receive" system. It’s a programming language for expressing complex ownership conditions, without needing a lawyer, a bank, or a third party that must be trusted. Every use case built on top of timelock is one step further toward a financial system that’s truly trustless.

Chapter 16 · 16.1
Before it can be trusted, a node must read all of Bitcoin’s history from the start
Initial Block Download — How a New Node Gets to Know Bitcoin

Imagine you just moved to a new city and have to read all the newspapers from the last 15 years before you can follow today’s news. That’s what a new Bitcoin node does: it must validate every block since the genesis block before it can be considered synced and trusted.

This process is called Initial Block Download (IBD). For a new node today, this means validating hundreds of thousands of blocks containing hundreds of millions of transactions. Depending on hardware, this process can take from a few hours to several days.

Headers-first: a clever strategy

Bitcoin client software (like Bitcoin Core or Bitcoin Knots) doesn’t immediately download all blocks from the start. It first downloads all the block headers, 80 bytes per block, from peers. For the entire blockchain, this is only about 70MB. From the headers, a node can verify the chain of proof-of-work without needing any transaction data at all.

After knowing which is the longest valid chain, only then does the node download blocks in parallel from many peers at once. This is far more efficient than the old approach of downloading just one block from one peer sequentially.

What is verified during IBD?

For each block, the node verifies: the proof-of-work is valid, the timestamp is within the allowed range, the block size doesn’t exceed the limit, all transactions are cryptographically valid, there’s no double spend, and the total coinbase output doesn’t exceed the allowed reward. This isn’t a light process, which is why IBD requires significant time and CPU.

assumevalid: a safe shortcut

Many Bitcoin client implementations include the hash of a particular block that has been verified by the broad community as a "safe point assumed valid." For blocks before this point, the node still downloads and executes all transactions to build the UTXO set, but no longer verifies the cryptographic signatures, which is the most CPU-intensive part. This shortens IBD significantly without sacrificing the security of the UTXO set.

Important: assumevalid isn’t blind trust. The node still verifies the entire block structure and the UTXO set. What’s skipped is only the signature verification for old blocks that have already been proven valid by millions of other nodes.

While IBD is in progress, the node should not be used to verify payments. It doesn’t yet have a full picture of the blockchain and can be tricked into accepting a transaction that has already been double-spent in a block it hasn’t validated. Check the "initialblockdownload" field via RPC to make sure the node is ready.

Chapter 16 · 16.2
A node trusts no one — it verifies everything itself
Block Verification — What a Node Checks Every Time a New Block Arrives

Every time a new block arrives from the network, a node doesn’t just accept it. It runs a long, strict series of checks before deciding whether the block is valid or not. This process is what makes Bitcoin trustless: you don’t need to trust anyone because your own node verifies everything.

Two layers of verification

Block verification happens in two layers. The first is header verification: the node checks the proof-of-work, timestamp, and basic block structure without needing to look at the transactions inside. This is fast and light. The second is full verification: the node checks every transaction one by one, ensuring there’s no double spend, all signatures are valid, and all consensus rules are met.

What gets checked?

Proof-of-work: the hash of the block header must be below the current difficulty target. This can’t be faked without expending real energy. Timestamp: no more than 2 hours in the future from the node’s time, and must be greater than the Median Time Past (MTP). Block size: total weight doesn’t exceed 4 million weight units. Coinbase transaction: the reward claimed by the miner doesn’t exceed the block subsidy plus total transaction fees. Every transaction: all inputs refer to a UTXO that exists and hasn’t been spent, all signatures are cryptographically valid, no transaction spends more than it receives.

Script validation: the most complex layer

For every transaction input, the node must run the Bitcoin script and verify that the locking script conditions are met by the provided unlocking script. This involves executing a stack-based virtual machine for every input in every transaction in every block. This is the most CPU-intensive part of the entire verification process.

Parallel verification

Modern Bitcoin client software verifies signatures in parallel using all available CPU cores. This is one reason better hardware speeds up IBD significantly. The more cores, the faster the signature validation process, which can number in the tens of thousands per block.

Every node that runs this verification is one independent vote that enforces Bitcoin’s consensus rules. No single entity can force these nodes to accept a block that violates the rules, even if that block has a valid proof-of-work.

Chapter 16 · 16.3
If you could keep only one folder from all of Bitcoin — keep the chainstate
The Chainstate Database — The Heart of Bitcoin State

If you delete all the blocks from your node’s hard drive but keep one small folder called chainstate, your node can still verify whether a new transaction is valid or not. That folder holds the entire "current state" of Bitcoin, all the UTXOs that exist right now, who owns them, and how much they’re worth.

What is chainstate?

Chainstate is the database that holds the UTXO set: the collection of all transaction outputs that have never been spent. Every time a new block is validated, the node updates the chainstate, new outputs are added, spent outputs are removed. This is a snapshot of current Bitcoin ownership.

LevelDB: A Very Organized Filing Cabinet

On disk, the chainstate is stored using LevelDB, a key-value database created by Google that’s very efficient for fast access. Imagine you have 184 million sheets of documents, where each sheet is one UTXO. If those documents were piled up haphazardly, finding one document could take a long time. LevelDB organizes those documents in order by their key, so a lookup can be done in milliseconds even with hundreds of millions of entries. That’s why a node can verify a new transaction very quickly without traversing the entire blockchain.

The key is the outpoint (txid + output index), the value is information about that UTXO: the value in satoshi, the locking script, whether it’s coinbase, and in which block it was confirmed.

Why does the UTXO set size matter?

Currently the UTXO set contains about 184 million entries and is about 11 GB on disk after LevelDB compression. The larger the UTXO set, the more RAM a node needs for efficient operation. This is one reason the Bitcoin community pays close attention to "UTXO bloat", the practice of creating many small, inefficient outputs.

dbcache: The Size of the Desk in RAM

One of the most important configuration parameters in bitcoin.conf is dbcache, the cache size for the chainstate database in MB. Imagine LevelDB as a physical filing cabinet in a warehouse (the hard disk). Every time the node needs to check a UTXO, it has to walk to the warehouse, open the drawer, grab the document, read it, then put it back. dbcache is the desk in front of the warehouse, the bigger the desk, the more documents can be accessed directly without going back and forth to disk. The default is only 450 MB, but with enough RAM, raising it to 4-8 GB can speed up IBD dramatically.

Undo data: how a node can roll back

Besides chainstate, the node also stores undo data for each block, the data needed to reverse that block’s effects in case of a reorg. Undo data contains all the UTXOs spent in that block, so if that block has to be disconnected, the node can return those UTXOs to the chainstate.

The total of all UTXOs in the chainstate must exactly match the total circulating Bitcoin supply. This can be verified by anyone at any time by running gettxoutsetinfo. There’s no central bank, no external audit needed, mathematics proves it.

Chapter 16 · 16.4
A node that saves storage but doesn’t compromise on verification security
Pruning — Discard Old Blocks, Stay Fully Validating

There’s a common misconception about running a Bitcoin node: that you need hundreds of gigabytes of storage to do it. This isn’t entirely true. Bitcoin has a feature called pruning that lets a node discard old blocks from disk after validating them, while still being able to fully verify new transactions.

What is a pruned node?

A node running in pruning mode still downloads and validates every block since the genesis block during IBD, there’s no shortcut. But after a block is validated and the UTXO set is updated, that block can be deleted from disk. What remains is only the chainstate (UTXO set) and a few recent blocks as a buffer. The result: a node that needs a minimum of about 550 MB of storage instead of 700+ GB for a full archival node.

What you lose with pruning

A pruned node can’t serve old blocks to other peers doing IBD. This means a pruned node doesn’t contribute fully as a relay for the network. Besides that, there are several RPC commands that can’t be run on a pruned node because the data they need is no longer on disk. This is what most often confuses new users.

But the most important thing remains

A pruned node is a fully validating node, not a light client and not an SPV node. The ability to verify new transactions, validate new blocks, reject invalid transactions and blocks, and maintain an accurate UTXO set all remain. Verification security isn’t reduced at all.

Configuring pruning

In bitcoin.conf, pruning is configured with the prune parameter in MB, with a minimum of 550 MB. A value of 0 means pruning is off. There are two modes: automatic, where the node manages itself based on a target size, and manual, where pruning is done via RPC to a particular block height.

A pruned node is very suitable for users who want to verify their own transactions without depending on a third party, but have limited storage. If storage is sufficient, running a full archival node is better for the health of the network because it can help new nodes doing IBD.

Chapter 16 · 16.5
Faster sync doesn’t mean less secure — if designed correctly
assumevalid and assumeUTXO — Faster Sync Without Sacrificing Trustlessness

We touched on assumevalid in 16.1 as one reason IBD can be shortened. This section explains how it actually works, along with its sibling assumeUTXO, and answers the objection that comes up most often: does this mean we are back to trusting the developers?

IBD can take hours or even days. Two Bitcoin features, assumevalid and assumeUTXO, are designed to speed up this process significantly. But both are often misunderstood: they’re not blind trust in the developers, but very carefully designed choices with verification mechanisms that remain strong.

assumevalid: Skip Signature Verification for Old Blocks

During IBD, the most CPU-consuming part is the cryptographic signature verification for every transaction input. For a blockchain hundreds of thousands of blocks long with hundreds of millions of transactions, this is very heavy work and can take dozens of hours.

assumevalid is the hash of a particular block hardcoded into the Bitcoin client software. For all blocks before this hash, the node still downloads all the data, validates the block structure, and builds the UTXO set fully, but doesn’t verify the cryptographic signatures. The logic: if millions of other nodes have already validated these signatures and the blockchain keeps running normally, the signatures must be valid.

Important: you can override this anytime. By running the flag -assumevalid=0, the node will verify every signature from block 0 without exception. This takes far longer but provides the most thorough verification.

assumeUTXO: Start from a UTXO Set Snapshot

assumeUTXO is a newer and more radical feature. Instead of building the UTXO set from the genesis block, the node can load a ready-made UTXO set snapshot from an external file. The node can immediately be used to verify new transactions while verifying the historical blockchain in the background.

The analogy: imagine you just joined a company. Rather than reading all the emails from 15 years ago before you can start working, you read a summary of the current situation first (the UTXO snapshot), start working right away, while slowly reading the historical archive in your free time.

Is this safe?

For assumevalid: if a malicious developer inserted the wrong block hash, the node would build a UTXO set that conflicts with the network and would be caught immediately. The thousands of developers and users who audit the source code become a strong layer of social verification.

For assumeUTXO: the snapshot hash is hardcoded and can be audited by anyone. If the snapshot contains the wrong UTXO, the background historical verification will eventually find the inconsistency. The design ensures that even if the snapshot is wrong, the node will self-correct.

assumevalid and assumeUTXO aren’t shortcuts that sacrifice security, but rather both are very carefully designed optimizations. Bitcoin’s security doesn’t depend on one node verifying everything, but on thousands of independent nodes all running the same consensus rules.

Chapter 16 · 16.6
Without your own node, you have to trust someone — and that contradicts the entire idea of Bitcoin
Why Run Your Own Node — and 10 Daily Commands

After understanding IBD, chainstate, block verification, pruning, and assumevalid, it’s time to answer the most fundamental question: why should you bother running your own node?

"Don’t trust, verify": Not an Empty Slogan

If you don’t run your own node, you have to trust someone. Maybe the exchange where you bought bitcoin. Maybe the block explorer you use to view transactions. Maybe the wallet connected to someone else’s node. Every time you trust a third party to verify a Bitcoin transaction, you create a point of failure that can be manipulated, hacked, or can lie.

Your own node removes all that dependence. You verify for yourself that the transaction you received really is on the blockchain, that there’s no hidden inflation, that the consensus rules you agreed to are actually enforced.

What does your node verify every day?

Every new block: the proof-of-work is valid, no transaction spends a UTXO that doesn’t exist, no miner claims more reward than they should, all consensus rules are met. Every transaction you receive: it really is on the blockchain, confirmed as many times as you see, with no data manipulation from a third party.

A node is your voice in the network

If one day there’s a proposal to change Bitcoin’s consensus rules, for example raising the supply limit or changing the mining algorithm, your node is what determines whether you follow that change or not. A node that isn’t upgraded will automatically reject blocks that violate the old rules. This is the mechanism that makes consensus changes in Bitcoin very hard to do without broad agreement from the users.

Contributing to the network

Every node that runs strengthens the Bitcoin network. An archival node helps new nodes doing IBD. A node that accepts inbound connections helps new peers find the network. The more independent nodes that run, the harder it is for anyone to censor transactions or manipulate data.

Running your own node is the most fundamental form of participation in Bitcoin. Not because it gives a direct financial benefit, but because it’s how you truly own and verify the bitcoin you hold, without trusting anyone.
