Chapter 17 · 17.1
Satoshi already thought about this in 2008 — how a phone can verify Bitcoin
The Problem SPV Solves

Imagine you want to verify that a check was really issued by a legitimate bank. There are two ways: first, you become a bank employee and access the entire database system to verify it yourself. Second, you ask the bank to show you proof of the transaction with an official stamp whose authenticity you can verify without entering the system.

A full node is the first way: full verification but it requires a big commitment. SPV is the second way: lighter verification but still reliable for most use cases.

Historical context: Satoshi already thought about this

In section 8 of the Bitcoin whitepaper (2008), Satoshi wrote about Simplified Payment Verification. He realized that not everyone would or could run a full node. For everyday users who just want to receive and send payments, there’s a lighter way: just verify that your transaction is in a valid block, without needing to validate the entire blockchain.

The key is in the block header. A Bitcoin block header is only 80 bytes per block, but contains the merkle root, a hash that represents all the transactions in that block. By using only the block headers (about 70 MB for the entire blockchain) plus a merkle proof for a particular transaction, you can prove that the transaction is in a valid block.

What can SPV verify?

An SPV client can verify that a transaction is in a particular block via a merkle proof, that the block has valid proof-of-work via the header, and that the block is part of the longest chain via the header chain. What SPV can’t verify without additional trust: whether the other consensus rules are met, whether the transaction was double-spent before entering the block, and whether the total Bitcoin supply is valid.

The trust assumption SPV needs

SPV isn’t trustless like a full node. It depends on the assumption that the majority of hashrate is honest. If the majority of miners collude, they can create a fake block that deceives the SPV client. But this assumption is the same as Bitcoin’s overall security assumption: as long as the majority is honest, SPV is safe for everyday payments.

Who is SPV suitable for?

For everyday payments of moderate amounts, SPV provides a good balance between security and convenience. For very large-value payments or for needs that require full verification, a full node remains the best choice.

SPV isn’t a bad compromise, but rather a deliberate trade-off that Satoshi thought about from the start. In a majority-honest system, SPV provides verification strong enough for most use cases. The key is understanding its limitations and choosing a level of verification that matches your needs and the value at stake.

Chapter 17 · 17.2
Proving one transaction out of millions — with just a few dozen bytes
Merkle Proof — Efficient Membership Proof

Imagine you live in a city of 10,000 residents and need to prove that your name is in the official residency register. There are two ways: first, show the whole book (650 pages) to the person who wants to verify. Second, show one small path from your name up to the official stamp on the first page, only 13 steps for 10,000 residents, not 10,000 pages.

That’s a merkle proof. Not proof by showing all the data, but proof by showing a path that can be cryptographically verified.

A different perspective from Chapter 3

In Chapter 4 we saw the merkle tree as a cryptographic structure: how transaction hashes are combined into one merkle root. Here we see it from the SPV client’s perspective: how your phone proves that your transaction is in a block it never fully downloaded.

The structure of a merkle proof

Suppose a block has 8 transactions. To prove that Tx3 is in this block, you don’t need all 8 transactions. You only need: the hash of Tx4 (Tx3’s pair at the first level), the hash of H(Tx1+Tx2) (the pair at the second level), and the hash of H(Tx5+Tx6+Tx7+Tx8) (the pair at the third level). These three hashes, combined with Tx3, are enough to reconstruct the merkle root. If the result matches the merkle root in the block header whose proof-of-work has been verified, the transaction is proven to be in that block.

Remarkable efficiency

For a block with n transactions, a merkle proof only needs log₂(n) hashes. A modern Bitcoin block can contain more than 3,000 transactions. Its merkle proof only needs about 12 hashes, 32 bytes each, totaling about 384 bytes. Compare that with downloading the entire block, which can reach 1-2 MB. If the transactions in a block double from 3,000 to 6,000, the proof only needs one additional hash.

How an SPV client uses a merkle proof

When your SPV wallet receives a payment, here’s what happens behind the scenes: the connected node sends the transaction along with its merkle proof. The SPV client takes the transaction hash, follows the merkle proof path, and reconstructs the merkle root. Then it compares that with the merkle root in the block header whose proof-of-work has been verified. If they match, the transaction is proven to be in that block.

Limitations of a merkle proof

A merkle proof proves that a transaction IS in a block, but doesn’t prove that the transaction is VALID. A transaction’s inputs could already have been spent earlier and the block containing that transaction would still be valid from a proof-of-work perspective. To detect a double spend, you need access to the UTXO set, which only a full node has.

The merkle proof is one of the most elegant cryptographic constructions in Bitcoin. With only a few dozen bytes, anyone can prove that a transaction is inside a block containing millions of bytes of data. This is a mathematical consequence of the deterministic and collision-resistant nature of a hash function.

Chapter 17 · 17.3
A mathematically elegant solution that turned out to leak on the privacy side
Bloom Filters — The Old, Problematic Way

An SPV client needs to tell a full node: "send me the transactions relevant to my address." But if the SPV directly says "I have address bc1q...xyz, send me transactions to that address," privacy leaks immediately because the full node knows exactly which address you own.

Bloom filters were Bitcoin’s first solution to this problem. Introduced in BIP 37 in 2012, they let an SPV client tell a node about relevant transactions without directly revealing the address.

What is a bloom filter?

A bloom filter is a probabilistic data structure that answers one question: "is element X in this set?" The answer "no" is always correct, if the bloom filter says it’s not there, it really isn’t. But the answer "yes" can be wrong (a false positive), the bloom filter can say "yes" for an element that isn’t actually in the set. This is intentional: false positives create ambiguity that protects privacy.

How a bloom filter works

A bloom filter is a bit array, starting with all bits zero. To add an element, you hash that element with several different hash functions, then set the resulting bits to 1. To query "is X there?", hash X with the same hash functions. If all the resulting bits are already 1, X might be there. If even one bit is still 0, X is definitely not there. The SPV client builds a bloom filter containing its addresses and sends it to a node. The node filters transactions and only sends the matching ones.

The privacy problem that made BIP 37 deprecated

Despite the clever design, bloom filters have a serious problem. The size and composition of the filter can reveal information about how many addresses the client owns. A malicious node can test millions of Bitcoin addresses against the filter and do statistical analysis to identify the addresses actually owned. Early BIP 37 implementations even had a weakness that let a full node determine the client’s addresses with surprising accuracy.

Besides the privacy problem, BIP 37 also burdened full nodes disproportionately, because a node has to filter every transaction for every connected SPV client, which can become a DoS attack.

Current status

BIP 37 is now considered deprecated. Many nodes disable BIP 37 support by default. A better solution, compact block filters (BIP 157/158), is already available and will be discussed in 17.4.

The bloom filter is an interesting example of a mathematically elegant solution that isn’t good enough in security practice. Privacy is a very hard property to maintain, even a system designed to protect privacy can leak information through unexpected channels.

Step 2: The node analyzes the filter size
From the filter size and the requested false positive rate, the node can estimate how many addresses are in the filter. A 64-byte filter with 1% fp usually contains 3-5 addresses.

Chapter 17 · 17.4
If you don’t need to tell anyone what you’re looking for, don’t do it
BIP 157/158 — Compact Block Filters: A Better Privacy Solution

BIP 37 lets the node filter for the client, so the node knows what the client is looking for. BIP 157/158 flips this logic: the client downloads filters and filters them itself. This simple shift creates a huge privacy difference.

The inverted logic

With BIP 37: the SPV client says to the node "I have this address, please filter for me." The node knows the address being searched. With BIP 157/158: the node creates a compact filter for each block that summarizes all the data in that block. The SPV client downloads this filter and checks for itself whether there’s any relevant data. If there is, only then does the client download the full block. The node never knows what the client is looking for.

What is a compact block filter?

BIP 158 defines a compact filter format using a data structure called a Golomb-Coded Set (GCS). A GCS is a probabilistic data structure that’s more efficient than a bloom filter with a more predictable false positive rate. For each block, the node creates a filter containing all the scriptPubKeys of the transaction outputs in that block. This filter is about 10-20 KB for a block with thousands of transactions.

BIP 157: The Filter Distribution Protocol

BIP 157 defines how these filters are distributed across the P2P network. There are two new message types: getcfheaders to request filter headers, and getcfilters to request filters for a particular block range. A client can download filter headers lightly first, then download the full filters only for the blocks it needs.

A trade-off to understand

An SPV client with BIP 157/158 has to download the filter for every block, totaling a few hundred MB to a few GB for the entire chain. This is larger than BIP 37, which only downloads relevant transactions. In exchange, the privacy gained is far better. This is a deliberate trade-off: trade bandwidth for privacy.

Implementation status

BIP 157/158 is already implemented in major Bitcoin client software. Neutrino is a Go light client implementation that uses BIP 157/158 and is used by Lightning Network mobile wallets like Phoenix and Breez.

BIP 157/158 shows how better protocol design can flip trust assumptions. By moving the filtering work from the node to the client, privacy increases drastically without sacrificing security. If you don’t need to tell anyone what you’re looking for, don’t do it.

Chapter 17 · 17.5
SPV can be deceived in certain scenarios — but how realistic and how expensive?
SPV vs Full Node Trade-off — How Big Is the Risk That SPV Can Be Deceived?

SPV doesn’t verify all consensus rules. But how big is the real risk? This is a question often answered wrong in two directions: some say SPV is as safe as a full node, others say SPV can’t be trusted at all. Both are wrong.

What can an attacker do to an SPV client?

The most realistic attack scenario is an eclipse attack: the attacker isolates the SPV client from the honest network and only connects it to nodes owned by the attacker. From this position, the attacker can hide incoming transactions or show a different chain. For a double spend, the attacker needs an eclipse attack AND significant hashrate to produce an alternative chain, which is very expensive and rare.

What an attacker CANNOT do

Without controlling the majority of the network’s hashrate, an attacker can’t create a transaction that spends bitcoin they don’t own because it needs a private key, create bitcoin out of nothing because it violates consensus that any full node can detect, or convince an SPV client to accept a block without valid proof-of-work because SPV still verifies the PoW header.

Confirmations as mitigation

The more confirmations you wait for, the more expensive it is for an attacker to carry out an attack. For everyday small-value transactions, 1-3 confirmations is already plenty. For large values, 6+ confirmations provide far stronger security even for SPV.

Practical conclusion

For 99% of everyday Bitcoin use by individuals, buying coffee, receiving a salary, sending to a friend, SPV provides more than enough security. A full node remains ideal for receiving large-value payments, running a business that accepts Bitcoin, and anyone who wants full self-verification without any trust assumptions.

Bitcoin’s security isn’t binary between "safe" and "unsafe," but rather a spectrum of trade-offs between convenience, resources, and the level of verification. SPV is a valid point on that spectrum, not an embarrassing compromise. What matters is understanding where that point is and choosing deliberately.

Chapter 17 · 17.6
SPV in the whitepaper and SPV in the app store are two different things
Light Clients in the Real World — Electrum, Neutrino, and Modern Wallets

Everything we learned in Chapter 17 about SPV, merkle proofs, bloom filters, and compact block filters isn’t a theoretical concept, but rather all of it is implemented in Bitcoin wallets used by millions of people every day. But real-world implementations are often more complex and varied than the pure SPV model Satoshi described in the whitepaper.

Electrum: SPV Hybrid with a Server

Electrum is one of the most popular Bitcoin wallets since 2011. Electrum doesn’t implement pure SPV, but rather connects to a network of Electrum servers that have already processed the blockchain and store the UTXO set. The Electrum client can query the server for balance, historical transactions, and UTXOs very quickly. If you run your own Electrum server on top of a full node, you get Electrum’s query speed with full-node-level privacy.

Neutrino: True BIP 157/158

Neutrino is a Bitcoin light client implementation in Go developed by Lightning Labs. It fully implements BIP 157/158 (compact block filters). Neutrino is used as the backend for several Lightning Network mobile wallets like Phoenix Wallet and Breez. To pay a Lightning invoice, those wallets use Neutrino to verify the channel state on the Bitcoin blockchain without downloading the entire blockchain.

Ordinary "SPV" Mobile Wallets: Most Use a Server

Many mobile wallets that claim "SPV" actually connect to a backend server controlled by that wallet’s developer. They don’t download the header chain or do any PoW verification at all, but rather just query the developer’s server API to get balance and transactions. This isn’t SPV, it’s custodial-lite: you hold the private key but verification is done by someone else.

Choosing the right one

There’s no single right answer for everyone. For 99% of everyday users with small amounts, an ordinary mobile wallet is already safe enough. For users who care about privacy and verification, Electrum with your own server or Neutrino is a far better choice. For large values or business needs, a full node remains the best choice.

What matters most is understanding the trust model of the wallet you use. "Self-custody" doesn’t always mean "trustless," because many self-custody wallets quietly require trust in a server operator or developer. Choose deliberately based on the value you store and the level of trust you need.

Chapter 18 · 18.1
Behind every Bitcoin transaction you send, there’s a very strict binary conversation between thousands of computers
P2P Architecture & Wire Message Structure

Chapter 8 explained Bitcoin’s P2P network in terms of what happens. Chapter 18 covers the how: which bytes exactly move between nodes. If Chapter 8 was the map of the city, Chapter 18 is its road signs and traffic rules.

Imagine two people talking over a walkie-talkie with a military protocol. Every transmission must start with the station identification code, followed by the command code, then the message body, then the verification code. You can’t just talk freely; if the format is wrong, the transmission is ignored. The Bitcoin wire protocol works exactly like that, except it’s not the human voice being sent, but binary bytes that follow very strict rules.

If you open Wireshark and look at the traffic between two Bitcoin nodes, you won’t see HTTP, no JSON, no REST API. What you see is a raw byte stream, a binary format designed for maximum efficiency, not human readability.

A network without a central server

Bitcoin runs on top of a pure, unstructured peer-to-peer network. There’s no central server, no coordinator, no single point of failure. Every node is both a client and a server, it receives data from other peers while also serving data to other peers. This is different from how the ordinary internet works, where you are the client and Google, YouTube, or your bank is the server.

Every node maintains two kinds of connections. Outbound connections (8 regular + 2 block-only) are connections you initiate yourself, where you choose the peer. Inbound connections (roughly 115, since Bitcoin Core caps total connections at 125 and 10 of those are already used by outbound) are connections initiated by other peers that come to you, if port 8333 is open. Outbound connections are more trusted because you choose who to talk to, rather than passively accepting anyone who comes knocking.

How does a node find someone to talk to?

When first run, a Bitcoin node doesn’t know anyone yet. It uses DNS seeds, like a special phone book, to get a list of IPs of active nodes. There are several DNS seeds maintained by trusted contributors. After connecting to a few peers, the node exchanges lists of acquaintances via addr messages, like friends recommending new acquaintances to each other. This list is stored in peers.dat for use on restart.

Anatomy of one Bitcoin message

Every Bitcoin P2P message, whatever its contents, always has the exact same header structure. It’s like a standard envelope that always has a "sender," "recipient," and "contents" field in the same place, so whoever receives the envelope immediately knows how to read it.

The magic bytes (4 bytes) are the network identifier code. Like the area code in a phone number: 0xF9BEB4D9 means "this is a Bitcoin mainnet message." If the first byte a node receives differs from what it expects, the connection is closed immediately without reading the rest.

The command (12 bytes) is the command name in ASCII text. "version", "inv", "tx", "block", always padded with null bytes up to 12 characters. Like an email subject that always has exactly the same length.

The length (4 bytes) tells the recipient how many payload bytes are coming. This is important so the recipient knows when one message ends and the next begins in the continuously flowing byte stream.

The checksum (4 bytes) is the first 4 bytes of SHA256(SHA256(payload)). If the payload is corrupted in transit, the checksum won’t match and the message is ignored. Like a serial number on a banknote that can detect forgery.

Services Flags: A Node’s Capability Business Card

Inside the version message, every node advertises what it can do via services flags. It’s like a LinkedIn profile listing skills: NODE_NETWORK means "I have the full blockchain and can serve historical blocks," NODE_COMPACT_FILTERS means "I support BIP 157/158 for modern SPV clients," NODE_WITNESS means "I support SegWit." Peers read these flags to decide what can be requested from that node.

Bitcoin’s binary, minimal wire format is a deliberate design decision. There’s no overhead from a text format like HTTP or JSON, every byte has a specific meaning. This lets a node process thousands of messages per second with very little CPU overhead. Simplicity at the protocol level is what makes complexity at the network level possible.

Chapter 18 · 18.2
Before they can exchange data, two nodes must first complete a three-step ritual
Handshake & Message Flow — The Language Two Nodes Use When They First Meet

Imagine two diplomats from different countries meeting for the first time. There’s a protocol to follow before they can discuss important matters: a formal introduction, identity verification, confirmation that both speak the same language, and only then move on to substance. Bitcoin nodes work exactly like that.

Handshake: three steps before they can talk

When two nodes first connect, they don’t immediately exchange transactions or blocks. There’s a three-step ritual that has to be completed first. The node that initiates the connection sends a version message containing the software version, services flags, timestamp, user agent, and the highest known block height. The receiving node replies with its own version. Then both send a verack as confirmation. After both veracks are received, the handshake is complete and the official communication session begins.

The nonce in the version message has a special function: detecting a self-connection. If a node receives a version with the same nonce it sent, it means it accidentally connected to itself through a relay or a strange network configuration. The connection is closed immediately.

Transaction lifecycle: from wallet to network

When you send a Bitcoin transaction from your wallet, three P2P messages work in sequence. First, the node announces the txid via inv without sending the full data, like a "new product available" poster without forcing everyone to grab it. A peer that doesn’t have the transaction yet replies with getdata. Only then is the full transaction sent via tx. A peer that already has the transaction from another node doesn’t need to respond at all, so there’s no redundant data transfer.

Propagation spreads like ripples in water: one transaction can reach the entire network in seconds via this flooding process.

Block propagation: three generations of mechanisms

When a miner finds a new block, propagation must be as fast as possible. Every second of delay increases the risk of another block being found before this one spreads, causing a stale block that wastes the miner’s reward.

The old way uses the classic inv/getdata/block, where the full 1-2 MB block must be sent to every peer that requests it. A better way is headers-first: send the 80-byte header first so the peer can verify the proof-of-work before deciding whether it needs the full block. The best way is compact blocks (BIP 152), discussed in 18.4: send a sketch of the block that can be reconstructed from the mempool, so only a small fraction of the data needs to be transferred.

Other supporting messages

getheaders requests block headers from a peer to build a picture of the chain quickly without downloading full blocks. addr and addrv2 share lists of known peer IP addresses, continuing the peer discovery process that started from DNS seeds. feefilter lets a node tell a peer the minimum fee it accepts in its mempool, so transactions with too low a fee aren’t sent at all.

The inv/getdata design that separates announcement from data delivery is a very important efficiency decision. Without it, every new transaction would be sent in full to all peers redundantly. With inv/getdata, each piece of data is only sent to the peer that actually needs it, saving network bandwidth significantly.

Chapter 18 · 18.3
A new node can’t just trust data from one peer — it has to know which chain is correct before starting to download
Block Sync — From One Block to the Whole Blockchain

In Chapter 16 we discussed IBD from the node’s perspective: what gets verified and how long it takes. Here we look at it from a different angle: what P2P messages are actually sent during the sync process, and why there are two sync strategies with very different efficiency.

Strategy 1: Blocks-first sync, the abandoned way

The most naive way is to request blocks one by one from a single peer. The node sends getblocks with a block locator, the peer replies with an inv containing up to 500 of the next block hashes, then the node requests each block via getdata and waits for it to be validated before requesting the next. The problem: the entire sync depends on a single peer. If the peer is slow, everything is slow. The node also can’t tell whether it’s on the correct chain until it has already downloaded many blocks.

Strategy 2: Headers-first sync, the modern way since 2015

Headers-first solves this problem by separating two phases. First phase: download all headers via getheaders. The peer replies with up to 2,000 headers per response (each header 80 bytes plus 1 byte varint, about 162 KB per response). Within a few minutes, the node has all the headers from genesis to the tip, about 70 MB total. From this header chain, the node can compute the accumulated proof-of-work of each chain offered by various peers and know which is valid, even before downloading a single full block.

Second phase: download blocks in parallel from many different peers. Since the order is already known from the header chain, the node can request blocks from any peer without the risk of being tricked by a wrong order.

Block locator algorithm

The block locator is a clever, economical list of hashes. The node doesn’t send the hashes of all the blocks it has, but rather chooses them exponentially sparse: the 10 most recent blocks one by one, then every 2 blocks, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, and so on up to the genesis block. This lets a peer efficiently find the chain divergence point even with a very long reorg, using only about 40 hashes, even for a chain hundreds of thousands of blocks long.

Minimum chain work threshold

For extra security, modern nodes have a minimum chain work threshold: the minimum accumulated proof-of-work a chain must have before it’s considered worth following. This prevents a node from being tricked into following a fake, very short chain with very little PoW, even before the header chain is fully verified.

The shift from blocks-first to headers-first is one of the biggest improvements in Bitcoin Core’s history (version 0.10.0, 2015). By separating chain verification from data download, IBD became far faster, safer, and more resistant to misbehaving peers.

Chapter 18 · 18.4
Why download data you already have? Compact blocks solve the biggest inefficiency in block propagation
Compact Blocks — Speeding Up Block Propagation (BIP 152)

Imagine someone sends you a copy of a 200-page newspaper, when you already have 198 of its pages. A waste of time and paper, right? That’s what happened with block propagation before compact blocks: every node had to download the full block (~1-2 MB) even though it already knew almost all the transactions in it from its own mempool.

The problem being solved

A node well-connected to the network usually already has 95-99% of the transactions in a block before the block is found. This is because transactions are propagated across the network when first sent, long before they enter a block. Compact blocks (BIP 152, 2016) take advantage of this fact: instead of sending the whole block, send just a list of short transaction IDs and let the recipient reconstruct the rest from its local mempool.

The cmpctblock message format

The cmpctblock message contains three main components. The block header (80 bytes) the same as usual, containing the proof-of-work, merkle root, and timestamp. Shortids of 6 bytes for each transaction in the block (much smaller than the 32-byte txid), created with SipHash-2-4 using a unique nonce per block so they’re only valid for this block. Prefill transactions, a few transactions sent directly without a shortid, especially the coinbase transaction, which is guaranteed not to be in any mempool.

The recipient matches each shortid against a transaction in its mempool. Found transactions are used directly to reconstruct the block. If a shortid doesn’t match, the recipient sends getblocktxn with a list of the transaction indices it needs, and the sender replies with blocktxn containing only those transactions.

High-bandwidth vs low-bandwidth mode

These two modes are negotiated via the sendcmpct message during the handshake. High-bandwidth mode (sendcmpct(1)): the node sends the cmpctblock unsolicited as soon as a new block is found, suitable for a maximum of 3 peers with trusted, low-latency connections. Low-bandwidth mode (sendcmpct(0)): the node announces via inv or headers first, and only sends the cmpctblock if the peer requests it via getdata.

Real-world impact

Compact blocks reduce the data transferred from ~1,500 KB to ~20-60 KB under normal conditions. This is equivalent to a 95-98% reduction in bandwidth for block propagation. Block propagation latency drops drastically because less data has to be transferred and verified.

Compact blocks are an elegant example of the principle "don’t send data the recipient already has." By taking advantage of the fact that the mempools of well-connected nodes are almost always in sync, BIP 152 turns block propagation from a bandwidth-heavy operation into a near-real-time one.

Chapter 18 · 18.5
If compact blocks solve block propagation, Erlay solves transaction propagation — with a very elegant mathematical approach
Erlay — More Efficient Transaction Propagation (BIP 330)

Imagine you live in a village of 1,000 residents. There’s fresh news: "The village head got married again." The old way: everyone who knows immediately tells all their neighbors. The same news can be heard by one person from 10 different people before they get a chance to pass it on. A waste of conversation. Erlay is a smarter way: exchange a list of news periodically, and only tell what’s genuinely new.

The flooding problem we have now

Currently transaction propagation uses a flooding mechanism via inv/getdata/tx. Every new transaction is announced to all peers via inv. The result: each transaction is announced on average 8-16 times to each node, almost all of it redundant. On a network with 10,000+ nodes and hundreds of thousands of transactions per day, the bandwidth overhead from this redundancy is very significant and limits how many connections a node can maintain without large bandwidth.

Set reconciliation: Erlay’s core idea

Erlay (BIP 330) introduces a technique called set reconciliation. For a small subset of chosen peers, the node still uses flooding as usual (fanout) to ensure fast propagation. For the other peers, the node periodically exchanges a very compact sketch of its transaction set using a data structure called minisketch. From the two exchanged sketches, both can learn which transactions are held by only one side, without needing to send the full list.

Minisketch: clever mathematics

Minisketch is an implementation of PinSketch, a set reconciliation technique built on BCH codes. It lets two parties learn the difference between their sets by transferring only as much data as the difference, not as much as the total set. If node A and node B each have 10,000 transactions and differ by only 50 transactions, the sketch sent is only about 50 elements in size, not 10,000. It’s like a small "fingerprint" of the collection that’s enough to mathematically reveal the difference.

Long-term impact

Erlay reduces transaction propagation bandwidth by about 40%. More importantly: because each peer connection needs less bandwidth, a node can maintain more peer connections without proportional overhead. More connections means a more decentralized network that’s more resistant to eclipse attacks. Transaction propagation latency barely changes because fanout to several peers is still done.

Erlay is an example of how mathematical theory (error-correcting codes and set reconciliation) can be applied to solve a practical problem in a P2P network. The result isn’t just bandwidth savings, but an improvement in network decentralization, which is one of Bitcoin’s most valuable properties.

Set reconciliation lets two nodes learn the difference between their transaction collections by exchanging only a tiny amount of data — without sending the entire list.
Minisketch analogy
You and your friend each have 10,000 songs. You want to know which songs only one of you has, but you don’t want to send a list of 10,000 songs. From those two fingerprints, you know exactly: "you have songs X and Y that I don’t have" — without ever sending the full list.
How Erlay works step by step:
1
Fanout: announce directly to 2-3 chosen peers
As usual (inv/getdata/tx), a new transaction is sent directly to a small number of chosen peers to ensure fast propagation to the network.
Like telling 2-3 trusted friends first so the news spreads quickly.
2
Accumulate: collect the difference for ~2 seconds
For the other peers, the node accumulates new transactions it has but hasn’t sent. Every ~2 seconds, one reconciliation round is done.
Like noting down all the new news for 2 seconds before sharing the list with your neighbors.
3
Sketch: send a transaction-set "fingerprint" via minisketch
The node sends a compact sketch of its transaction set using minisketch (a PinSketch implementation). Its size is proportional to the number of differences, not the total set size.
Like exchanging fingerprints of a song collection — small but enough to know the difference.
4
Decode: find the difference from the two sketches via XOR
The recipient combines the received sketch with its own. The XOR operation reveals the difference set without needing to send larger data.
Two fingerprints combined produce a list of differences directly and mathematically.
5
Request: ask only for transactions that are genuinely missing
After knowing the difference, the node requests via getdata only the txids it doesn’t have. No redundancy.
Only after knowing which songs are missing do you ask for those specific songs.
Erlay’s impact on decentralization:
Because each peer connection needs less bandwidth with Erlay, a node can maintain more peer connections without proportional overhead. More connections means a more decentralized network that’s more resistant to eclipse attacks.
Implementation status (as of 2025):
Erlay has been merged into Bitcoin Core as an optional feature. Both peers must support BIP 330 to use set reconciliation. During the transition period, a node that supports Erlay can still operate normally with old nodes using ordinary flooding.
Chapter 18 · 18.6
You can verify transactions without your identity being known — but transaction propagation can expose your IP address before the transaction enters a block
Dandelion & Transaction Privacy (BIP 156)

We mentioned Dandelion in 8.3 as the most widely discussed answer to the privacy problem in propagation. Here we look at how it works, and also at why it still has not made it into Bitcoin Core.

Imagine you’re standing in the middle of a crowd and shout "I have this letter!" Everyone immediately knows you’re the sender. That’s what happens with Bitcoin transaction propagation today: the node that first spreads a transaction to the network is almost certainly the sending node.

How transaction propagation exposes the sender’s IP

When you create a transaction, your node is the first to spread it via flooding. An attacker running many nodes can observe from which node a transaction is first seen. The node that first broadcasts a transaction to many different peers is most likely the original source. This isn’t a theoretical attack, and blockchain analytics companies have long used this technique to link Bitcoin transactions to the sender’s IP address.

Dandelion: stem phase and fluff phase

Dandelion (BIP 156) solves this problem in an elegant way. Its name comes from the dandelion flower: a thin stem at first, then bursting out in all directions. In the stem phase, a new transaction isn’t immediately flooded to all peers. Instead, it’s forwarded to one peer at random, then that peer to one more peer, for several hops. During the stem phase, the transaction doesn’t enter the normal mempool, but is only forwarded silently. In the fluff phase, after a few hops, one node randomly decides to start spreading the transaction normally via flooding. The node that starts the fluff isn’t the original sender, so an attacker can’t determine the true source.

Dandelion++: A Refinement of the Original Version

The original BIP 156 has a weakness: if an attacker is on the stem path, they can trace it. Dandelion++ fixes this by choosing a different stem peer for each transaction from a stable, random subset of peers, so an attacker can’t predict or influence the stem path.

Implementation status

Dandelion++ hasn’t been merged into Bitcoin Core because of implementation complexity and concerns about potential new DoS attacks that could be exploited via the stem phase. Instead, Bitcoin Core uses a simpler technique: transactions are sent with a random delay to make timing analysis harder, though not as effective as Dandelion.

Privacy in Bitcoin isn’t just about hiding transaction amounts or on-chain identity, but also about hiding where a transaction originates at the P2P network level. Dandelion is one of the cleverest attempts to solve this problem without sacrificing transaction propagation speed.

Dandelion splits transaction propagation into two very different phases. The stem phase is hidden, the fluff phase is like ordinary flooding but from an unexpected point.
Why is it called Dandelion (the dandelion flower)?
A dandelion flower has a thin, long stem, then at its tip tiny seeds scatter in all directions when the wind blows (fluff). A Bitcoin transaction in Dandelion moves exactly like that: silent and linear at first, then bursting out across the entire network from one unexpected point.

Chapter 19 · 19.1
A miner is paid by two sources with very different characters — and the proportion will change drastically over time
Anatomy of Miner Revenue — Block Reward, Fee, and Coinbase Transaction

Before talking about mining economics, we first need to understand where a miner’s money actually comes from. The answer is simple but often misunderstood: a miner gets two sources of income with very different characters.

Block reward: bitcoin minted by the protocol

The block reward is new bitcoin created in each block according to a schedule fixed since the genesis block. This isn’t money taken from anyone, but genuinely newly minted by the protocol. Currently the block reward is 3.125 BTC per block. This amount is halved every 210,000 blocks (about 4 years) in a process called the halving.

Transaction fees: a fluctuating open market

The second source of income is transaction fees from all the transactions included in a block. A fee is the difference between the total input and total output of a transaction, and what "disappears" from the UTXO set automatically becomes the property of the miner who includes that transaction in a block. Unlike the block reward, which is fixed and predictable, fees are very fluctuating. Transaction senders compete to get into the next block by offering a fee high enough to attract a miner’s interest.

Coinbase transaction: the only way new bitcoin is created

The block reward is claimed by the miner through the coinbase transaction, the first transaction in every block that has no input from any UTXO. This is the only transaction that can create new bitcoin, and it’s valid under the consensus rules. The coinbase output can’t be spent for the next 100 blocks, known as the coinbase maturity rule, to protect the ecosystem from a situation where a block is orphaned after the miner has already spent the reward.

A proportion that changes over time

Currently the block reward dominates miner income, about 95-99% of total revenue. This will change with the next halvings. Eventually, according to the schedule fixed since the genesis block, the block reward will reach zero around the year 2140 and miners will depend entirely on fees. Whether fees alone are enough to secure the network is one of the most important open questions in Bitcoin economics.

Why this matters for network security

Miner revenue is what pays for hashrate. High hashrate means a 51% attack becomes very expensive. If miner revenue drops because the Bitcoin price falls or the block reward shrinks without a sufficient rise in fees, hashrate can drop and the network becomes more vulnerable. Understanding where a miner’s money comes from is the foundation for understanding Bitcoin’s economic security.

These two sources of miner revenue aren’t a coincidence, but a deliberate design. The block reward ensures miners have a strong incentive early on when transactions are still few. Fees ensure the incentive remains after the block reward runs out. The big question is whether the transition from block reward to fees as the main source can go smoothly without sacrificing network security.

Why is the coinbase output amount verified strictly?
Every full node verifies that the total output of the coinbase transaction doesn’t exceed the allowed block reward plus the total fees from all transactions in the block. If a miner tries to create more than allowed, the block is immediately rejected by the entire network. This is one of the most fundamental consensus rules — there’s no way to mint bitcoin beyond the schedule fixed since the genesis block.
Chapter 19 · 19.2
No matter how many or how few miners are active, Bitcoin always finds one block every 10 minutes — how does this happen?
Difficulty Adjustment — How Bitcoin Maintains 10 Minutes

We covered how difficulty adjustment works back in 5.4. There the question was technical: what the mechanism does. Here the question is economic: what it does to a miner’s money, and why this is the mechanism that keeps mining from ever truly dying out.

One of the most elegant mechanisms in Bitcoin is difficulty adjustment: a system that automatically adjusts how hard it is to find a new block, so that on average one block is found every 10 minutes, no matter how many or how few miners are active.

Why 10 minutes?

Ten minutes is a deliberate trade-off. Too fast means a new block is found before the previous block has had time to spread across the network, increasing the risk of accidental forks and giving an advantage to miners with the fastest connections. Too slow means the first confirmation of a transaction takes too long. Ten minutes gives enough time for block propagation across the network while still providing reasonably fast confirmation.

The difficulty adjustment mechanism

Every 2,016 blocks (about 2 weeks if the average stays at 10 minutes), the entire network automatically recalculates the difficulty target. The method: compute how long the last 2,016 blocks took, compare it with the target of 20,160 minutes (the ideal 2 weeks), then adjust proportionally.

If the last 2,016 blocks were completed in 7 days because hashrate rose, difficulty is raised so blocks again take 10 minutes on average. If they were completed in 28 days because hashrate fell, difficulty is lowered. There’s an important limit: difficulty can’t rise or fall more than 4x in a single adjustment, to prevent extreme changes that could destabilize the network.

The difficulty target as a number

The difficulty target is a 256-bit number that must be greater than the hash of a valid block. The smaller the target number, the harder it is to find a valid hash because the miner has to try more combinations before finding a hash small enough. There’s no central server computing the difficulty, because every node computes it itself from the same blockchain data and, because the process is deterministic, all nodes get an identical number.

Economic implications

Difficulty adjustment makes Bitcoin self-regulating on the production side. If the Bitcoin price rises and more miners join, difficulty rises and the cost per block rises too until profitability returns to equilibrium. If the price falls and miners leave, difficulty falls so mining becomes economical again for the remaining miners. This is also what makes Bitcoin’s emission schedule predictable: even if hashrate changes drastically, the halving still occurs every ~210,000 blocks because difficulty adjustment maintains 10 minutes per block.

Difficulty adjustment is one of Satoshi’s most important innovations that often doesn’t get enough attention. Without it, Bitcoin couldn’t function as a predictable system: the emission schedule could be chaotic, block propagation could be inconsistent, and the entire consensus mechanism could break. The simplicity of its formula hides how fundamental the role it plays is.

Calculation steps:
5-epoch simulation — stabilizing toward equilibrium:
Bitcoin’s difficulty adjustment formula is simple but powerful. There’s one important restriction: the change can’t be more than 4× in a single epoch.
// Difficulty Adjustment Formula
// Run every 2,016 blocks by every node independently

target_time = 2016 × 10 // 20,160 minutes = ~14 days
actual_time = timestamp[2016] - timestamp[0] // in minutes

ratio = actual_time / target_time

// Limit: the ratio can’t be more than 4× or less than 1/4×
ratio = max(0.25, min(4.0, ratio))

new_target = old_target × ratio
// Larger target = easier difficulty
// Smaller target = harder difficulty
Why does the 4× limit matter?
Without a limit, a very large hashrate surge could make difficulty rise too drastically in one epoch. The 4× limit ensures gradual stabilization — at most a few epochs to return to equilibrium even with a very extreme hashrate change.
Decentralized calculation
There’s no central server computing the difficulty. Every node computes it itself from the same blockchain data and, because it’s deterministic, all nodes get an identical number. A block with the wrong difficulty is rejected by all nodes.
Implementation detail: off-by-one
The timestamps compared are between the first and last block of each epoch, not the genesis block. The genesis block (#0) has a hardcoded timestamp so the first epoch causes no problem. This is an example of how real implementations often have details not present in the high-level description.
Chapter 19 · 19.3
Every 210,000 blocks, the block reward is cut in half — and this brings the most important open question in long-term Bitcoin economics
Halving & Security Budget — What Happens When the Block Reward Approaches Zero?

The halving is one of the most fundamental mechanisms in Bitcoin: every 210,000 blocks, the block reward is cut exactly in half. This isn’t a decision made by anyone, but happens automatically according to rules embedded in the protocol since the genesis block.

The halving schedule is already certain

First halving at block #210,000 (November 2012): the block reward dropped from 50 BTC to 25 BTC. Second halving at block #420,000 (July 2016): dropped to 12.5 BTC. Third halving at block #630,000 (May 2020): dropped to 6.25 BTC. Fourth halving at block #840,000 (April 2024): dropped to 3.125 BTC. The total bitcoin that can ever exist is 21 million, the result of summing a geometric series: 210,000 blocks × 50 BTC × (1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + ...) = 21 million BTC.

Security budget: the key concept

The security budget is the total miner revenue in a given time period. It’s an economic measure of how expensive an attack on the network is: the higher the security budget, the more hashrate miners can buy, and the more expensive it is for an attacker to gather enough hashrate for a 51% attack. The security budget consists of the block reward in BTC multiplied by the BTC price at the time, plus the total fees collected. Currently the block reward dominates about 95-99% of the total security budget.

The open question: are fees alone enough?

When the block reward approaches zero in the next century, miners will depend entirely on fees. Whether fees will be enough to maintain high hashrate is one of the most important and genuinely unanswered questions in Bitcoin economics. Some argue that as adoption grows, transaction volume and total fees per block will naturally increase. Others argue that the fee per transaction may not be high enough to replace the block reward, especially if layer-2 solutions take many transactions away from layer-1. No one can answer this with certainty today because it depends on many unpredictable variables.

What can be known now

The proportion of fees in the total security budget slowly rises with each halving, not because fees spike drastically, but because the block reward keeps shrinking. Whether this trend will continue at a sufficient pace is a question only time and future data can answer.

The block reward will approach zero around the year 2140, more than 100 years from now. Many aspects of the Bitcoin ecosystem in 2140 can’t be predicted from 2025. What’s certain: the halving mechanism is a consensus rule that can’t be changed without the agreement of the entire network, and the question of the long-term security budget will remain relevant with each subsequent halving.

Chapter 19 · 19.4
Solo mining is nearly impossible for a small miner today — pools exist to solve the variance problem, not to reduce total income
Mining Pool Economics — Why Do Miners Join a Pool?

Solo mining Bitcoin today is statistically almost impossible for a small miner. With network hashrate reaching hundreds of exahash per second, a miner with one modern ASIC producing 100 terahash per second has a probability of finding a block once every few hundred years. Mining pools solve this problem by combining the hashrate of many miners and splitting the reward proportionally.

How a mining pool works

The pool operator runs a full node and prepares the block template. Miners who join receive work from the pool: they’re asked to find a hash that meets a target far easier than the actual network target. A hash that meets this easier target is called a share, as proof that the miner is genuinely working. When one of the miners finds a hash that meets the actual network target, the pool gets the block reward and distributes it to all members based on how many shares each contributed.

Payment schemes: PPS, PPLNS, and FPPS

PPS (Pay Per Share) pays a miner for every valid share, regardless of whether the pool actually finds a block. The pool bears all the variance risk. More stable for the miner but the pool usually takes a higher fee. PPLNS (Pay Per Last N Shares) pays a miner based on the shares contributed within a certain window before a block is found. The miner shares the variance, the pool fee is lower, and it’s more profitable for consistent miners. FPPS (Full Pay Per Share) is like PPS but includes an estimate of transaction fees, not just the block reward.

Pool fee and its implications

The pool takes a small percentage of the total reward as an operational fee, usually 1-3%. The long-term total income between solo mining and pool mining is theoretically the same if the hashrate is the same, but a pool provides far more consistent and predictable income because of the far lower variance.

Implications for decentralization

Mining pools improve the efficiency and income stability of small miners, but the pool operator who manages the block template has influence over which transactions get included in a block. Miners who join a pool delegate this decision to the pool operator. The concentration of hashrate in large pools is something the community watches from the perspective of network decentralization.

A pool doesn’t increase miners’ total income in aggregate, the total reward from the network stays the same. What a pool does is redistribute the reward from an irregular pattern (solo) into a consistent, predictable stream. This is a trade-off between variance and a slight centralization at the block template level.

Chapter 19 · 19.5
Does a rational miner always follow the protocol? Selfish mining shows that under certain conditions, the answer is no
Selfish Mining & Miner Behavior — When Does a Rational Miner Deviate from the Protocol?

Bitcoin’s basic assumption is that a rational miner will always follow the protocol because that’s what’s most profitable. But is this always true? Selfish mining is a strategy that shows that under certain conditions, a miner can gain more by deviating from the honest mining protocol.

Honest mining vs selfish mining

Honest mining is the default strategy: when a miner finds a new block, they immediately propagate it to the entire network. All miners start working on top of the latest block simultaneously and the probability of getting a reward is proportional to each one’s hashrate. Selfish mining, first formally analyzed by Eyal and Sirer in 2013, is a strategy in which a miner with significant hashrate hides a newly found block instead of immediately propagating it. The miner keeps working secretly on top of this hidden block while the rest of the network is still working on the old block.

Why selfish mining can be profitable

If the selfish miner can find a second block before the network finds one block, they have a two-block lead. When the longer chain is finally published, all the work of the rest of the network is orphaned and the selfish miner gets more than their proportional share. Eyal and Sirer’s analysis shows that selfish mining can be profitable if a miner has more than about 33% of the network hashrate, depending on network connectivity.

Mitigation: fast propagation shifts the threshold

The faster a block spreads across the network, the smaller the window for a selfish miner to exploit their lead. Compact blocks and fast propagation technologies like FIBRE directly raise the hashrate threshold needed for selfish mining to be profitable. Besides that, unusual block patterns can be detected by nodes and researchers monitoring the network, and a large pool caught doing selfish mining can lose the trust of the miners who join it.

Fee sniping: another form of miner behavior

Fee sniping is another scenario: a miner with large hashrate can try to reorganize the last block to grab a very high transaction fee in that block. This is more relevant in the future when fees become the dominant component of miner revenue. Bitcoin Core has already implemented a default locktime to reduce the incentive for fee sniping by making transactions invalid in blocks before a certain height.

Selfish mining isn’t just academic theory, but a reminder that Bitcoin’s incentive design must keep being analyzed as network conditions change. The larger the proportion of fees in total revenue, the more important it is to understand how miner incentives can shift. What keeps Bitcoin healthy isn’t just cryptography, but the economic design that makes honest behavior the most rational strategy.

There are several mechanisms that naturally limit or prevent selfish mining — both technical and economic.
TECHNICAL SOLUTION #1 — FASTER PROPAGATION
Compact blocks & FIBRE narrow the selfish mining window
The faster a block spreads across the network, the smaller the window for a selfish miner to exploit their lead. Compact blocks and fast propagation technology directly raise the hashrate threshold needed.
Like gossip that spreads very fast — there’s no longer any advantage to withholding information because everyone already knows within seconds.
TECHNICAL SOLUTION #2 — ANOMALY PATTERN DETECTION
Nodes and researchers can detect unusual block patterns
Selfish mining leaves a statistical trail: a higher orphan rate, blocks arriving in bursts after quiet periods, and suspicious timestamp patterns. The community monitoring the network can identify suspected pools.
Like traffic police detecting a cheating racer from camera footage — the trail remains even if they aren’t caught directly.
ECONOMIC SOLUTION — REPUTATION AND SOCIAL INCENTIVES
A pool that gets caught loses miners and all its income
A large pool depends on the trust of the thousands of miners who join it. If caught doing selfish mining, miners can move to another pool. Losing hashrate is far more expensive than the short-term gain from selfish mining.
Like a business that cheats — it might profit once in a while, but losing customers is far more expensive than the gain from the cheating itself.
LIMITING FACTOR — HIGH VARIANCE
Selfish mining increases the variance of the miner’s own income
There are periods where the hidden block is orphaned by the network before it can be published. The selfish miner loses the reward in that period. High variance makes income more unpredictable even for the perpetrator.
Like a speculator vs a long-term investor — the former might profit big once in a while, but can also lose big.

Chapter 19 · 19.6
Bitcoin mining is a global industry that follows cheap energy, depends on highly specialized hardware, and operates through a protocol that determines who controls the contents of a block
The Mining Ecosystem — Hardware, Energy, and Protocol

Bitcoin mining in the real world is an industry very different from the simple picture of "computers guessing numbers." It involves specialized hardware designed for one purpose, highly economic energy decisions, geographic distribution that follows electricity prices, and a communication protocol that determines who has control over block content.

ASIC: hardware born from one purpose

An ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) is a chip designed specifically to run one operation: the SHA256 double hash as fast as possible with as little energy as possible. The key efficiency metric of an ASIC is joules per terahash (J/TH): how much energy is needed to produce one terahash. The first generation of Bitcoin ASICs around 2013 needed more than 1,000 J/TH. The best modern hardware today is already in the range of 15-20 J/TH, an efficiency improvement of more than 50-fold in a decade. Miners with old hardware are economically forced out when the Bitcoin price falls or difficulty rises, because the electricity cost exceeds the income.

Energy and geographic distribution

Bitcoin mining is a competition in energy efficiency. The miners who survive are those who can get the cheapest electricity: hydro plants with excess capacity, geothermal energy, flare gas from oil fields, or solar energy in remote areas. The global hashrate distribution changes significantly with regulation. After China banned mining in 2021, the hashrate that was once dominant in China migrated to the United States, Kazakhstan, Russia, and elsewhere within months. This shows that mining is very geographically mobile and the Bitcoin network is resistant to local regulation because hashrate can move to another jurisdiction.

The Stratum protocol: who controls the block template

Stratum is the communication protocol between the pool server and the mining hardware. In Stratum v1, still dominant today, the pool operator assembles the block template and decides which transactions are included. The miner only receives work in the form of a header to hash, without control over the block content. Stratum v2 introduces job negotiation: an individual miner can choose their own transactions and only ask the pool to validate their work. This significantly improves decentralization because control of the block template is no longer centralized in the pool operator.

These three aspects are interconnected: hardware efficiency determines where a miner can operate economically, geographic distribution determines the network’s resistance to regulation, and the communication protocol determines how decentralized the decisions about block content are. Understanding all three together gives a far more complete picture of how Bitcoin mining really works in the real world.

Stratum is the communication protocol between the pool and the hardware. Its version determines who has control over block content.

STRATUM V1 — DOMINANT TODAY
The pool controls the block template

The miner only receives work in the form of a header to hash

A contractor who only knows "dig a hole here" without knowing what for.

The miner can choose their own transactions
Job negotiation: the miner can assemble their own block template
The pool only validates that the hash work is correct
Communication is encrypted — safer from interception
Significantly improves decentralization of the block template
A contractor who can choose their own materials and design — the boss only checks the final quality.

Chapter 20 · 20.1
All of Bitcoin stands on mathematics that can’t be manipulated — the two structures that form its foundation are the hash function and elliptic curve cryptography
Foundations: Cryptography & Identity

Hash functions

A hash function takes input of any size and produces a fixed-size output that’s unpredictable and irreversible. Bitcoin uses SHA256 extensively: for mining (the double SHA256 of the block header), for addresses (SHA256 then RIPEMD160), and for the Merkle tree (the double SHA256 of each pair of hashes). The most important properties of a hash for Bitcoin are collision resistance (no two different inputs produce the same hash within a reasonable time) and the avalanche effect (one changed input bit produces a completely different hash).

Elliptic curve cryptography

Bitcoin uses the secp256k1 curve. A private key is a random 256-bit number. A public key is a point on the curve produced by multiplying the private key with the generator point G. This operation is one-way: from private key to public key is easy, the reverse is computationally impossible. A Bitcoin address is a hash of the public key, not the public key itself, adding an extra layer of protection.

ECDSA and Schnorr

ECDSA is the signature scheme Bitcoin has used from the start. It proves that the sender owns the private key matching the public key in the UTXO being spent, without revealing the private key itself. Schnorr signatures, activated together with Taproot in 2021, are more efficient and elegant: the signatures are linear so they can be aggregated. MuSig enables n-of-n multisig that looks identical to a single signature on chain, improving privacy and efficiency at the same time.

From key to address

A private key produces a public key via ECC. The public key is hashed to produce an address. Each address generation uses a different format: P2PKH (legacy, starts with 1), P2SH (starts with 3), P2WPKH (bech32, starts with bc1q), P2TR (bech32m, starts with bc1p). The format isn’t just aesthetics, but determines the Script that locks the UTXO and how that UTXO can be spent.

HD wallets and seed phrases

BIP32 defines a deterministic hierarchy: one seed produces the entire key tree deterministically. BIP39 defines the representation of the seed as 12 or 24 words. BIP44 defines the standard derivation path. The result: one seed phrase can recover the entire wallet in any wallet software that follows these standards.

Key numbers: a 256-bit private key with about 10^77 possibilities. SHA256 produces a 32-byte output, RIPEMD160 produces 20 bytes for legacy addresses. A Schnorr signature is only 64 bytes vs ECDSA’s 71-72 bytes. BIP39 seed phrase: 12 words equal 128-bit entropy, 24 words equal 256-bit entropy.

Chapter 20 · 20.2
The UTXO is the basic unit of Bitcoin ownership, and Script is the language that determines its spending conditions
Transactions & Script

UTXO and transactions

The UTXO (Unspent Transaction Output) is the basic unit of Bitcoin ownership. Every transaction consumes old UTXOs as inputs and creates new UTXOs as outputs. There’s no balance stored in one place, but rather the balance is the sum of all UTXOs that can be unlocked with the keys you own. Each UTXO is locked by a scriptPubKey and unlocked by the scriptSig or witness of the transaction that spends it.

Fee and timelock

The fee isn’t written explicitly: it’s the difference between total input and total output. The miner who includes the transaction in a block claims this difference. The fee rate is measured in satoshi per virtual byte because transactions differ in size. Timelocks enable transactions that can only be executed in the future. nLocktime works at the transaction level (absolute time), nSequence works at the input level (relative time). OP_CLTV and OP_CSV move these conditions into the Script itself so they apply to anyone trying to spend.

Bitcoin Script

Script is a stack-based language that determines the spending conditions of a UTXO. P2PKH asks for a signature and public key. P2SH hides the actual script behind a hash. P2WPKH moves the signature data to the witness field. P2TR enables key path spending that looks like an ordinary signature, or script path spending that reveals one of many hidden conditions via MAST. Tapscript runs inside the Taproot path with OP_CHECKSIGADD for more efficient multisig and OP_SUCCESS for future upgrades. Miniscript is a structured language on top of Script that enables automated analysis and safe script composition.

PSBT

PSBT (BIP 174) separates the role of transaction composer and signer, enabling safer multisig and hardware wallet workflows. The wallet software composes the transaction and exports it as a PSBT file. The hardware wallet reads, verifies, signs, and returns it. After all signatures are collected, the PSBT is finalized and broadcast.

Key numbers: 1 sat/vByte is the default minimum relay fee. SegWit gives a discount: witness data counts as 1/4 weight. P2PKH is about 148 vBytes per input, P2WPKH about 68 vBytes, P2TR key path about 57.5 vBytes (the most efficient). The OP_RETURN data limit is per-node relay policy, not a consensus rule (long-standing convention: 80 bytes).

Chapter 20 · 20.3
Proof of Work makes writing transaction history computationally expensive and cheap to verify
Consensus & Mining

Proof of Work

A miner repeatedly changes the nonce in the block header until the block hash meets the difficulty target. Because the hash can’t be predicted, there’s no shortcut. The entire network can verify that this work was done with just one hash operation, while the miner has to try billions of possibilities to find it.

Difficulty adjustment

Every 2,016 blocks, the network computes how long the last blocks took, compares it with the target of 20,160 minutes, then adjusts proportionally. The 4× per-epoch change limit prevents destabilization from extreme hashrate surges. Every node computes the adjustment independently and deterministically, with no coordination.

Halving and security budget

The halving happens every 210,000 blocks, the block reward shrinking by exactly half. This schedule produces a maximum total supply of 21 million BTC as a geometric series. The block reward is currently 3.125 BTC after the fourth halving in April 2024. The security budget is the total miner revenue, which determines how expensive an attack is. Open question: are fees alone enough when the block reward approaches zero around the year 2140?

Mining pools and selfish mining

A pool combines the hashrate of many miners to reduce income variance. PPS pays per valid share regardless of whether the pool finds a block. PPLNS pays based on shares in the last window, with the miner sharing the variance. FPPS is like PPS but includes an estimate of transaction fees. Selfish mining is a strategy of hiding a found block to gain a chain lead, profitable above a threshold of about 33% hashrate, limited by fast propagation, detection, and reputation risk.

Key numbers: target block time 10 minutes. A difficulty epoch is every 2,016 blocks, about 2 weeks. The maximum adjustment limit is 4× per epoch. Total supply 21,000,000 BTC. Halving every 210,000 blocks, about 4 years. Selfish mining threshold about 33% of network hashrate.

Chapter 20 · 20.4
The Bitcoin network is P2P with no central server — information flows through thousands of interconnected nodes
Network & Nodes

P2P and peer discovery

The Bitcoin network is P2P with no central server. Each node connects to a number of peers and forwards transactions and blocks to other peers. Peer discovery starts from hardcoded DNS seeds, then grows through addr and addrv2 messages. Default connections: 8 outbound, up to 125 total. The handshake between two nodes starts with the version and verack messages.

Efficient propagation

Compact blocks (BIP 152) reduce block propagation bandwidth by sending only transaction shortIDs, so a node that already has the transactions in its mempool doesn’t need to re-download. Erlay (BIP 330) uses set reconciliation for more efficient transaction propagation, reducing bandwidth by up to 40%. Dandelion (BIP 156) improves propagation privacy with a stem phase (a single path) before the fluff phase (normal broadcast).

Full nodes and sync

A full node downloads and verifies the entire blockchain from genesis. IBD uses headers-first: download all headers first, validate the chain of work, then download blocks. assumevalid skips script verification for old blocks already known to be valid. assumeUTXO lets a node sync from a verified UTXO set snapshot, without sacrificing the long-term security model.

SPV and light clients

SPV stores only block headers and verifies transactions via a Merkle proof. The bloom filter (BIP 37) is the old way that leaks privacy to the server. The compact block filter (BIP 157/158) is the modern solution: a per-block filter downloaded and checked locally without telling the server which transactions are being searched for.

Key numbers: block header 80 bytes. The entire header chain is currently about 70 MB. Outbound connections are usually 8 full-relay; modern implementations add dedicated block-relay connections. A BIP 158 compact block filter is typically tens of KB for a full modern block — still far lighter than downloading whole blocks. Erlay saves about 40% bandwidth vs ordinary flooding. Coinbase maturity 100 blocks before it can be spent.

Chapter 20 · 20.5
The Lightning Network enables instant off-chain payments, while privacy techniques make it harder to trace on-chain transactions
Layer 2 & Privacy

Lightning Network

The Lightning Network is a network of payment channels on top of Bitcoin. Two parties lock funds in an on-chain multisig (the funding transaction), then exchange off-chain commitment transactions that update the balance without broadcasting to the network. A channel can be closed cooperatively (immediately final) or unilaterally (requiring a wait for the CSV timelock to give the other party time to respond if there’s cheating).

HTLC and routing

An HTLC (Hash Time Locked Contract) enables multi-hop payments: each hop only forwards the payment if it can reveal the preimage of a particular hash, and if it isn’t claimed within a certain time the funds return. Routing in Lightning is source routing with onion encryption: the sender determines the entire path, each hop only knows its predecessor and successor.

On-chain privacy

Privacy in Bitcoin is hard because the blockchain is public and transparent. CoinJoin combines inputs from many users in one large transaction with equal-sized outputs, breaking the link between input and output without trust. Payjoin includes an input from the recipient so chain analysis can’t easily identify who the sender is and how much was sent. Silent Payments (BIP 352) enable a static address that produces a unique address for each payment without coordination, eliminating address reuse.

Key numbers: a Lightning channel is a 2-of-2 multisig on-chain. HTLC timeout is usually 40-144 blocks per hop. Onion routing has a maximum of 20 hops. CoinJoin outputs are all equal-sized for an effective anonymity set. Silent Payments: one static address produces infinite unique addresses per payer.

Chapter 20 · 20.6
Bitcoin has no CEO — protocol changes happen through a process involving many parties with a de facto veto at every layer
Governance & The Future

BIPs and the change process

A BIP (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal) is a formal document describing a proposed change. Anyone can submit a BIP, but no one can force it to be implemented. A change that doesn’t get broad support from users, developers, miners, and businesses won’t be successfully activated. This is a feature, not a bug.

Soft fork and hard fork

A soft fork is a change that tightens the consensus rules, where old nodes still accept new blocks as valid. A hard fork loosens the rules, so old nodes will reject new blocks and the network splits. Bitcoin has only ever successfully done soft forks since 2013. SegWit was activated in 2017 after a long process via UASF. Taproot was activated in 2021 with Speedy Trial, more smoothly because there was broad consensus from the start.

Open questions

Are fees alone enough for the long-term security budget when the block reward approaches zero? No one can answer this with certainty; it depends on adoption, price, transaction volume, and the structure of the ecosystem in the future. Active proposals under discussion: OP_CTV for simple covenants, OP_VAULT for safer self-custody, ANYPREVOUT for eltoo as a simpler Lightning alternative. None of these are activated yet.

What doesn’t change

Amid all the debate about the future, some things are already settled: the total supply of 21 million BTC can’t be changed without a hard fork that won’t get support. Proof of Work is the consensus mechanism that’s maintained. Network decentralization is a value guarded together. Changes must be backward-compatible or they won’t happen.

Key numbers: the first BIP is BIP 1 by Amir Taaki (2011). SegWit active at block #481,824 (August 2017). Taproot active at block #709,632 (November 2021). The block reward reaches zero around the year 2140 as a mathematical consequence of the halving schedule fixed since the genesis block.

Block #840,000 is Bitcoin’s 4th halving block. The block reward dropped from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC automatically according to the schedule embedded in the protocol since the genesis block. The block header is 80 bytes that summarize the entire block. This is what the miner hashes to prove proof of work. Click each field for an explanation.
Total header: 80 bytes (4 + 32 + 32 + 4 + 4 + 4). The double SHA256 of these 80 bytes is the block hash — this is what must meet the difficulty target.
The Merkle tree is a hash structure that connects all the txids to one Merkle root stored in the block header. Click each node for an explanation.

Merkle proof: to prove a single transaction is in a block, just provide the hashes along the path from leaf to root — the entire block isn’t needed. This is what SPV wallets use.

Press Mine to start searching for a valid nonce.
1
The miner changes the nonce in the block header (4 bytes, 0 to ~4 billion). Each nonce change produces a completely different hash.
2
The double SHA256 of the 80-byte header is computed. The result is 32 bytes (64 hex characters). It can’t be predicted; the only way is to try.
3
The hash is compared with the target. If the hash is smaller than the target (enough leading zeros), the block is valid and the miner gets the reward.
4
Real Bitcoin difficulty requires 19+ leading zeros, with a probability of 1 in 2^76. The entire network tries trillions of hashes per second to reach this every 10 minutes on average.
